title: Pets in Illinois Affordable Housing Trust Fund Units
bodyText:
If a multifamily rental unit of 500 square feet or more was acquired, built or rehabilitated with money from the Illinois Affordable Housing Trust Fund after January 1, 2022 and is designated as affordable housing for low- and very low-income families, the tenant must be allowed to keep at least 2 cats or one dog weighing under 50 pounds, whatever its breed or height, in the home, in line with other State laws.

The rule doesn't cover service animals (which have their own protections), a dog found dangerous or vicious under the Animal Control Act, supportive living facilities, or elderly housing (housing for people 62 or older, housing where at least 80% of units have someone 55 or older, or a qualifying government program for the elderly).

Your pet policy for these units may require compliance with noise and sanitation standards, registration of the pet with you, restraint in common areas, prompt waste removal, vaccination and sterilization, and enforcement of violations. You are not liable for injuries caused by a tenant's permitted household pet except for willful and wanton misconduct. Any pet deposit is part of the security deposit, and any non-optional pet fee or pet rent must appear on the lease's first page.

title: Rental Fee Transparency and Junk-Fee Ban
bodyText:
For residential leases entered into after the law's effective date (official records give January 1, 2027; the Act's own text says July 1, 2026), every non-optional fee, one-time or recurring, must appear explicitly on the first page of the lease, or the tenant is not liable for it. A listing must disclose non-optional fees clearly and conspicuously (or through an accompanying web link), and the lease or listing must say whether utilities are included in rent.

No landlord or lease may require:
- an application fee, including background checks, over $50 (a landlord may charge the actual cost of a third-party background check above $50 only if it paid the cost up front and bills the applicant with receipts within 14 days, or the fee is waived, and the fee can never be a basis for eviction in the first lease year)
- a fee at application that duplicates screening costs or covers costs unrelated to screening
- a fee for modifying or renewing a lease
- a fee for an eviction notice or for filing an eviction before the court grants an eviction order (court costs and filing fees remain recoverable)
- a fee for after-hours maintenance requests
- a fee for contacting the owner or manager about maintenance, the lease or the tenancy
- a maintenance travel fee
- a maintenance-hotline fee
- a fee for routine maintenance and upkeep
- a pest-abatement fee where the tenant in no way contributed to the infestation
- a fee for a move-in or move-out walk-through.

Renaming a fee does not avoid the law. Leases for units in owner-occupied premises of 6 units or fewer are exempt. Local governments may regulate fees, but only in a way at least as restrictive. A tenant may sue for injunctive and monetary relief, attorney's fees and costs.

title: Application Fees and Reusable Screening Reports
bodyText: Under the rental-fee law (for leases entered into after its effective date, January 1, 2027 in official records; the Act's own text says July 1, 2026), an application fee, including background checks, may not exceed $50, subject to the third-party background check exception described in the rental-fee law, and no additional fee at application may duplicate screening costs. If a prospective tenant offers a reusable tenant screening report that a consumer reporting agency prepared at the tenant's request and expense within the previous 30 days, that is available to the landlord at no cost, and that includes all the criteria the landlord consistently uses in screening (at least the applicant's name, contact information, verification of source of income, last known address and eviction history), the landlord may not charge a fee to access the report or an application screening fee. The landlord may require the applicant to state that there has been no material change in the report's information, and may still collect and process an application of its own as long as it charges no screening fee for it. A local rule that protects prospective tenants more controls.

title: Rent Payment Methods
bodyText:
For leases and agreements executed after January 1, 2024, a landlord may not require a tenant or applicant to pay any amount due under a residential lease, renewal or extension by electronic funds transfer, including automatic recurring transfers; beginning 90 days after that date, a violation is an unlawful practice under the Consumer Fraud and Deceptive Business Practices Act.

For leases executed after January 1, 2025, a landlord that collects rent through a third-party payment portal that charges a transaction fee must let the tenant pay by paper check or cash delivered to the landlord or its business office, or by another means that carries no fee.

A landlord of a building or complex of 100 or more units with an on-site business office that keeps regular hours must accept rent there during those hours without any penalty, fee or charge for paying that way (it may refuse cash), and a conflicting lease term is void.

title: Late Fees
bodyText:
Illinois has no statewide statute that caps residential late fees or requires a grace period; the lease sets the fee, subject to the general contract rule against penalties.

Because a late fee is a charge the tenant may have to pay, the library lists it in the first-page fee box that the rental-fee law requires for leases entered into after its effective date (January 1, 2027 in official records; the Act's own text says July 1, 2026). Some local ordinances, including Chicago's, limit late fees; they are not covered here.

title: Rent Control Preemption
bodyText: No Illinois unit of local government, including a home rule unit, may enact, maintain or enforce an ordinance or resolution that would have the effect of controlling the amount of rent charged for leasing private residential or commercial property. Local governments may still manage and control residential property in which they have a property interest.

title: Rent Increases
bodyText: No Illinois statute sets a notice period or a cap for residential rent increases. During a fixed term rent changes only as the lease provides; in a month-to-month tenancy the landlord can end the tenancy on 30 days' written notice and offer new terms. A rent increase made because a tenant complained, organized or used a legal right in good faith is retaliation. A landlord may not raise rent to recover utility payments a tenant lawfully deducted after the landlord failed to pay a landlord-paid utility.

title: Rent Receipts
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires a landlord, including a mobile home park owner, to give rent receipts. Some local ordinances, including Chicago's, require receipts for cash; they are not covered here.

title: Taxes on Rent
bodyText: Illinois' Hotel Operators' Occupation Tax does not reach rent from a permanent resident, defined as a person who occupies or has the right to occupy any room or rooms in a hotel for at least 30 consecutive days. No state tax on ordinary long-term residential rent was found. Short stays in rooms may be taxable; local hotel and rental taxes are not covered here.

title: Notice for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: Any time after rent is due, the landlord may serve a written demand for the rent stating that unless payment is made within a stated time, not less than 5 days after service, the lease will be terminated. If the tenant does not pay within that time, the landlord may treat the lease as ended and file an eviction without further notice or demand, and may join a claim for the rent due. Partial payments of the amount demanded do not invalidate the notice if the notice prominently states: "Only FULL PAYMENT of the rent demanded in this notice will waive the landlord's right to terminate the lease under this notice, unless the landlord agrees in writing to continue the lease in exchange for receiving partial payment." The landlord may agree in writing to continue the lease for a partial payment. Collecting past-due rent after the eviction is filed does not invalidate the suit. For a property with a federally backed mortgage or in a covered federal program, give a 30-day notice to vacate as well before filing (see the federal CARES Act row).

title: Interest on Unpaid Amounts
bodyText: Illinois' Interest Act lets a creditor receive interest at 5% a year on money due on a written instrument, such as a lease, from the time it becomes due, and on money withheld by an unreasonable and vexatious delay. The writer of a dishonored check is also liable for interest at the rate in the Interest Act.

title: Security Deposit Return Rules and Penalties
bodyText:
A landlord who keeps any part of a residential security deposit for damage must, within 30 days after the tenant vacates or the tenant's right of possession ends, whichever is later, give the tenant an itemized statement of the damage and the estimated or actual cost of each repair or replacement, with paid receipts (or copies), by personal delivery, postmarked mail to the last known address, or email to a verified email address the tenant provided. If costs are estimated, the paid receipts follow within 30 days after the statement.

The landlord may charge the reasonable cost of its own labor. Costs the written lease specifies for cleaning, repair or replacement may be withheld if they are for damage beyond normal wear and tear and reasonable; the statement must reference the amount and include a copy of that part of the lease. If receipts cannot be produced through no fault of the landlord, a verified statement with other evidence of cost may be used.

Without a proper statement and receipts, the whole deposit must be returned within 45 days of the tenant vacating. A landlord is not liable where the tenant gave no mailing or email address.

A court that finds the landlord refused to give the statement, or gave it in bad faith, and failed to return the deposit on time, awards twice the deposit due plus court costs and reasonable attorney's fees. A tenant does not forfeit a deposit solely because of an eviction for criminal activity or drug use, although the deposit may pay the sheriff's eviction fees in a criminal-activity eviction.

title: Interest on Security Deposits
bodyText:
A landlord of residential property with 25 or more units, in one building or a complex on contiguous parcels, must pay interest on any security deposit held more than 6 months.

The rate is the rate the largest commercial bank (by total assets) with its main banking premises in Illinois paid on minimum-deposit passbook savings accounts as of December 31 of the year before the rental agreement began, computed from the date of the deposit.

Within 30 days after the end of each 12-month rental period the landlord must pay accumulated interest of $5 or more, in cash or as a credit against rent, unless the tenant is in default; all unpaid interest is due when the tenancy ends.

A landlord who willfully fails or refuses to pay is liable for an amount equal to the deposit, plus court costs and attorney's fees. The Act does not apply to public housing. Some local ordinances, including Chicago's, have their own interest rules (not covered).

title: No Security Deposit Limit
bodyText: Illinois sets no statewide limit on the amount of a residential security deposit. The Human Rights Act bars increasing the customary deposit for a person with a disability, and a restoration escrow for a disability-related modification is limited to the reasonable cost of restoration. Local ordinances are not covered here.

title: Security Deposits When the Property Is Sold or Foreclosed
bodyText: When a landlord sells, leases, transfers or otherwise disposes of residential property (other than to a lienholder), the new owner becomes liable to the tenant for any security deposit, including statutory interest, and prepaid rent the tenant paid, and the former owner remains jointly and severally liable. When a deposit is actually transferred to the holder of a foreclosure certificate of sale or deed, or to the purchaser at a foreclosure sale, that holder or purchaser is liable for it and must, within 21 days after receiving the deposits and the tenants' names and addresses, post a written notice on the main entrance of each affected unit stating that it has acquired the deposit.

title: Unclaimed Security Deposits
bodyText: Under Illinois' Revised Uniform Unclaimed Property Act, a security deposit is 'property'. A deposit the landlord owes but cannot return (for example, because the tenant cannot be found or does not cash the refund) is presumed abandoned under the Act's catch-all period, the earlier of 3 years after the owner first has a right to demand it or the obligation to pay it arises, and the Act then gives the landlord, as holder, duties toward the State that are not covered here.

title: Repairs and Habitability
bodyText:
Illinois has no general statute that sets a residential landlord's repair or habitability duty; Illinois courts recognize an implied warranty of habitability in residential leases, and local building and housing codes apply.

Statutes add specific duties: working smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, heating and cooling standards in 55-and-older housing, paying landlord-paid utilities, rekeying between tenants in Cook County, a tenant's limited right to repair and deduct, and minimum living standards (including heat, cooling, pest control and keeping the premises fit for human habitation) for housing financed under the Illinois Affordable Housing Program.

It is also a crime (criminal housing management) for an owner or manager to recklessly let a residential property's physical condition or facilities become or remain in a condition that endangers anyone's health or safety, and the State's Attorney may obtain an order diverting rents into a court escrow for repairs. A landlord may not use a lease clause to excuse itself from liability for its own negligence in operating or maintaining the property.

title: Tenant Repair and Deduct
bodyText:
If a repair is required by the lease or by a law, rule or local ordinance and its reasonable cost is no more than the lesser of $500 or half a month's rent, the tenant may notify the landlord in writing, by registered or certified mail or other restricted delivery, at the landlord's or agent's address shown in the lease (or the last known address), of the tenant's intention to have the repair made at the landlord's expense.

If the landlord does not make the repair within 14 days after notice, or sooner in an emergency, the tenant may have it made in a workmanlike manner by a licensed and insured tradesperson and, after giving the landlord a paid bill from an unrelated tradesperson or supplier, deduct the cost (up to those limits and the customary price) from rent.

The right does not apply if the tenant, family or a guest caused the condition. The tenant is responsible for damage caused by its contractor.

The Act does not apply to public housing, condominiums, cooperative housing corporations, owner-occupied rental property of 6 or fewer units, or mobile homes. Home rule units may not diminish these rights.

title: Heating and Cooling in 55-and-Older Housing
bodyText: In residential rental property limited to people 55 or older, where a heating or cooling system serves the whole premises, the landlord must: run the cooling system from June 1 through September 30 whenever the heat index exceeds 80 degrees Fahrenheit; and, from October 1 through May 31, keep heat at no less than 68 degrees between 6 a.m. and 10 p.m. when the outside temperature falls below 55 degrees, and no less than 62 degrees between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m. If there is no premises-wide cooling system, the landlord must provide at least one cooled indoor common gathering space, free to all tenants, when the heat index exceeds 80 degrees (a property with no such space is exempt).

title: Rekeying Between Tenants (Cook County)
bodyText:
In counties of more than 3,000,000 people (Cook County), after a unit with a written lease is vacated and on or before the day a new tenant takes possession, the landlord must change or rekey the lock (replace the lock or cylinder, change a combination or electronic code, or otherwise change the means of access). A landlord who fails to do so is liable for damages from a theft attributable to the failure. The duty does not apply if the written lease gives the tenant the right to change or rekey the lock, to an owner-occupied building of 4 or fewer units, or to a room in an owner-occupied home.

Statewide, the owner of a rental building of 5 or more units whose construction began after the peephole statute took effect (enacted in 1967) must provide and maintain a peephole in each unit's entrance door; a tenant may sue to compel it, and each violation is a petty offense ($25 to $100 per unit, each day a separate offense). Hotels, motels, dormitories and similar buildings are excluded.

title: Landlord-Paid Utilities
bodyText:
Where an agreement requires the landlord to pay for water, gas or electric service, the landlord must pay on time so service continues through the lease. If the landlord does not pay, the tenant (or all tenants served by a common meter) may end the lease, or pay the utility if nonpayment jeopardizes service and deduct the payment from rent; the landlord may not raise rent to recover lawful deductions.

A utility must give tenants of buildings with 3 or more apartments notice before shutting off service for the landlord's nonpayment, and must restore service to a tenant who pays the past-due amount, or who puts the account in the tenant's own name, meets the utility's credit or deposit rules and agrees to pay future bills. Tenants who receive a utility's termination notice, or the utility, may also ask a court to appoint a receiver to collect rents and pay current utility bills. A tenant billed for service outside the unit because of the landlord's violation may recover it (trebled if knowing or intentional, plus attorney's fees if the utility award exceeds $3,000).

title: Tenant-Paid Utilities on a Shared Meter
bodyText:
A landlord may not rent a unit where the tenant pays the utility company directly for service that also serves common areas or other units, unless, before offering a lease or renewal, taking a deposit or otherwise agreeing to rent:
- the landlord gives a written statement of the areas and uses served by the tenant's meter (including foreseeable ones)
- gives copies of the unit's utility bills for the previous 12 months, unless the tenant waives them in writing
- does not ask the tenant to collect from neighbors
- states in writing any rent reduction offered for usage outside the unit.

A landlord may not switch from landlord-paid to tenant-paid utilities, or from master-metered to individually metered tenant-paid utilities, during a lease term; it must give at least 30 days' notice, and for tenants under a lease the notice must come at least 30 days before the lease expires, unless both sign a written amendment. Inconsistent lease terms are void.

title: Disability Modifications and Accommodations
bodyText:
A landlord must permit, at the expense of a person with a disability, reasonable modifications of the premises needed for full enjoyment of them, and must make reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices and services. Where reasonable, the landlord may condition a modification on the tenant agreeing to restore the interior at the end of the tenancy (reasonable wear and tear excepted), on a reasonable description of the work, and on assurances that it will be done in a workmanlike manner with required permits.

The landlord may not increase the customary security deposit for a person with a disability, but where necessary to ensure restoration funds it may negotiate payments into an interest-bearing escrow account, over a reasonable period, of a reasonable amount not exceeding the restoration cost, with the interest going to the tenant. Refusing to rent to, or discriminating against, a blind, hearing-impaired or physically disabled person because of a guide, hearing or support dog is also a civil rights violation.

title: Illinois Rules That Depend on Property Size or Type
bodyText: Several Illinois rules turn on the size or type of the property, not the landlord's whole portfolio: the rental-fee law exempts leases in owner-occupied premises of 6 units or fewer; the repair-and-deduct law exempts owner-occupied property of 6 or fewer units, condominiums, cooperatives and public housing; the Human Rights Act's housing exemptions cover an owner-occupied building of 4 or fewer units and rooms in an owner-occupied home (but never discriminatory advertising), and an owner-occupied building of 4 or fewer units may decide on sexual orientation (these exemptions reach only the general prohibitions in Section 3-102, not the disability provisions); the Cook County rekey duty exempts owner-occupied buildings of 4 or fewer units; the posted manager-and-insurer notice applies to buildings of more than 4 units with no resident or on-site owner or manager; deposit interest applies to properties of 25 or more units; the on-site rent-payment rule applies to 100 or more units with an on-site office; the Safe Homes Act excludes public housing except Housing Choice Vouchers; the radon disclosure excludes units on the third story or higher; and a pool, spa or bathing beach at an apartment or condominium building or association with 5 or more living units must be licensed under the Swimming Facility Act. Each rule is described in its own row.

title: Landlord Entry
bodyText: No Illinois statute sets a general notice period or other rules for a landlord's entry into a leased house or apartment; the lease governs, subject to the tenant's common-law right of possession. Specific statutes require the tenant to give access to correct smoke and carbon monoxide alarm deficiencies the tenant reported. Some local ordinances, including Chicago's, set entry notice rules; they are not covered here.

title: Ending a Tenancy: Notices by Tenancy Type
bodyText:
Illinois notice rules depend on the kind of tenancy.
- Fixed term: no notice is needed; the tenant must leave when the term ends.
- Year to year: 60 days' written notice ending at the end of the year, which may be given at any time in the 4 months before the last 60 days.
- Week to week, where the tenant holds over without special agreement: 7 days' written notice.
- Any other term of less than a year, including month to month: 30 days' written notice.
- Unpaid rent: a written demand giving at least 5 days to pay.
- Breach of any other lease term: a 10-day written notice to quit, which the statute does not require to offer a chance to cure and gives a suggested form for.
- Use of the premises for a felony or Class A misdemeanor, or drug activity: the landlord may void the lease and give 5 days' written notice to vacate.

After a foreclosure, a new owner may end a bona fide lease only at the end of its term, and a month-to-month or week-to-week lease, with at least 90 days' written notice, except on the ordinary grounds such as nonpayment, breach or criminal activity.

Demands and notices are served by delivering a copy to the tenant, leaving it with a person 13 or older residing on or in possession of the premises, certified or registered mail with a returned receipt, or, if no one is in actual possession, posting it on the premises.

Once a tenancy is ended by one of these notices, no further demand is needed before filing.

If your property has a federally backed mortgage or is in a covered federal housing program, federal law may require 30 days' written notice to vacate first (see the federal CARES Act row).

title: How Legal Notices Are Delivered
bodyText: Eviction demands and termination notices must be served by one of the methods in the Code of Civil Procedure: personal delivery; leaving a copy with a person 13 or older residing on or in possession of the premises; certified or registered mail with a returned receipt from the addressee; or, if no one is in actual possession, posting on the premises. The statute does not list email. The deposit statement may be emailed to a verified email address the tenant provided. Illinois' Uniform Electronic Transactions Act lists no exclusion for landlord-tenant notices; its other provisions, including when the parties must have agreed to deal electronically, are not covered here. The repair-and-deduct notice goes by registered or certified mail or other restricted delivery.

title: The Eviction Process
bodyText: An Illinois eviction is a court action under Article IX of the Code of Civil Procedure; the complaint states that the landlord is entitled to possession and the defendant unlawfully withholds it. Under Illinois Supreme Court Rule 139, the landlord must attach to the complaint the notice or demand the case rests on, with proof of service, and, for a case based on breach of a written lease under the 10-day notice statute, a copy of the lease or its relevant portions (or, if unavailable, an affidavit on the Supreme Court's standardized form). Under Rule 99.2 (effective March 1, 2026), circuits may run residential eviction mediation or diversion programs, which must give litigants reasonable time to reach counsel and mediation before a default or eviction judgment. A claim for rent may be joined; unrelated claims may not. Either party may demand a jury despite any lease waiver. An eviction order may not be enforced more than 120 days after it is entered unless the court extends it on the landlord's motion, which must include a statutory notice to the tenant. Tenants may raise defenses including domestic or sexual violence, immigration status, retaliation and servicemember protections, described in their own rows.

title: Minors May Not Be Named in an Eviction
bodyText: An eviction complaint may not name a minor (a person under 18 who has not been emancipated) as a defendant. A complaint that names a minor must be dismissed in its entirety against all defendants and immediately sealed, although the landlord may refile against defendants who can properly be named (the court may not waive the refiling fees). A minor willfully and wantonly named may recover reasonable attorney's fees, actual damages and $1,000 in liquidated damages.

title: Sealing of Eviction Court Files
bodyText: A court may seal an eviction court file if it finds the landlord's case sufficiently without basis in fact or law (including lack of jurisdiction) that sealing is clearly in the interests of justice and not outweighed by the public's interest in the record. Sealing is mandatory for eviction cases against a tenant after a foreclosure under the 90-day foreclosure-tenant statute or the foreclosure-possession provision, and for cases dismissed because a minor was named as a defendant.

title: Criminal Activity: Voiding the Lease and Expedited Eviction
bodyText:
If a tenant or occupant uses or permits use of the premises for a felony or Class A misdemeanor, the lease becomes void at the landlord's option; if the tenant does not leave within 5 days after written notice to vacate, the landlord may file an eviction (or, with consent, assign the right to file to the State's Attorney or corporation counsel), and a resulting eviction order may be stayed no more than 7 days unless all parties agree.

A separate emergency procedure lets a landlord of privately owned or housing-authority property seek possession on a verified complaint alleging direct evidence of drug activity, an unlawful firearm, or listed violent or sex crimes on the premises with the knowledge or consent of those named: no predicate notice is required, the hearing is held after 14 days' notice, and continuances and stays are limited to 7 days.

Where the landlord and tenant signed HUD's drug-free housing addendum or a similar document, a Class X felony charge on the premises followed by a probable-cause finding or indictment lets the landlord void the lease on 5 days' posted notice.

A tenant does not forfeit the security deposit solely because of these evictions (in a criminal-activity eviction it may pay the sheriff's fees). If your property has a federally backed mortgage or is in a covered federal housing program, federal law may require 30 days' written notice to vacate first (see the federal CARES Act row).

title: Drug Use on the Premises
bodyText: If a tenant or occupant uses the leased premises, or permits them to be used, for unlawfully possessing, storing, making, growing, delivering, using, selling or giving away controlled substances, the lease becomes void at the landlord's option. The landlord may post a written notice (on circuit clerk forms) requiring the occupants to vacate within 5 days, then file an eviction or assign the right to file to the State's Attorney. If a controlled substance is found or used anywhere in an apartment, there is a rebuttable presumption that a tenant or occupant used or possessed it or permitted its use. The tenant does not forfeit the security deposit solely because of this eviction.

title: No Self-Help Evictions or Utility Shutoffs
bodyText: Illinois law prohibits entering land or buildings except where the law allows entry, and then only peaceably, not by force. A landlord recovers possession through the court eviction process. A landlord may not cause or request utility service to tenants in an occupied building to be interrupted, discontinued or terminated, whether by not paying utility bills it is responsible for or by tampering with equipment or lines, except temporary shutoffs for emergencies such as gas leaks or fire, or, on 7 days' written notice to each affected tenant, for building repairs or rehabilitation. A tenant whose service is cut off in violation recovers a full rent abatement for the period plus consequential damages, and where the landlord acted deliberately, recklessly or in bad faith, statutory damages up to $300 per tenant (or $5,000 divided among affected tenants, if less).

title: Tenant's Property After an Eviction
bodyText:
No Illinois statute sets what a landlord must do with a residential tenant's belongings after an eviction order is carried out or after the tenant leaves; the sheriff enforces eviction orders and courts may direct the handling of property. The library's property-left-behind clause gives a contract procedure for property left after the tenant moves out. The landlord's statutory right of distress for rent is a separate court-supervised process.

Illinois sets no period for the tenant to collect belongings left after moving out; giving at least 10 days after a written notice is the cautious choice.

title: Duty to Mitigate When a Tenant Leaves Early
bodyText: When a tenant defaults, including by leaving before the lease ends, the landlord must take reasonable measures to mitigate the damages it can recover from the tenant, such as trying to re-rent. No Illinois statute defines when a house or apartment is abandoned.

title: Holding Over After the Lease Ends
bodyText:
A tenant who willfully holds over after the term ends and after the landlord's written demand for possession owes the landlord, for the time the landlord is kept out, double the yearly value of the premises, recoverable in a civil action. A tenant who gives notice of intent to leave on a date when the lease allows it, and then does not leave, owes double the rent that would otherwise be due. The landlord may instead accept rent and continue the tenancy.

These double amounts apply only in those two cases. No statute sets an amount for any other holdover, such as a tenant who stays on before any written demand for possession or without acting willfully; the landlord then recovers its actual damages, such as the reasonable rental value, unless the lease sets a measure. The library offers an optional daily holdover charge for those cases; it does not apply after a termination for nonpayment of rent, and it cannot be collected for the same days as either double amount.

title: Distress for Rent (Landlord's Statutory Seizure Remedy)
bodyText: Illinois still allows distress for rent: a landlord may seize a tenant's personal property found in the county where the tenant lives for rent due, but only the tenant's own property, and must immediately file the distress warrant and an inventory with the circuit clerk, after which a court case follows. The right continues for 6 months after the term ends. Property exempt from judgment enforcement is exempt from distress (except crops on the leased premises). Landlords also have a statutory lien on crops grown on leased land. The procedure is technical and court-supervised; a lease clause is not needed to use it.

title: Tenants in Foreclosure and Receivership
bodyText: After a foreclosure, the mortgagee, receiver, certificate or deed holder, or foreclosure-sale purchaser who takes control may end a bona fide lease only at the end of its term, and a month-to-month or week-to-week lease, with at least 90 days' written notice; an individual who buys at the judicial sale and will live in the unit as a primary residence may end the lease on at least 90 days' written notice. The successor keeps the ordinary grounds to end a tenancy, including nonpayment, breach of the lease, holding over and criminal activity. Eviction files against tenants under this rule are sealed. A holder or purchaser who receives tenants' security deposits is liable for them and must post a notice on each unit within 21 days. A court-appointed receiver may not reject an unexpired lease where the tenant occupies the premises as the tenant's primary residence. A foreclosure buyer, mortgagee in possession or receiver who doesn't give occupants the required written notice may not collect rent from a known occupant, or end the tenancy for not paying it, until the notice is served, and an occupant who already paid the current period's rent to the owner or manager isn't liable for it again. A receiver must accept rent from occupants and payments from a third party or a rental assistance program toward an occupant's housing.

title: Unauthorized Occupants and Squatters
bodyText: Nothing in Illinois' eviction Article prevents law enforcement from enforcing criminal trespass, or from removing persons or property from premises when there is a criminal trespass. Whether a person is a trespasser or an occupant who must be evicted through the courts depends on the facts; a landlord should not remove someone who may be a tenant without a court order.

title: No Statewide Just-Cause Requirement
bodyText: Illinois has no statewide law requiring a landlord to have good cause to end or not renew a residential tenancy. One exception: multi-family housing assisted by the Illinois Affordable Housing Trust Fund may not evict tenants without good cause. A fixed-term lease ends when the term expires, and a periodic tenancy can be ended with the statutory notice, as long as the landlord's reason is not retaliatory, discriminatory, based on domestic or sexual violence or immigration status, or otherwise unlawful. Some local ordinances may add protections (not covered).

title: When a Tenant Dies
bodyText: Illinois has no statute that ends a residential lease when a tenant dies or gives an estate a special right to terminate; the lease continues against the estate under general law, and the landlord's duty to mitigate applies. A tenant's belongings are handled under Illinois estate law.

title: Retaliation Is Prohibited
bodyText: A landlord may not knowingly end a tenancy, raise rent, decrease services, sue or threaten to sue for possession, or refuse to renew because the tenant in good faith: complained of code violations to a government agency, elected representative or official; complained of code violations or illegal landlord practices to a community organization, or sought its help; asked the landlord for repairs required by a code, ordinance, regulation or the lease; organized or joined a tenants' union or similar group; testified about the premises' condition; or exercised any right or remedy provided by law. A retaliating landlord faces the tenant's defense to its action and a civil action in which the tenant may end the lease and recover the deposit, interest and prepaid rent, recover possession, and recover the greater of 2 months' rent or twice the damages, plus attorney's fees. Evidence of protected activity within one year before the landlord's action creates a rebuttable presumption of retaliation, unless the activity began after the landlord's action. The landlord's action is not retaliatory if it had a legitimate non-retaliatory basis or began before the protected activity.

title: Safe Homes Act: Leaving Because of Domestic or Sexual Violence
bodyText: A tenant who leaves the premises is not liable for rent for the period after leaving if a court finds either that, when the tenant left, the tenant or a household member was under a credible imminent threat of domestic or sexual violence at the premises and the tenant gave written notice of that reason before or within 3 days after leaving; or that the tenant or a household member was a victim of sexual violence on premises the landlord owns or controls, the tenant left as a result, and the tenant gave written notice before or within 3 days after leaving, stating the reason and the date and providing medical, court or police evidence or a statement from a victim services or rape crisis organization, with the violence having occurred within 60 days before the notice (or as soon as practicable if the tenant could not reasonably give notice sooner). Rent owed before the tenant left remains owed. The Act's rights cannot be waived or modified in any lease or separate agreement. It does not apply to public housing, except the Housing Choice Voucher program. In an eviction, it is also a defense that the landlord's demand for possession is based solely on the tenant's or a household member's status as a victim, or on an incident of violence against them, with supporting evidence; the landlord may still seek possession against the perpetrator.

title: Safe Homes Act: Lock Changes
bodyText: All tenants on a written lease may give the landlord written notice asking for a lock change if one of them reasonably believes a tenant or household member is under a credible imminent threat of domestic or sexual violence at the premises. If the threat comes from someone not on the lease, the notice must include medical, court or police evidence or a statement from a victim services, domestic violence or rape crisis organization; if it comes from a person on the lease, it must include a plenary order of protection or plenary civil no contact order granting the tenant exclusive possession (and that person's signature is not needed). Within 48 hours after receiving the notice and evidence, the landlord must change the locks or give permission to change them, and must make a good-faith effort to give the tenant a key within 48 hours. The landlord may charge a fee no more than the reasonable price customarily charged for changing a lock. If the landlord does not act within 48 hours, the tenant may change the locks in a workmanlike manner with locks of similar or better quality and must try to give the landlord a key within 48 hours. The landlord is not liable to third parties who cannot enter because of the change. The tenant may get an injunction if the landlord interferes.

title: Safe Homes Act: Confidentiality
bodyText: A landlord may not disclose to a prospective landlord that a tenant or household member exercised rights under the Safe Homes Act, or any information the tenant provided in doing so, unless the disclosure is required by law, occurs in a civil proceeding under the Act, or the victim (or the victim's parent or guardian) consents in writing. Giving the landlord evidence of violence does not waive any confidentiality or privilege the victim has with a third party. A landlord who discloses in violation is liable for actual damages up to $2,000, and a successful tenant may be awarded attorney's fees and costs.

title: Calling Police or Emergency Services
bodyText: No Illinois municipality or county may enact or enforce an ordinance or regulation that penalizes tenants or landlords (through fines, license action, subsidy termination, or termination or nonrenewal of a lease) because of a contact to police or emergency services made to prevent or respond to domestic or sexual violence, or made by or about a person with a disability for a disability-related purpose, or because of domestic or sexual violence, or related criminal activity, against a tenant, household member or guest. In an eviction, it is a defense that the demand for possession is based solely on a tenant's or household member's status as a victim of domestic violence, sexual violence, dating violence or stalking, or on an incident of such violence. A landlord may bar a person who is not a tenant or household member by a written notice to the tenant that says the person is no longer allowed on the premises and that inviting the person onto the premises may be treated as a breach of the lease, whether or not the lease says so; it is a defense to an eviction on that ground if the tenant or household member who was a victim of domestic violence, sexual violence, stalking or dating violence did not knowingly consent to the entry, or a valid court order permitted it.

title: Immigration Status
bodyText: Unless required by law or court order, a landlord may not threaten to disclose, or disclose, information about a tenant's immigration or citizenship status to anyone, including immigration or law enforcement agencies, to harass or intimidate the tenant, retaliate for the exercise of rights, or influence the tenant to leave, and may not bring an action for possession based solely or in part on the tenant's immigration or citizenship status. A tenant may recover actual damages, a civil penalty of up to $2,000 for each violation, attorney's fees and costs. A waiver of these rights is void. It is also a defense to an eviction that the demand for possession is based solely or in part on the tenant's immigration status, or, after the lease has begun and the tenant has taken possession, on the tenant's failure to provide a Social Security number, credit-report information or a form of identification the landlord accepts. Landlords may still comply with legal obligations (including rental-assistance programs and court orders), verify a prospective tenant's financial qualifications, give notices about lease violations, and collect rent. Immigration status is also a protected class under the Human Rights Act; inquiry or use is allowed only in compliance with State or federal law.

title: Servicemember Rights
bodyText: An Illinois resident servicemember (any component of the U.S. Armed Forces or any state's National Guard) who enters military service of more than 29 consecutive days after signing a lease, or who while in service receives orders for a permanent change of station or to deploy for at least 90 days, may terminate a residential lease, as may a family member living with the servicemember, by giving the landlord copies of the orders. Termination takes effect 30 days after notice, or, if rent is paid monthly, 30 days after the next rent due date after the notice; the landlord must refund unearned prepaid rent and the security deposit, less actual damages the lease allows it to deduct. A landlord's refusal to accept a proper termination is a civil rights violation. In a residential eviction, if military service materially affects a servicemember tenant's ability to pay, the court may, and on the tenant's motion must, stay the case for 90 days or adjust the rental obligation. A second Illinois statute, the Service Member Residential Property Act, also lets a service member who enters military service of 180 days or more, or receives orders for a permanent change of station or a deployment of at least 90 days, end a residential lease by written notice with a copy of the orders (and lets the immediate family end it if the service member is killed on active duty); the tenant then owes rent only to the termination date and no other rent or liquidated damages, though still liable for damage the tenant caused, advance rent must be refunded within 30 days, and a tenant may sue to enforce the Act and recover attorney's fees. Federal law (the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act) gives additional protections.

title: Illinois Human Rights Act: Housing
bodyText: The Illinois Human Rights Act makes it a civil rights violation, in renting, to refuse to rent, alter terms, refuse offers or negotiation, misrepresent availability, publish or use an application, notice, advertisement, record or inquiry indicating a preference, or use criteria or methods with a discriminatory effect not necessary to a substantial, legitimate, nondiscriminatory interest, because of actual or perceived race, color, religion, national origin, ancestry, age, sex, marital status, order of protection status, disability, military status, sexual orientation (which includes gender-related identity), pregnancy, reproductive health decisions or unfavorable military discharge, or because of familial status, immigration status, source of income or arrest record. Exemptions include rental in a building of 4 or fewer units where the owner lives in one, rental of rooms in a private home where the owner or family lives, reasonable occupancy limits, religious organizations, single-sex rooms, conduct toward persons convicted of illegal manufacture or distribution of controlled substances, housing for older persons (familial status only), an owner-occupied building of 4 or fewer units deciding on sexual orientation, and inquiry into arrest records or immigration status authorized by or in compliance with State or federal law. The owner-occupied and private-room exemptions never permit discriminatory advertising or inquiries. These exemptions apply only to the general prohibitions in Section 3-102; they do not excuse disability discrimination, refusals of reasonable modifications or accommodations, or discrimination over guide, hearing or support dogs. Separately, the Illinois Constitution gives all persons the right to be free from discrimination on the basis of race, color, creed, national ancestry and sex in the rental of property, enforceable without any statute (the General Assembly may set reasonable exemptions and add remedies), and says that persons with a physical or mental handicap shall be free from discrimination in the rental of property. How courts apply these sections to private landlords alongside the Human Rights Act and its exemptions is case law not reviewed here.

title: Source of Income
bodyText: Source of income, defined as the lawful manner by which a person supports themselves and their dependents, is a protected class in Illinois housing; it is generally read to include housing vouchers and other lawful assistance. A landlord may not refuse to rent, set different terms, advertise a preference, or use screening criteria with a discriminatory effect because of it. The Human Rights Act's owner-occupied (4 or fewer units) and private-room exemptions apply, but not to advertising.

title: Applications and Inquiries
bodyText: It is a civil rights violation to use a rental application form, or to make a record or inquiry in connection with a prospective rental, that indicates any preference, limitation or discrimination based on a protected class under the Illinois Human Rights Act, including familial status, immigration status, source of income and arrest record, or an intention to make one. This applies even to landlords otherwise exempt as owner-occupants of small buildings or renters of rooms. Inquiry into arrest records or immigration status is allowed only where State or federal law authorizes it or it complies with that law.

title: Assistance Animals
bodyText:
A housing provider asked to make an exception to a pet policy for an assistance animal may require reliable documentation of the disability and disability-related need only if they are not readily apparent or known. Documentation must be in writing, from a person with whom the requester has a therapeutic relationship, and describe the disability-related need; the provider may offer a form but may not deny a request for not using it.

The provider may deny or rescind the accommodation for undue financial and administrative burden, fundamental alteration, or, after an individualized assessment with reliable objective evidence, if the specific animal poses a direct threat to others' health or safety, or causes substantial physical damage to others' property, that another reasonable accommodation cannot reduce or eliminate, or has shown a pattern of uncontrolled behavior the handler has not effectively corrected.

The resident pays for damage the animal causes beyond reasonable wear and tear, as for any other resident, but may not be charged a pet deposit or pet fee or required to carry special insurance. The housing provider is not liable for injuries caused by an assistance animal permitted as a reasonable accommodation. A guide, hearing or support dog may not be refused or subjected to different terms.

title: Misrepresenting an Assistance Animal
bodyText: No Illinois statute penalizes a person for misrepresenting an animal as an assistance or service animal in order to obtain housing. The Criminal Code's service-animal access section covers public places of accommodation, not rental housing. A housing provider may rely on the Assistance Animal Integrity Act's documentation rules.

title: Radon: Tenant Testing and Termination Rights
bodyText:
For leases entered into on or after January 1, 2024, of units below the third story, a tenant has 90 days from the start of the lease to conduct a radon test and must give the landlord copies of the results within 10 days. If the result exceeds the Illinois Emergency Management Agency's Radon Action Level and the landlord chooses not to mitigate, the tenant may terminate the lease; the landlord may hire a radon contractor to retest within 30 days of learning the results, and a contractor's result may disprove the hazard (results are valid 2 years unless the building is renovated).

If the landlord never provided the pamphlet, records and disclosure form, the tenant may test at any time during the lease and, if a hazard is shown and the landlord does not dispute it or mitigate, may within 60 days either have a radon contractor mitigate with the landlord's express consent or terminate the lease.

Mitigation must be done by a licensed radon contractor; a tenant who mitigates with the landlord's express consent may deduct the cost from rent in equal parts over the rest of the lease. A landlord may not withhold the deposit for radon testing or mitigation after a tenant terminates for lack of the disclosure, except for an improper installation the tenant made without consent. Neither side is required to test or mitigate.

title: Illinois Lead Rules for Rentals
bodyText:
In addition to the federal lead disclosure, before entering into a residential lease an owner of a residential building with units built before 1978 must give the prospective tenant the Illinois Department of Public Health's lead information brochure.

An owner who has received a lead mitigation notice for a unit must, before renewing that unit's lease, give the current tenants a copy of the mitigation notice and inspection report (unless a certificate of compliance has been obtained), and must mitigate the hazard and obtain a certificate of compliance before entering into a new lease of that unit; a buyer of such a unit who received notice of the mitigation order has the same duty. An owner who receives a mitigation notice must also post the Department's notices at every building entrance until the hazard is mitigated.

If you violate the Act, the State's Attorney may charge you with a Class A misdemeanor and must take measures so that tenants of the affected units withhold rent from you until the mitigation is done; no tenant may be evicted because rent is withheld under the Act. The Department's rules add a written notice to each new tenant after a hazard was found.

title: Mold
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires a residential landlord to disclose or remediate mold. The Mold Remediation Registration Act addresses registration of mold remediation businesses, not landlords. Local codes and the common-law warranty of habitability may apply.

title: Bed Bugs
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires a residential landlord to disclose bed bugs or sets treatment duties. For leases it covers, the rental-fee law bars charging a tenant a pest-abatement fee where the tenant in no way contributed to the infestation. Chicago has its own bed bug ordinance (not covered).

title: Methamphetamine Contamination
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires a residential landlord to disclose prior methamphetamine manufacture or contamination to a tenant. Drug activity on the premises lets the landlord void the lease. If your lease gives the tenant an option to buy a property of 1 to 4 units, or a condominium or cooperative unit, the Residential Real Property Disclosure Act's seller report applies, and it asks whether you are aware the property was used to manufacture methamphetamine.

title: Renting a Condominium Unit
bodyText:
When a condominium unit is leased, the Condominium Property Act, the declaration, bylaws, other condominium instruments and rules that relate to the use of the unit or the common elements apply to the tenant and are deemed incorporated in every lease executed or renewed on or after August 30, 1984.

The unit owner must deliver a copy of the signed lease (or a memorandum of an oral lease) to the association board by the date of occupancy or 10 days after signing, whichever is first. Units in a common interest community are treated the same way under the Common Interest Community Association Act.

If you do not follow the leasing rules, a condominium association may sue you and your tenant together to keep the tenant out or evict the tenant, the board may sue a tenant directly for breaking the association's rules, and a condominium board may evict your tenant if you fall behind on assessments.

title: Converting a Rental Building to Condominiums
bodyText: Before a building is submitted to the Condominium Property Act as a conversion condominium, every tenant must receive a notice of intent at least 30 days and not more than a year before the declaration is recorded, together with a schedule of selling prices and an offer to sell the tenant's unit, open at least 30 days (except units to be vacated for rehabilitation). Tenants whose leases would expire within 120 days after the notice may extend on the same terms until the 120 days end by written notice within 30 days. The developer must tell each tenant whether the tenancy will be renewed and on what terms. For 120 days the tenant has a right of first refusal to buy the unit on substantially the same terms as a signed contract, exercisable within 30 days after notice of the contract. Occupied units may be shown only a reasonable number of times, at appropriate hours, and only in the last 90 days of an expiring tenancy. An owner who converts without the notice is liable to a tenant who moves out because of non-renewal for moving expenses up to $1,500, 3 months' rent and attorney's fees. Lease terms contrary to or waiving these rights are void.

title: Notices in Federally Subsidized Buildings
bodyText: If you own federally subsidized housing (a building with a HUD or Farmers Home mortgage, mortgage insurance or rent subsidy under the listed federal programs, or a Section 8 contract), Illinois requires written notices to tenants. Before signing any lease in a building with a Section 8 contract that the Illinois Housing Development Authority does not administer, give each prospective tenant written notice of the date the Section 8 contract expires. If you may prepay the federally insured or held mortgage, post a notice in the building and deliver it personally or by certified mail to every tenant at least 12 months before the earliest prepayment date, and give a copy to every prospective tenant; if you intend to prepay, give a second notice at least 9 months before, posted and delivered the same way and given in writing to prospective tenants during the notice period. Both notices go to the local clerk and the Illinois Housing Development Authority too, on forms the Authority prescribes. An owner who fails to give a required tenant notice owes that tenant $1,000. Federal program rules may require more and are not covered here.

title: Towing From Rental Property
bodyText:
Except as provided in the relocation-towing chapter of the Vehicle Code, the owner or lessor of private property, or a person it authorizes, may have a motor vehicle abandoned or left unattended on the property without permission removed by a towing service, without liability for the costs of removal, transportation or storage or for damage caused by them.

A tenant's own vehicle parked with permission is not towed under this provision; enforcing lease parking rules against it may require other authority. The Vehicle Code's relocation-towing sign rule and its residential exception are described in the parking-rules notice row; local towing ordinances and the rest of that chapter are not covered here.

title: Tenant Right to Install EV Charging
bodyText:
In a single-family home or multifamily building that has parking spaces, and notwithstanding the lease, an Illinois tenant may install, at the tenant's expense and for the tenant's own use, a level 1 or level 2 receptacle or outlet or a level 2 electric vehicle charging system, subject to the landlord's bona fide safety requirements, registration within 30 days, reasonable aesthetic rules, and the tenant's written agreement to the landlord's design specifications, a licensed electrical contractor and insurance.

The landlord may charge only for electricity used (including network fees), a reasonable access fee, a restoration security deposit, installation costs where the landlord installs at the tenant's request, and a reasonable fee to reserve a shared-area space. A tenant-installed system remains the tenant's property. A landlord who willfully violates the statute owes actual damages and a civil penalty up to $1,000, and a prevailing tenant plaintiff recovers attorney's fees.

title: Cannabis in Rentals
bodyText: A landlord may prohibit a tenant from cultivating cannabis, may prohibit smoking cannabis on the premises, and is not required to allow a tenant to use cannabis on the property. A landlord may not refuse to lease to or penalize a person solely for being a registered medical cannabis patient or caregiver, unless required to avoid violating federal law or losing a federal monetary or licensing benefit, and a landlord is not penalized under State law for leasing to a cardholder or a lawful adult user.

title: Lease Terms Illinois Law Voids or Limits
bodyText: Illinois voids or overrides several kinds of residential lease terms: a clause exempting the landlord from liability for injury or property damage caused by the negligence of the landlord or its agents or employees in operating or maintaining the property; a jury-trial waiver in an eviction case; a requirement to pay by electronic funds transfer; for leases the rental-fee law covers, the fees it bans and any non-optional fee not listed on the lease's first page; a waiver or modification of Safe Homes Act rights; a waiver of Immigrant Tenant Protection Act rights; a utility term inconsistent with the Rental Property Utility Service Act's shared-meter and payment-arrangement rules; a term conflicting with the right of large complexes' tenants to pay at the on-site office; a lease term blocking a tenant's electric vehicle charger that complies with the statute; and a term contrary to or waiving condominium-conversion rights. A power to confess judgment in a lease is doubtful: the confession-of-judgment ban covers consumer transactions involving goods, services or intangibles, and its application to real-property leases was not confirmed.

title: Attorney's Fees
bodyText: Illinois has no general statute on attorney's-fee clauses in residential leases; a lease may provide for fees, and the shared default clause awards them to the prevailing party to the extent the law permits. Several tenant-protection statutes award fees to tenants, including those on security deposits, deposit interest, retaliation, the summary of rights, Safe Homes lock changes and confidentiality, immigrant tenant protection, utility violations over $3,000, EV charging, the rental-fee law (for leases it covers) minors named in evictions, and servicemember lease terminations. Some local ordinances, including Chicago's, restrict landlord fee clauses (not covered).

title: Illinois Statutory Forms and Required Wording
bodyText: Illinois supplies these forms or required words, which should be used as printed: the flood disclosure form (in the lease and before signing); the Disclosure of Information on Radon Hazards to Tenants form; the lease sentence on use of the premises for a felony or Class A misdemeanor; the sentence a 5-day rent demand must prominently state about partial payment; the suggested 10-day notice to quit; the notice in a motion to extend an eviction order past 120 days; the Department of Human Rights summary of rights attached as the lease's first pages; the 'Concession Granted' legend for a lease that does not state a rent concession; the disclosure of a recorded wind or solar noise waiver to a tenant before a new lease; and a broker landlord's or agent's written disclosure of real estate licensee status. Courts also publish standardized eviction forms and affidavits.

title: What This Illinois Research Covers
bodyText: The Illinois rows cover state statutes and the Illinois Supreme Court rules named in them for residential leases of houses and apartments. They do not cover mobile home lots (the Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Rights Act), farm leases, hotels and short stays, public housing rules, federal law beyond the lead disclosure, or local ordinances. Several Illinois local governments have their own landlord-tenant ordinances with additional duties, including the City of Chicago, Cook County, Evanston, Urbana and Mount Prospect, and home rule units may regulate further where state law allows. A landlord renting in one of those places must also follow the local ordinance.

title: Landlords Who Are Child Sex Offenders
bodyText: If a landlord who lives in the building is a child sex offender and rents to a person who did not tell the landlord that they are a parent or guardian of a child under 18, the tenant may not terminate the lease on later discovering the landlord's status. Such a landlord may not knowingly rent another unit in the building where they live to a parent or guardian of a child under 18 (a Class 4 felony, for leases entered into after January 1, 2009), and refusing to rent to such a person does not violate the Human Rights Act. Illinois does not require landlords to disclose sex offenders living nearby.

title: Firearms
bodyText: Illinois' concealed carry law lets the owner of private real property of any type prohibit carrying concealed firearms on property under the owner's control, with the statutory sign posted unless the property is a private residence; a licensee may still keep a firearm in a locked vehicle in a prohibited parking area. The statute does not say whether a leased unit is under the landlord's control or the tenant's, so whether a lease may bar a tenant's lawful firearm inside the unit is not settled here. Housing authorities may treat illegal use of a firearm as grounds for termination. The library offers no firearm clause for Illinois.

title: Flags and Signs
bodyText: No Illinois statute gives a residential tenant a right to display a flag, political sign or religious item that a lease may not restrict. Condominium and common-interest association rules on displays for unit owners are not covered here. The shared common-area clause's carve-out for displays the law protects has no Illinois statute to apply to.

title: Copies of the Lease
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires a landlord of a house or apartment to give the tenant a copy of the signed lease (the mobile home statute has its own rule). A condominium unit owner who leases the unit must give the association board a copy of the signed lease by occupancy or within 10 days of signing, whichever is first, and an owner in a common interest community must do the same for the association unless the community instruments provide otherwise.

title: Requiring Renter's Insurance
bodyText: No Illinois statute regulates a landlord's requirement that a tenant carry renter's insurance. Insurers may not refuse, cancel or surcharge a renter's policy based solely on the breed of a dog the tenant keeps (with exceptions). A landlord may not require special insurance for an assistance animal, and a tenant installing an EV charger must name the landlord as an additional insured when asked. A lease clause cannot excuse the landlord from liability for its own negligence.

title: Deaths or Crimes on the Property
bodyText: No Illinois statute addresses a landlord's own duty to tell a prospective tenant about a death, crime or similar event on the property. The Real Estate License Act provides that no cause of action arises against a real estate licensee for failing to disclose that an occupant had HIV or another medical condition, or that the property was the site of an act or occurrence that had no effect on its physical condition or environment. General fraud and misrepresentation law may apply to a direct question.

title: When the Tenant Causes Damage
bodyText:
Illinois law leaves much of the cost of tenant-caused damage with the tenant but sets no measure for the landlord's lost rent. No Illinois statute lets the tenant of a house or apartment stop paying rent or move out because a fire or other casualty made the home unlivable, and the library's optional casualty clause gives no termination or rent reduction for damage caused by the tenant, household members or guests.

A tenant may not use the repair-and-deduct remedy for a condition caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a family member or another person on the premises with the tenant's consent.

The landlord may keep from the security deposit the cost of repairing damage the tenant caused, including the reasonable cost of the landlord's own labor, if within 30 days after the later of the move-out date and the end of the tenant's right of possession it gives an itemized statement with the actual cost and paid receipts, or with an estimated cost followed by paid receipts within 30 days; the landlord may sue for the rest.

If the lease ends because of the damage, no statute measures the landlord's lost rent; the landlord must take reasonable measures to mitigate the damages it can recover, and the library offers an optional clause that sets the measure.

Tenants keep the remedies that turn on the landlord's own failure: if the landlord does not pay for water, gas or electric service it is required to pay for, the tenant may end the lease or, if the nonpayment puts the service at risk, pay for it and deduct the payment from rent, and a tenant gets a full rent abatement when the landlord causes utility service to be cut off by not paying a landlord-paid utility bill or by tampering (temporary shutoffs for emergencies such as fire, or for repairs on 7 days' written notice, are allowed).

Whether Illinois courts treat a tenant as covered by the landlord's fire insurance, and how the common-law warranty of habitability and constructive eviction apply to tenant-caused damage, are case law not reviewed here.

title: Waiving Habitability
bodyText: Illinois has no statute that sets a general habitability standard for leased houses and apartments, so no statute says whether a lease may waive one, lets a tenant accept named defects for a rent reduction, or requires a separate document for any such agreement. The standard comes from Illinois case law, which recognizes an implied warranty of habitability in residential leases; this library has not reviewed that case law, including what it says about waiver. Cautious course: don't put a clause in your lease in which the tenant gives up the right to a home fit to live in, accepts known defects in exchange for lower rent, or takes over your duty to keep the property fit; assume a court won't enforce it. Two statutes do limit such clauses: a term excusing you from liability for your own negligence in operating or maintaining the property is void, and the heating and cooling standards for 55-and-older housing apply whatever the lease says, since no statute lets them be waived. If the housing is financed under the Illinois Affordable Housing Program, the program's minimum standards, including keeping the premises fit for human habitation, are a condition of the funding. Whatever the lease says, it is a crime (criminal housing management) for an owner or manager to recklessly let the property's condition or facilities become or remain dangerous to anyone's health or safety, and the State's Attorney may have rents paid into a court escrow for repairs. Local codes and ordinances, including Chicago's and Cook County's, set their own standards.

title: Which Habitability Duties a Lease May Shift
bodyText: No Illinois statute lists habitability duties that a lease may or may not shift to the tenant, and no statute lets a lease waive a water or hot-water supply duty where the property has no well or utility water; Illinois has no statutory duty to supply water or hot water to a leased house or apartment at all. The duty to keep the home fit to live in comes from Illinois case law (the implied warranty of habitability). Cautious course: a lease may assign routine upkeep to the tenant (yard work, snow removal, replacing light bulbs and filters), but keep structural, heating, plumbing, electrical, water and safety items your responsibility, and don't write a clause excusing you from liability for your own negligence in operating or maintaining the property, which Illinois law voids. If the tenant pays utilities directly on a meter that also serves other areas, the statutory disclosure and rent-reduction rules for shared meters apply and can't be changed by the lease. Local codes and ordinances may set further rules.

title: How Serious a Defect Must Be
bodyText: No Illinois statute defines which defects are material to habitability or ties a general tenant remedy to how serious a defect is, because Illinois has no habitability statute for leased houses and apartments; the courts decide under the implied warranty of habitability. The statutes that do give tenants remedies use their own triggers instead of a materiality test: the repair-and-deduct right is limited by cost (the lesser of $500 or half a month's rent) and excludes conditions the tenant caused; utility shutoff remedies turn on whether service was interrupted; and the flood-disclosure remedy applies when an undisclosed flood damages the tenant's property, affects the habitability of the unit or affects the tenant's access. Cautious course: treat any loss of heat, water, power, sanitation, security or structural soundness, and any code violation, as serious and fix it promptly; treat cosmetic items as ordinary repairs under the lease.

title: Presumptions About Habitability
bodyText: No Illinois statute creates a presumption about habitability, such as a presumption that a unit with a code violation is uninhabitable or that a landlord who fails to repair within a set time acted in bad faith. The one presumption Illinois landlord-tenant law does create is about retaliation: if, within one year before an alleged retaliatory act, the tenant engaged in protected activity (such as complaining about code violations or asking for repairs the code or lease requires), that evidence creates a rebuttable presumption that your action was retaliatory, unless the tenant's activity began after your action. Cautious course: keep complete records of repair requests and what you did, and document a legitimate, non-retaliatory reason for any rent increase, non-renewal or eviction that follows a complaint.

title: Tenant Rights a Lease Cannot Waive
bodyText: Illinois has no general rule that a tenant's rights cannot be waived and no single list of banned lease terms. Instead, particular statutes void or override particular terms. A lease term has no effect, or the statute applies anyway, where it: excuses you from liability for injury or property damage caused by your or your employees' negligence in operating or maintaining the property; waives a jury trial in an eviction (either side may still demand a jury); waives or modifies Safe Homes Act rights for survivors of domestic or sexual violence; waives the Immigrant Tenant Protection Act's protections; conflicts with the shared-meter utility rules; conflicts with the right of tenants in buildings or complexes of 100 or more units to pay at an on-site office; is contrary to or waives condominium-conversion rights; blocks a tenant's electric vehicle charger that meets the statute; requires payment by electronic funds transfer; or takes away the right of a tenant who agreed to deal electronically to refuse later electronic transactions. For leases covered by the rental fee law (leases entered into after its effective date, which is July 1, 2026 under the law's own text or January 1, 2027 under the General Assembly's records, so treat it as covering leases entered into on or after July 1, 2026; leases in owner-occupied buildings of 6 or fewer units are excluded), a non-optional fee not listed on the lease's first page can't be collected, and the listed junk fees can't be required at all. Other statutory rights, including those under the Landlord Retaliation Act, the security deposit acts and the repair-and-deduct law, have no anti-waiver sentence; whether a lease may waive them is for the courts. Cautious course: never put a clause in your lease that waives or narrows a right a statute gives the tenant.

title: Shorter Notice for Showings
bodyText:
Illinois has no statute that sets a notice period before you enter a leased house or apartment, for showings or for any other purpose, so there is no statutory notice for a tenant to waive and no rule that a shorter showing notice be in a separate signed document.

The notice is what your lease says; the library's entry clause gives 24 hours, and the optional showings clause lets you set a shorter notice and fixed hours for showings near the end of the tenancy.

One statute does limit showings: if the building is being converted to a condominium, a tenant-occupied unit may be shown to prospective purchasers before its first sale only a reasonable number of times, at appropriate hours, and only during the last 90 days of the tenancy, and a lease term contrary to or waiving that rule is void. Some local ordinances, including Chicago's, set their own entry-notice rules; follow them where they apply.

title: Jury Trial Waivers
bodyText: A jury-waiver clause doesn't work in an Illinois residential lease. In any case relating to premises used as a residence, either you or the tenant may demand a jury trial, whatever the lease or any other contract says about waiving one. The Illinois Constitution keeps the right to a jury trial as it has historically existed. A jury isn't automatic, though: under the general civil procedure rule, a plaintiff who wants a jury must file a demand when the case is filed and a defendant no later than its answer, or the party gives up the jury. So in an eviction the case is tried by the judge unless someone files a timely demand. Don't put a jury waiver in your lease; the library doesn't offer one for Illinois. Illinois has no general statute on jury waivers in standard-form contracts; its consumer-contract jury-waiver rules cover payday loans, refund anticipation loans and home repair contracts, not leases.

title: Clauses Excusing the Landlord's Negligence
bodyText: Illinois voids any lease term, or any agreement made with or alongside a lease, that exempts you from liability for injury to people or damage to property caused by your negligence, or that of your agents, employees or servants, in operating or maintaining the rented premises or the building or land they are part of. The rule covers personal injury and property damage in residential leases; only a non-residential lease may exempt a landlord from liability for property damage. The term isn't just unenforceable against the tenant who signed it: the statute declares it void as against public policy. The statute doesn't address a clause making the tenant indemnify you, or limits on liability for harm you didn't cause; whether those are enforceable is for the courts. Cautious course: limit any indemnity or release in your lease to harm caused by the tenant, the tenant's household and guests, and say expressly that it doesn't cover your own negligence. The library's Illinois clauses on insurance, parking, storage and pets use versions without a landlord-liability disclaimer for this reason. Separately, in Cook County, if you don't rekey a unit between tenants as required and a theft results, you are liable for the theft damages.

title: Unconscionable Lease Terms
bodyText: No Illinois statute lets a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable term in a residential lease of a house or apartment, and none lets a court revise or end a lease because circumstances have made it excessively burdensome. The Uniform Commercial Code's unconscionability rule for leases covers leases of goods (movable things), not leases of real estate. Unconscionability in a residential lease is a common-law doctrine decided by the courts. Illinois's Consumer Fraud and Deceptive Business Practices Act prohibits unfair or deceptive practices in trade or commerce, which it defines to include property of every kind, real or personal; whether and how it reaches a residential lease is for the courts, but some landlord statutes expressly make a violation a Consumer Fraud Act violation (for example, requiring electronic rent payment). Cautious course: assume a court can refuse to enforce a one-sided term that a tenant had no real chance to negotiate, and treat deceptive or unfair leasing conduct as exposed under the Consumer Fraud Act. Use the library's Illinois clauses, which avoid terms Illinois law voids, and don't add your own penalty, waiver or liability-shifting terms.

title: Charges for Eviction Notices and Filings
