bodyText: For leases covered by Illinois's rental fee law (leases entered into after its effective date, which is July 1, 2026 under the law's own text or January 1, 2027 under the General Assembly's records, so treat it as covering leases entered into on or after July 1, 2026; leases in owner-occupied buildings of 6 or fewer units are excluded), neither you nor the lease may require the tenant to pay a fee or fine for an eviction notice, or for filing an eviction case before the court grants an eviction order. That rule doesn't stop you from recovering court costs and filing fees as the court allows, and you can't avoid it by calling the charge something else. A tenant may sue over a violation for an injunction, money, attorney's fees and costs. The same law bars using an unpaid application or background-check fee as a ground for eviction during the first year of the lease. For leases the fee law doesn't cover, no Illinois statute bans an eviction charge, but whether a fixed charge is an unenforceable penalty is decided under case law. Cautious course for every lease: don't put a flat "eviction fee," "notice fee" or "legal processing fee" in the lease; recover only what the court awards (court costs and, where the lease and law allow, attorney's fees), and list any non-optional charge on the lease's first page.

title: Preset Damages in the Lease
bodyText:
No Illinois statute says when a residential lease may fix in advance the damages a tenant owes for a breach, such as a lease-break or early-termination fee or a flat charge for a default, and no statute sets a test for when such an amount is an unenforceable penalty. Courts decide that under the common law; the Uniform Commercial Code's liquidated-damages rule covers leases of goods, not real estate.

Statutes do settle three points. First, the Security Deposit Return Act lets a written lease set a dollar amount for cleaning, repairing or replacing a listed component, which you may then withhold from the deposit for damage beyond normal wear and tear, if the amount is reasonable to restore the property (see the library's optional cost-schedule clause).

Second, when a servicemember ends a lease under the Service Member Residential Property Act, the tenant owes prorated rent to the termination date and the cost of damage the tenant caused, but no other rent and no liquidated damages.

Third, for leases covered by the rental fee law, every non-optional fee must be listed on the lease's first page or the tenant isn't liable for it, and fees for renewing or modifying a lease or for an eviction notice are barred.

Cautious course: charge actual, documented costs; use a preset amount only where a statute authorizes it or as a reasonable estimate of a loss that would be hard to measure, never as a penalty; and put any preset charge on the lease's first page.

title: Accepting Rent After a Notice
bodyText:
Illinois's statute answers this only for unpaid rent. After you serve a written demand for rent (at least 5 days to pay), partial payments that don't add up to the full amount demanded by the end of the notice period don't cancel the demand, but only if the demand prominently states: "Only FULL PAYMENT of the rent demanded in this notice will waive the landlord's right to terminate the lease under this notice, unless the landlord agrees in writing to continue the lease in exchange for receiving partial payment."

You may agree in writing to continue the lease for a partial payment. Collecting past-due rent after you file the eviction doesn't invalidate the case. If the tenant pays the full amount demanded within the notice period, the lease isn't terminated.

For every other situation, including accepting rent after a 10-day notice for a non-rent breach, after a notice ending a month-to-month tenancy, or with knowledge of a breach, no statute decides whether acceptance waives the notice or the breach; Illinois courts decide, and a lease non-waiver clause may not be enough.

Cautious course: after serving any notice other than a rent demand, refuse rent for any period after the notice, or return it promptly with a written statement that you are not waiving the notice; and put the statutory statement in every rent demand. The library offers an optional Illinois clause stating that acceptance doesn't waive a breach, notice or case.

title: Penalties for Using Prohibited Lease Terms
bodyText: Illinois has no general penalty for knowingly putting a prohibited term in a residential lease. Most Illinois bars simply make the term void, so a tenant can ignore it: for example, a clause excusing your own negligence, a jury waiver in an eviction, or a waiver of Safe Homes Act rights. A few statutes attach consequences to the term or the conduct itself. Under the rental fee law (for the leases it covers), a lease may not require a banned fee, and any person alleging a violation may sue for an injunction, money, attorney's fees and costs. Requiring a tenant to pay by electronic funds transfer is an unlawful practice under the Consumer Fraud and Deceptive Business Practices Act, which allows a private suit for actual damages and attorney's fees and civil penalties of up to $50,000 in an action by the Attorney General or a State's Attorney. Rental Property Utility Service Act violations can bring trebled damages for knowing or intentional violations, and statutory damages for deliberate or reckless utility shutoffs. A landlord who willfully violates the EV charging rules owes actual damages and a civil penalty of up to $1,000, and immigration-related harassment or eviction carries a civil penalty of up to $2,000 per violation. Whether the Consumer Fraud Act's general ban on unfair or deceptive practices, or its separate ban on non-disparagement clauses in consumer contracts, reaches a residential lease is for the courts. Cautious course: use the library's Illinois clauses as written and don't add terms that misstate a tenant's rights.

title: Waiving or Shortening a Notice to Quit
bodyText: No Illinois statute lets a residential lease waive or shorten the notices required before an eviction: the written demand giving at least 5 days to pay unpaid rent, the 10-day notice for other lease breaches, and the 7-day, 30-day or 60-day notices that end week-to-week, month-to-month and year-to-year tenancies. The statutes are written as minimums, and whether a lease may waive them is for the courts. Two points are settled by statute: when a fixed-term lease ends on its own terms, no notice or demand is needed before filing; and the week-to-week and other short-term notice rules apply where the tenant holds over "without special agreement," which leaves room for the lease to address what happens at the end of the term. Cautious course: don't rely on a lease clause waiving a notice. Serve the statutory demand or notice, by an approved method, before every eviction other than at the end of a fixed term, and keep proof of service, since the notice and proof of service are attached to the eviction complaint. The library doesn't offer a notice-waiver clause for Illinois.

title: Confession of Judgment Clauses
bodyText: A confession-of-judgment clause lets a landlord get a court judgment against the tenant without a lawsuit the tenant can defend. Illinois bars such a clause in any instrument used in a consumer transaction made after September 24, 1979: the power is void and any judgment based on it is unenforceable. The statute defines a consumer transaction as a sale, lease, assignment, loan or other disposition of goods, a consumer service or an intangible to an individual for personal, family or household purposes. It doesn't mention leases of real estate, so whether it reaches a residential lease of a house or apartment is unresolved by statute and decided by case law. Illinois's eviction statutes provide no confessed judgment for possession, and other statutes ban confession clauses in many consumer contracts (payday loans, rental-purchase of goods, motor vehicle leases, home solicitation sales other than real-property rentals). Cautious course: don't put a confession-of-judgment clause in a residential lease; recover rent and possession through an eviction case, where a claim for rent may be joined. The library doesn't offer one for Illinois.

title: Waiving Homestead and Property Exemptions
bodyText: Illinois's homestead exemption can protect a tenant, not only an owner: every individual is entitled to a homestead of up to $50,000 in a lot and buildings, a condominium or personal property "owned or rightly possessed by lease or otherwise" and occupied as a residence. A release or waiver of the homestead is valid only if it is in writing and signed by the individual and the individual's spouse, if any (or if possession is abandoned or given under a conveyance); an instrument waives the homestead only if it contains a clause expressly doing so, and one spouse's waiver doesn't bind the other unless the other joins in it. Separately, household goods, clothing, pets, medications, a vehicle up to $3,600, tools of the trade, benefits and other listed personal property are exempt from judgments, attachment and distress for rent, and no Illinois statute provides for waiving those exemptions in a lease. Anyone who seizes exempt property by distress is liable for double its value. Cautious course: don't put a homestead or exemption waiver in your lease; the library doesn't offer one for Illinois. Collect unpaid rent through an eviction case or a money judgment, and if you use distress for rent, never take exempt property.

title: Changing the Casualty and Mitigation Rules by Lease
bodyText:
Illinois has no statute on what happens to a residential lease when fire or another casualty damages the home, so there is no statutory casualty rule for a lease to change: the lease decides, and the library offers an optional Illinois casualty clause for that.

Mitigation is different. When a tenant defaults, including by leaving early, Illinois requires you to take reasonable measures to mitigate the damages you can recover, such as trying to re-rent. The statute doesn't say whether a lease may waive or narrow that duty, and no statute says it can't; the courts decide.

Cautious course: don't put a clause in your lease saying you have no duty to re-rent or that the tenant owes all remaining rent regardless; assume you must make reasonable efforts, and keep records of advertising and showings. The library's default clause promises mitigation to the extent the law requires. Don't use a casualty clause that keeps the tenant paying full rent for a home that can't be lived in.

title: Tenant Remedies When the Landlord Breaches
bodyText: Illinois has no general statute listing a tenant's remedies when a landlord fails to keep the lease or the home in repair; those remedies, including rent abatement and damages for breach of the implied warranty of habitability, come from case law. Specific statutes give tenants these remedies: repair and deduct for small repairs the lease or a code requires (up to the lesser of $500 or half a month's rent, after 14 days' written notice, in buildings the law covers); if you fail to pay a utility the lease makes your responsibility, the tenant may end the lease or pay the bill and deduct it from rent; if you cause a utility shutoff, a full rent abatement for the period, consequential damages and, for deliberate or reckless conduct, statutory damages; damages for shared-meter violations, trebled if knowing or intentional; retaliation remedies; ending the lease and recovering damages after an undisclosed flood; ending the lease or mitigating with your consent and deducting the cost after a radon hazard you don't mitigate; double the deposit for a bad-faith or missing itemized statement; Cook County rekeying theft damages; under the Lead Poisoning Prevention Act, rent withheld from you, through the State's Attorney, until required lead mitigation is done, with no eviction for that withholding; and remedies for Safe Homes lock-change, immigration-status, EV-charging, rental-fee, servicemember and condominium-conversion violations, each described in its own row. Separately, it is a crime (criminal housing management) for an owner or manager to recklessly let a residential property's condition or facilities endanger anyone's health or safety, and the State's Attorney may obtain a court order paying rents into an escrow for repairs; that law does not itself let tenants stop paying rent. In an eviction case, the tenant may raise defenses but generally can't join unrelated claims, and a tenant who did not follow every repair-and-deduct step can't defend by saying the rent was withheld under that law. Cautious course: respond promptly and in writing to repair requests and keep records.

title: Smoke Drift and Common-Area Smoking
bodyText:
No Illinois statute addresses smoke drifting from one unit into another, or a lease clause in which the tenant gives up claims about drifting smoke. The Smoke Free Illinois Act exempts private residences, including apartments and condominium units, so it doesn't ban smoking inside a unit.

It does ban smoking in any place of employment, defined as any area under an employer's control that employees must enter, leave or pass through while working, including common areas, and an enclosed area includes lobbies and corridors. So where your employees or building staff work in or pass through enclosed hallways, lobbies, laundry or other common areas, smoking there is banned, and as the owner you must reasonably assure that it is; smoking is also banned within 15 feet of the entrances, exits, opening windows and air intakes of those areas.

Whether the Act reaches common areas of a building with no employees, as a "public place," isn't settled by the statute's words. Local ordinances may go further.

Cautious course: don't rely on a waiver of smoke-drift claims, since a court could treat persistent smoke as a habitability or nuisance problem; a no-smoking rule is the safer tool. Use the library's Smoking Policy clause, which bans smoking (including cannabis and vaping) anywhere on the property; Illinois law expressly lets you prohibit smoking cannabis on the premises.

title: No General Statement of Tenant Rights
bodyText: Illinois has no "truth in renting" law: no state-prepared statement of general landlord and tenant rights that you must give tenants, and no statute voiding lease terms just because they misstate the law. Illinois instead requires three narrower handouts. Starting January 1, 2026, the Illinois Department of Human Rights' summary of housing protections for survivors of domestic and sexual violence must be attached as the first page of every written residential lease, including renewals, with each tenant signing an acknowledgment at the bottom of each page; a landlord who fails to comply owes the tenant actual damages up to $2,000 or $100, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees. For housing built before 1978, the Department of Public Health's lead brochure goes to prospective tenants. And on request, you must give the radon guide for tenants and the radon disclosure form. Separately, specific statutes void particular lease terms (see the library's row on terms Illinois law voids). Local ordinances, such as Chicago's, require their own summaries; they are not covered here.

title: Blank Spaces in the Lease
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires every blank in a residential lease to be completed before it is signed, or treats an unfilled blank as a breach. Illinois has blank-space rules only for other contracts, such as motor vehicle leases and retail installment contracts. Two Illinois rules still make blanks matter. Under the rental fee law (for leases it covers), a non-optional fee not explicitly stated on the lease's first page can't be collected, so a blank fee line on page 1 means no fee. And a cost schedule for deposit deductions works only for the dollar amounts the written lease actually specifies. Statutory disclosures with blanks to fill in, such as the flood disclosure, must be completed to give the information the statute requires. Cautious course: fill in every blank, or write "None" or "N/A," before anyone signs, and give the tenant a complete copy.

title: What an Illinois Lease Must Contain
bodyText: Illinois has no statute listing everything a residential lease must contain, but several statutes require specific content. In or with every written lease: (1) the Illinois Department of Human Rights summary of housing protections for survivors of domestic and sexual violence, attached as the first page, with each tenant signing each page (from January 1, 2026); (2) for leases covered by the rental fee law, every non-optional fee on the lease's first page, and whether utilities are included in rent; (3) the flood disclosure, in the lease or renewal and signed by both parties, where the property is in a FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area or you know of flooding, and for every lower-level unit that has flooded in the last 10 years; (4) the statutory notice that use of the premises for a felony or Class A misdemeanor lets you void the lease; (5) if tenants pay a share of a master-metered utility, the written allocation formula; and (6) federal lead-paint disclosures for housing built before 1978. Other content is conditional or optional: the drug-free housing addendum needed for the Class X felony remedy; the building manager and insurer notice, which may go in the lease instead of being posted, for buildings of more than 4 units with no on-site owner or manager; and a schedule of cleaning and repair costs you may deduct from the deposit. Illinois does not require the lease's start and end dates on its first page. Before offering a lease where the tenant pays a utility on a meter that also serves other areas, you must give a written statement and other information. Local ordinances (Chicago, Cook County and others) add their own requirements.

title: Initials and Conspicuous Print
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires a residential tenant to initial particular lease terms, or requires any lease term to be printed in bold, capital letters or a minimum type size. Illinois's initialing and conspicuous-print rules apply to other documents, such as self-storage agreements, car rentals and utility-company shutoff notices. Two statutory forms that go with a lease do call for initials or signatures: the radon disclosure form has the landlord and the tenant initial each statement that applies, and each tenant signs the bottom of every page of the domestic and sexual violence summary attached to the lease; the flood disclosure is signed by both parties. Cautious course: although initials aren't required, having each tenant initial every page and any unusual term (a fee, an optional clause, a waiver) is good evidence the tenant saw it.

title: Plain Language in the Lease
bodyText: Illinois has no plain-language law for residential leases: no readability test, no rule that a lease be divided into captioned sections, and no consumer-contract statute of that kind that reaches leases. Illinois's plain-language rules cover other contracts and documents, such as pre-need funeral and cemetery contracts, agricultural production contracts and some utility and insurance disclosures, and a state task force is studying whether to extend plain-language principles to private contracts. Some Illinois lease rules do turn on clarity: under the rental fee law (for leases it covers), non-optional fees must be explicitly stated on the first page and disclosed clearly and conspicuously in listings, and the flood disclosure must be made clearly. Cautious course: write the lease in short, clear sentences with headings; a court reading an unclear term may construe it against the party who wrote it.

title: No Consumer Restrictions Statement
bodyText: Illinois has no statute requiring a residential lease to carry a front-page statement listing the terms that restrict the tenant's rights (the "statement of consumer restrictions" some states require), no readability test for leases, no Attorney General preapproval process for lease forms and no dollar threshold for such a rule. The closest Illinois requirements are front-page placement rules for other content: the domestic and sexual violence summary attached as the lease's first page, and, for leases covered by the rental fee law, every non-optional fee on the first page. Cautious course: keep restrictive terms visible and clearly labeled; the library's Illinois clauses mark optional terms.

title: Notices That Must Be in Writing
bodyText: Illinois requires writing for the notices that matter most. Your notices: the demand for unpaid rent (at least 5 days); the 10-day notice to quit for other lease breaches, signed by you or your agent; the 7-day, 30-day and 60-day notices ending week-to-week, month-to-month and year-to-year tenancies; the notice to vacate after voiding a lease for criminal activity; the itemized deposit statement (by personal delivery, postmarked mail or email to a verified address the tenant gave you); 7 days' written notice before a utility shutoff for repairs; and any agreement to continue the lease for a partial rent payment. Agreements: a lease amendment shifting utilities to the tenant must be in writing and signed by both of you. Tenant notices: a repair-and-deduct notice (by registered or certified mail or other restricted delivery), a Safe Homes notice when leaving because of domestic or sexual violence and a written lock-change request, a flood-disclosure termination, and a servicemember's termination notice with orders. Eviction demands and notices are served by handing a copy to the tenant, leaving it with a household member 13 or older, certified or registered mail with return receipt, or posting if no one is in possession. For other notices, such as entry, the lease decides; the library's Illinois leases use written notice throughout. Whether a notice the law requires in writing may be sent by text or email instead of paper turns on electronic-records law, so use paper and the statutory service methods for eviction notices.

title: Leases Longer Than One Year Must Be in Writing
bodyText: Under Illinois's Frauds Act, a lease (an interest in land) for a term longer than one year can't be enforced against a party unless the lease, or a note or memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by that party or by an agent the party authorized in writing. The same Act requires a signed writing for any agreement that can't be performed within one year. The consideration (the rent) doesn't have to be stated in the writing. Illinois has no separate rule for leases of five years or more. A lease of one year or less can be oral, but the library's leases are always written and signed by every tenant and the landlord. Recording: an instrument authorized to be recorded takes effect against creditors and later buyers without notice only from the time it is recorded; whether a tenant's possession gives a buyer notice of an unrecorded lease is for the courts, so a tenant under a long lease may want to record it or a memorandum of it. Whether an assignment or surrender of a long lease needs a signed writing turns on how courts apply the Act; put every assignment, sublease and surrender in a signed writing.

title: Formalities for Longer Leases
bodyText: For a residential lease longer than one year, Illinois requires a signed writing: the Frauds Act makes such a lease unenforceable against a party who didn't sign it, and an agent signing for a party needs written authority. Illinois doesn't require a seal, the owner's own signature, a notary or recording for a residential lease to be valid between the landlord and tenant, and it isn't a community-property state with a spouse-joinder rule for leases. One spouse rule may matter. If the property you rent out is a married owner's homestead, a release, waiver or conveyance of the homestead is valid only if it is in writing and signed by both spouses, unless possession is given under the conveyance, and one spouse's release doesn't bind the other unless the other joins. Illinois's Conveyances Act treats leasing as a way of conveying land, but no statute says whether a lease of a homestead is a conveyance of it. Cautious course: if the rented home is, or may still be, a married owner's residence, have both spouses sign the lease; for any lease over one year, have every landlord and tenant sign, and use a written power of attorney for any agent who signs. This row doesn't cover lease-term limits that apply to public bodies, trustees, guardians or estate representatives.

title: Waiving Security Deposit Rights
bodyText: Illinois has no statute that says a tenant cannot waive the security deposit rules in a lease, and none that says a tenant can. The Security Deposit Return Act and the Security Deposit Interest Act contain no anti-waiver sentence, and Illinois has no general statute that voids lease waivers. That silence does not make a waiver lawful: whether a court would enforce a lease term giving up the 30-day itemized statement, the 45-day return, the doubled-deposit penalty or deposit interest is a question of case law. Some rules protect the deposit outright: a tenant does not forfeit the deposit solely because of an eviction under the criminal-activity, drug-nuisance or Class X felony provisions (in a criminal-activity eviction the deposit may still pay the sheriff's eviction fees). The cautious course is to put no deposit waiver, forfeiture, longer return period or nonrefundable-deposit term in the lease, and to follow the return rules in the library's deposit clauses. Some local ordinances, including Chicago's, have their own deposit and anti-waiver rules (not covered). Searched: the Illinois Compiled Statutes, the Illinois Constitution and the list of the 104th General Assembly's Public Acts. Not searched: the Administrative Code, court rules, local ordinances and case law.

title: Paying a Deposit in Installments
bodyText: Illinois has no statute that gives a tenant the right to pay a security deposit in installments, and none that stops you from agreeing to it. If you allow installments, write the schedule into the lease's amounts-due terms and treat every installment you receive as part of the security deposit, held and returned under the Security Deposit Return Act. Offer the same deposit terms to every applicant: the Human Rights Act makes it a civil rights violation to alter the terms or conditions of a rental because of a protected characteristic, including source of income, and bars increasing the customary security deposit for a person with a disability. Local ordinances are not covered. Searched: the Illinois Compiled Statutes, the Illinois Constitution and the list of the 104th General Assembly's Public Acts. Not searched: the Administrative Code, court rules, local ordinances and case law.

title: Last Month's Rent and the Deposit
bodyText: Illinois has no statute that limits collecting last month's rent in advance, and none that lets a tenant use the security deposit as the last month's rent or stops a lease from forbidding it. Illinois law does recognize rent paid in advance in three places: if you sell or otherwise transfer the property, the new owner becomes liable to the tenant for any prepaid rent and you remain liable with the new owner; if a servicemember ends the lease under the military termination right, you must return any unearned rent paid in advance; and if a tenant ends the lease because of unlawful retaliation, you must return all prepaid rent. The cautious course: if you collect last month's rent, label it in the lease as prepaid rent for the last month, separate from the security deposit, and list it with the other amounts due at signing; and if you do not want the deposit used as rent, say so in the lease (the library's security deposit clause says the deposit does not relieve the tenant of paying rent). Local ordinances are not covered. Searched: the Illinois Compiled Statutes, the Illinois Constitution and the list of the 104th General Assembly's Public Acts. Not searched: the Administrative Code, court rules, local ordinances and case law.

title: Move-Out Notice and the Deposit Clock
bodyText: Illinois does not make the return of a security deposit depend on the tenant giving notice of moving out, returning the keys or giving a forwarding address. Your deadlines run from the later of the day the tenant vacates and the day the tenant's right of possession ends: 30 days to deliver the itemized statement of damage with paid receipts (or estimates, with receipts to follow within 30 days), and, without a proper statement, 45 days after the tenant vacates to return the whole deposit. The one protection the statute gives you: if the tenant gives you no mailing address or email address, you are not liable for damages or penalties caused by that failure. The cautious course: ask in the lease and at move-out for a forwarding mailing address in writing (and a verified email address if the tenant wants email delivery), record the date the tenant vacated and the date possession ended, and count your deadlines from the later date without waiting for keys or a notice. A lease may still require notice to end a month-to-month tenancy; that is a termination rule, not a condition of the deposit return. Searched: the Illinois Compiled Statutes, the Illinois Constitution and the list of the 104th General Assembly's Public Acts. Not searched: the Administrative Code, court rules, local ordinances and case law.

title: Where Security Deposits Are Held
bodyText: Illinois does not require an owner who holds its own tenants' security deposits for a house or apartment to keep them in a separate, escrow or interest-bearing account, to tell the tenant where the money is held, or to keep it apart from the owner's other funds. Different rules apply in these cases. A licensed real estate broker or property manager who holds deposits for an owner must keep them in a special account, separate from personal and other business accounts, until the tenancy transaction ends, unless the parties direct otherwise in writing or a court orders a release; the account must not bear interest unless the law requires interest or the parties require it in writing; and this rule does not reach deposits held by the sole owner of the property. A landlord of 25 or more units in one building or complex must pay interest on deposits held more than 6 months (see the deposit interest row). If a disability-related modification requires a restoration agreement, any money the tenant pays toward restoration goes into an interest-bearing escrow account, capped at the reasonable cost of restoration, with the interest going to the tenant. If you sell or transfer the property, the new owner is liable for the deposits. Mobile home parks have their own trust-account rules, and some local ordinances, including Chicago's, have holding rules (not covered). Good practice everywhere: keep deposits in an identified account and keep records of each tenant's deposit so you can return it on time.

title: Deposit Amount Standards
bodyText: Illinois has no statute that requires a landlord, of any size, to post or hand out the standards it uses to decide how much security deposit to charge, and no statewide cap on the amount. What limits you is fair housing law: the Human Rights Act makes it a civil rights violation to alter the terms or conditions of a rental because of a protected characteristic (which in Illinois includes source of income, immigration status and arrest record as well as the federal classes), and you may not increase the customary security deposit for a person with a disability. Illinois also lets the written lease state fixed costs for cleaning, repairing or replacing particular components, which you may then withhold from the deposit for damage beyond normal wear and tear (the library's optional cost-schedule clause). The cautious course: if you use more than one deposit amount (for example by unit type, pet or screening result), write the standard down, apply it the same way to every applicant and keep it on file. Local ordinances are not covered. Searched: the Illinois Compiled Statutes, the Illinois Constitution and the list of the 104th General Assembly's Public Acts. Not searched: the Administrative Code, court rules, local ordinances and case law.

title: No Fast-Track Deposit Procedure
bodyText: Illinois has no fast-track procedure for security deposit disputes and no special rule that lets you settle a deposit early or differently when a tenant abandons the unit, dies, is evicted or ends the lease early. The ordinary rules apply in every case: within 30 days after the later of the day the tenant vacates and the day the right of possession ends, deliver the itemized statement of damage with receipts (or estimates followed by receipts within 30 days), or return the whole deposit within 45 days after the tenant vacates. A tenant evicted for certain criminal or drug activity, or after a Class X felony charge, does not forfeit the deposit for that reason alone. A dispute over the deposit goes to court as an ordinary money claim, usually in small claims; the Illinois Supreme Court's small claims rules govern that procedure. If the tenant has died, see the library's row on a tenant's death; if you cannot find the tenant to return the money, see the row on unclaimed deposits. Searched: the Illinois Compiled Statutes, the Illinois Constitution and the list of the 104th General Assembly's Public Acts. Not searched: the Administrative Code, court rules, local ordinances and case law.

title: Fees in Place of a Security Deposit
bodyText: Illinois has no statute on deposit alternatives: nothing authorizes, bars or regulates a monthly fee, surety bond or insurance product offered in place of a security deposit, and nothing requires you to let a tenant switch back to a deposit. The rental fee law still reaches such a fee for leases it covers: every non-optional fee must be stated on the first page of the lease or the tenant is not liable for it, a landlord may not rename a fee or charge to avoid the law, and the law exempts owner-occupied buildings of 6 units or fewer. The cautious course: if a tenant must pay a deposit-alternative fee (or chooses it in place of a required deposit), list it on the first page with its amount; offer the choice on the same terms to every applicant; and describe accurately what the fee does, since it usually buys the landlord's protection, not the tenant's, and the tenant may still owe you for damage beyond what the product pays. Money a tenant pays that you hold to secure rent or damage and could return is a security deposit, whatever it is called, and should be handled under the deposit return rules. Insurance and credit-reporting rules for these products are not covered. Searched: the Illinois Compiled Statutes, the Illinois Constitution and the list of the 104th General Assembly's Public Acts. Not searched: the Administrative Code, court rules, local ordinances and case law.

title: Holding Deposits Before the Lease
bodyText: Illinois has no statute on holding deposits or other money taken to reserve a unit before a lease is signed: nothing authorizes, caps or bars them, and nothing says when they must be returned. Three rules bear on them. First, for leases the rental fee law covers, the application fee (including background checks) is capped at $50, and you may not charge, at the time of application, an additional fee or fine that duplicates screening costs or covers costs unrelated to screening, so a nonrefundable holding fee collected with the application is risky. Second, if a tenant's meter will also serve common areas or other units, you must give the written statement of what the meter serves, and the past 12 months of bills (unless waived in writing), before offering the lease or accepting a security deposit. Third, if a licensed broker or property manager takes the money once a lease has been agreed, it is held as escrow money in a separate account. The cautious course: take a holding deposit only under a short written agreement that says how long the unit is held, that the money is credited to the first month's rent or the security deposit if the lease is signed, and that it is refunded if you decline the applicant or do not offer the lease as agreed; once credited to the security deposit it is handled under the deposit return rules. Searched: the Illinois Compiled Statutes, the Illinois Constitution and the list of the 104th General Assembly's Public Acts. Not searched: the Administrative Code, court rules, local ordinances and case law.

title: Nonrefundable Deposits and Fees
bodyText:
Illinois has no statute that allows, bars or requires a special notice for a nonrefundable deposit or fee.

Two rules decide how such a charge works. First, money you hold to secure the payment of rent or to pay for damage is a security deposit under the Security Deposit Return Act, and you may keep it for damage only by giving the itemized statement with receipts within 30 days; calling part of a deposit nonrefundable does not take it outside those rules, and no statute lets you keep it without that statement.

Second, for leases the rental fee law covers, a nonrefundable fee the tenant must pay is a non-optional fee that must be stated on the first page of the lease, or the tenant is not liable for it; a fee the law bars (such as a move-in or move-out walk-through fee, a routine maintenance fee, a lease renewal fee or a pest fee where the tenant did not contribute to the infestation) stays barred whatever it is called, because a landlord may not rename a fee to avoid the law.

The cautious course: never make any part of the security deposit nonrefundable; charge a nonrefundable fee only for a lawful purpose, list it with its amount on the first page, and use the library's optional nonrefundable-fees clause so the lease says which payments are fees and which are deposit. You may not charge a pet fee or pet deposit for an assistance animal. Owner-occupied buildings of 6 units or fewer are exempt from the fee law. Searched: the Illinois Compiled Statutes, the Illinois Constitution and the list of the 104th General Assembly's Public Acts. Not searched: the Administrative Code, court rules, local ordinances and case law.

A fee for pest abatement or removal can't be listed as a nonrefundable fee at all, because a fee fixed at signing can't depend on whether the tenant later contributed to an infestation. A third-party background check that actually costs more than $50 is billed to the applicant, with the provider's receipts within 14 days, only if you paid it up front; it is never listed as a lease fee.

title: Separate Notice of Nonrefundable Charges
bodyText: Illinois has no statute that requires a separate written notice, signed acknowledgment or special wording before you charge a nonrefundable fee or treat any payment as nonrefundable. What the law does require, for leases the rental fee law covers, is that every non-optional fee appear on the first page of the lease, or the tenant is not liable for it; a separate notice does not take the place of that first-page listing. The rules on nonrefundable deposits and fees are explained in the library's row on nonrefundable deposits and fees. Searched: the Illinois Compiled Statutes, the Illinois Constitution and the list of the 104th General Assembly's Public Acts. Not searched: the Administrative Code, court rules, local ordinances and case law.

title: Fees Must Be on the First Page
bodyText: For leases the rental fee law covers, every non-optional fee you charge, one-time or recurring, must be stated explicitly on the first page of the lease; if it is not, the tenant is not liable for it. Your listing must also disclose non-optional fees clearly and conspicuously (or through a web link that accompanies it), and the lease or listing must say whether utilities are included in rent. Fees the law bars may not be charged at all, even if they are listed. Illinois does not require the lease to show rent and fees as one labelled total, does not set a notice period for adding a fee during the term, and does not cap a markup on a third-party service, except that a landlord who allocates a master-metered utility bill among tenants by formula may not collect more for the building than the utility charges. Because a fee is collectible only if it is on the first page, don't add a new fee during the term; put any new fee on the first page of the renewal lease. The law exempts leases for units in owner-occupied buildings of 6 units or fewer. The library prints the required fee box at the top of the lease.

title: Fees for Services
bodyText: Illinois has no general statute that bars a landlord from charging for a service it does not provide, but the rental fee law bars a list of service-type fees outright for leases it covers: fees for after-hours maintenance requests; for contacting the owner or manager about maintenance, service, the lease or the tenancy; for travel to do maintenance or safety repairs; for a maintenance hotline or calls to it; for routine maintenance and upkeep of the unit; for pest abatement where the tenant in no way contributed to the infestation; and for a move-in or move-out walk-through. Renaming one of these fees does not take it outside the ban. Any other service or amenity fee is allowed only if it is stated on the first page of the lease. Whether the Consumer Fraud Act reaches a fee for a service the tenant never receives is a question of case law not reviewed here; the cautious course is to charge a service or amenity fee only for a service the tenant actually receives, describe it in the lease, and stop or credit the fee for any period it is not available. Owner-occupied buildings of 6 units or fewer are exempt from the fee law. Searched: the Illinois Compiled Statutes, the Illinois Constitution and the list of the 104th General Assembly's Public Acts. Not searched: the Administrative Code, court rules, local ordinances and case law.

title: Are Fees Rent?
bodyText: No Illinois statute defines rent for a house or apartment lease or says that fees the lease calls additional rent count as rent. That matters because the 5-day demand that lets you end a lease for nonpayment is a demand for rent, and in an eviction case a claim for rent may be joined but other matters not germane to possession may not. Other lease defaults, such as an unpaid fee, can support a 10-day notice to quit for breach of the lease. The rental fee law adds one express limit for leases it covers: a third-party background check fee may never be the basis for an eviction action within the first year of the lease, and no fee is owed at all unless it is on the first page of the lease. No court decision was reviewed on whether a lease can turn fees into rent. The cautious course: put only unpaid rent in a 5-day demand; collect late fees, damage charges and other fees separately (by written demand, a 10-day notice for a material lease default, or a separate money claim); and don't rely on an additional-rent sentence, so the library offers no such clause. Subsidized tenancies follow their program's rules. Searched: the Illinois Compiled Statutes, the Illinois Constitution and the list of the 104th General Assembly's Public Acts. Not searched: the Administrative Code, court rules, local ordinances and case law.

title: No Statewide Late Fee Cap
bodyText: Illinois has no statewide statute that caps a late fee on a house or apartment lease, sets a grace period before one may be charged, or limits a daily late fee. The lease sets the fee, subject to the common-law rule against penalties, so the cautious course is a fee that is a reasonable estimate of what late payment costs you. Three statutes still bear on late fees: for leases the rental fee law covers, a late fee is collectible only if it is stated on the first page of the lease (the library lists it in the first-page fee box); a landlord of 100 or more units with an on-site office that keeps regular hours must accept rent there and may not charge a penalty or fee for paying that way when the payment is otherwise timely; and mobile home parks have their own grace-period rule. Some local ordinances, including Chicago's, cap late fees (not covered). Searched: the Illinois Compiled Statutes, the Illinois Constitution and the list of the 104th General Assembly's Public Acts. Not searched: the Administrative Code, court rules, local ordinances and case law.

title: Pet Deposits, Fees and Pet Rent
bodyText:
Illinois has no statute that caps or regulates pet deposits, pet fees or pet rent for house and apartment leases, with one exception: you may not charge a pet-related deposit, pet fee or other pet assessment, or require special liability insurance, for an assistance animal, even if you charge pet owners; you may charge for damage the animal causes, beyond reasonable wear and tear, as you would for any other resident.

A refundable pet deposit secures against damage, so treat it as part of the security deposit and return it under the deposit return rules (the library's pet clause says so).

For leases the rental fee law covers, pet rent or a nonrefundable pet fee is collectible only if it is stated on the first page of the lease; once a pet is approved, pet rent is a recurring non-optional fee. Mobile home parks have their own pet-fee rule (not covered). Searched: the Illinois Compiled Statutes, the Illinois Constitution and the list of the 104th General Assembly's Public Acts. Not searched: the Administrative Code, court rules, local ordinances and case law.

title: Statutory Caps on Charges
bodyText: Illinois caps very few charges in a house or apartment lease. The one dollar cap on a fee: for leases the rental fee law covers, an application fee, including background checks, may not exceed $50 (a higher actual third-party background check cost may be billed only on the law's conditions), and a list of other fees is barred outright. There is no statewide cap on rent (and no local government may control rent), on the security deposit, on late fees or on pet fees (but no pet deposit, pet fee or other pet assessment may be charged for an assistance animal; see the pet-fee row). A few statutes limit particular charges without a dollar cap: under a master-metered utility allocation formula, the total collected from the building may not exceed the utility's bill; an electric vehicle charging fee is limited to the actual cost of electricity used, a reasonable access fee (and any network fee), installation costs where you install at the tenant's request, a restoration deposit and a reasonable fee to reserve a shared parking space; and a Safe Homes Act lock-change fee may not exceed the reasonable price customarily charged for changing a lock. Other figures in the landlord-tenant statutes limit the tenant's remedies or set your liabilities rather than your charges: the repair-and-deduct remedy is limited to the lesser of $500 or half a month's rent; deposit interest applies only to properties of 25 or more units (on deposits held more than 6 months), must be paid within 30 days after each 12-month rental period once it has reached $5 (unless the tenant is in default), and must be paid in full, whatever the amount, when the tenancy ends; and statutory damages apply for violations of the deposit, retaliation, utility, Safe Homes, summary-of-rights, immigrant-tenant and EV-charging laws (each described in its own row). Local ordinances, including Chicago's, may cap fees (not covered). For a dishonored check, the law makes the writer liable for $25 or your actual collection costs, whichever is greater, rather than capping a fee, and to recover more than $25 without a lawsuit you must first send a written demand by certified mail (see the returned payments clause). Searched for figures: the residential landlord-tenant acts; the deposit, late-fee and rent-control rows record their own whole-code searches.

title: Passing Government Fees to Tenants
bodyText: Illinois has no statewide rental registration, licensing or inspection fee for houses and apartments, and no statute that allows, bars or limits passing a government fee on to a tenant. Such fees come from local ordinances. If you want a tenant to reimburse a local registration, licensing or inspection fee, the rental fee law governs it for leases it covers: the reimbursement is a non-optional fee, so it must be stated on the first page of the lease, with its amount, or the tenant is not liable for it; and calling it something else does not change that. Don't pass on a fine, a reinspection fee or a permit fee caused by your own violation. Owner-occupied buildings of 6 units or fewer are exempt from the fee law. Searched: the Illinois Compiled Statutes, the Illinois Constitution and the list of the 104th General Assembly's Public Acts. Not searched: the Administrative Code, court rules, local ordinances and case law.

title: Passing Government Fines to Tenants
bodyText:
No Illinois statute bars you from asking a house or apartment tenant to reimburse a government fine, penalty or abatement charge, and none makes a tenant liable to you for one; the lease decides.

For mobile home parks the law limits pass-throughs to fines incurred because of the tenant's actions, which is a sensible model everywhere: require reimbursement only for a fine or charge caused by a condition or violation the tenant, a household member or a guest caused or permitted, never for a condition you are responsible for, such as a building-code violation.

For leases the rental fee law covers, two further limits apply: you may not charge a pest-abatement fee where the tenant in no way contributed to the infestation, and a reimbursement the tenant must pay should also be listed among the conditional charges on the first page of the lease, since a non-optional fee not on the first page cannot be collected. The library offers an optional tenant-caused fines clause. Searched: the Illinois Compiled Statutes, the Illinois Constitution and the list of the 104th General Assembly's Public Acts. Not searched: the Administrative Code, court rules, local ordinances (which may impose nuisance or code fines on owners) and case law.

title: No Fees for Eviction Notices
bodyText: For leases the rental fee law covers, you may not charge a tenant a fee or fine for an eviction notice, or for filing an eviction action before the court grants an eviction order. That covers a fee for preparing or serving a 5-day rent demand, a 10-day notice for a lease default or a termination notice in an eviction. You may still recover court costs and filing fees, including the sheriff's or process server's statutory fees, as the court awards them in the case. No Illinois statute authorizes a charge for serving other notices, and a preset charge for a breach is risky under the common-law rule against penalties; the library offers no notice-service fee clause. Owner-occupied buildings of 6 units or fewer are exempt from the fee law, but the cautious course there too is to charge no notice fee and recover only court-awarded costs.

title: Collection Costs
bodyText:
Illinois limits what a collection agency may add to a tenant's unpaid balance. A licensed collection agency may not collect any interest, charge or fee beyond the actual debt unless the agreement that created the debt (the lease) expressly authorizes it or a law does; a contingency or hourly collection fee that the tenant pays under the lease is allowed unless it is unreasonable, and the state agency that licenses collection agencies is to decide what is reasonable, though its rules set no figure yet, so keep any percentage modest.

So if you plan to use a collection agency, the lease must say so expressly; the library's optional collection-costs clause does that.

For a bounced check, the writer owes $25 or your costs of collection, whichever is greater, and to collect more than $25 without a lawsuit you must first send a certified-mail demand (see the returned-payments clause).

For leases the rental fee law covers, a collection charge the tenant must pay should be listed among the conditional charges on the first page, and you may not charge a fee for an eviction notice or for filing an eviction before the court grants an eviction order, although court costs and filing fees remain recoverable. Attorney's fees are covered in their own row.

title: Tampering With Smoke and CO Alarms
bodyText:
Illinois makes tampering with a smoke detector or carbon monoxide alarm a crime: tampering with, removing, destroying or disconnecting an installed detector or alarm, or removing its batteries, except during inspection, maintenance or replacement, is a Class A misdemeanor on a first conviction and a Class 4 felony after that.

No Illinois statute sets, allows or bars a lease fee for tampering. For leases the rental fee law covers, a tampering charge is not one of the barred fees, but it is collectible only if it is listed on the first page of the lease.

A flat fee unrelated to your cost risks being treated as an unenforceable penalty, so the library does not offer one: recover the actual, documented cost of repairing, replacing or reinstalling a detector the tenant disabled, and use the optional detector-care clause alongside the required smoke and carbon monoxide alarm clause, which sets the tenant's statutory testing, battery and written-notice duties. Never leave a disabled detector unrepaired. Searched: the Illinois Compiled Statutes, the Illinois Constitution and the list of the 104th General Assembly's Public Acts. Not searched: the Administrative Code (including State Fire Marshal rules), court rules, local ordinances and case law.

title: Carpet Cleaning at Move-Out
bodyText:
Illinois has no statute on carpet cleaning at move-out. Two rules decide what you may do.

First, you may keep part of the security deposit for damage, but only damage beyond normal wear and tear, with the itemized statement and receipts; and if the written lease states a dollar cost for cleaning, repairing or replacing a component such as carpet, you may withhold that amount for damage beyond normal wear and tear if it is a reasonable cost of restoring the property to its condition when the lease began (the library's optional cost-schedule clause).

Second, for leases the rental fee law covers, you may not charge a fee for the routine maintenance and upkeep of the unit, and renaming a fee does not avoid the ban, so a flat move-out carpet-cleaning fee charged whatever the carpet's condition is risky.

The cautious course: don't require professional carpet cleaning in every case; charge for carpet cleaning or replacement only where the carpet is soiled or damaged beyond normal wear and tear, either at actual cost with receipts or at a reasonable amount stated in the lease's cost schedule. Searched: the Illinois Compiled Statutes, the Illinois Constitution and the list of the 104th General Assembly's Public Acts. Not searched: the Administrative Code, court rules, local ordinances and case law.

title: Who Collects Rent Keeps the Duties
bodyText: Some states provide that whoever receives the rent keeps the landlord's duty to maintain the property, whatever a lease, assignment, deed or mortgage says. Illinois has no general statute like that, and no statutory habitability duty for it to protect (see the habitability row). Three Illinois rules point the same way in particular cases: a court-appointed receiver of a building that violates local building codes may use the rents for maintenance, repair and rehabilitation despite any assignment of rents; a receiver appointed in a mortgage foreclosure may collect the rents, but that does not affect a residential tenant's legal rights about safety and habitability; and when a landlord's unpaid utility bill puts tenants' service at risk, a court may appoint a receiver to collect the rents and pay the utility. The cautious course: assume the duty to keep the home fit and to make repairs stays with whoever acts as landlord and collects the rent, so that assigning rents to a lender, or having a manager or master tenant collect them, does not let anyone collect rent free of those duties; make any management agreement require the manager to handle repairs, and tell the tenant in the lease whom to contact for repairs. Searched: the Illinois Compiled Statutes, the Illinois Constitution and the list of the 104th General Assembly's Public Acts, including general property and obligations law with no landlord or tenant words. Not searched: the Administrative Code, court rules, local ordinances and case law (including the implied warranty of habitability).

title: No Lockouts for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: No. Illinois law gives a landlord of a house or apartment no right to lock out a tenant who is behind on rent, even with advance notice, an opt-in lease clause or keys available on request. Illinois forbids entering land or buildings except where the law allows, and then only peaceably, not by force; a person put out of possession by a forcible entry may sue to be restored. The lawful route for unpaid rent is the written 5-day demand and, if the rent is not paid, an eviction case in court; only a court order, enforced by the sheriff, removes a tenant. Don't put a lockout clause in the lease, and never change the locks, remove doors or belongings, or cut off utilities to force a tenant out (see the self-help eviction row). Lock changes in Illinois law are a tenant's right under the Safe Homes Act, not a landlord's remedy, and self-storage lockouts under the storage lien law do not apply to dwellings. Chicago's ordinance has its own lockout rules (not covered). Searched: the Illinois Compiled Statutes, the Illinois Constitution and the list of the 104th General Assembly's Public Acts. Not searched: the Administrative Code, court rules, local ordinances and case law.

title: Utility Deposits
bodyText: Utility deposits on a residential gas, electric or water account are mainly between the utility and its customer. If the account is in the tenant's name, the utility takes and refunds any deposit under the Illinois Commerce Commission's rules: a residential deposit may not exceed one-sixth of the estimated annual charges, it earns interest, and the utility must refund it with interest after 12 months of on-time service (fewer than four late payments, no disconnection for nonpayment) or when the customer ends service, generally within 30 days. If you have a written arrangement with the utility to put service in your name between tenants, the utility may not bill you for an amount a tenant owes. Illinois statutes add these points: an electric or gas utility may not require a deposit from a low-income residential customer or applicant for standard service unless it has proof of tampering in the past 5 years; a utility must defer its initial credit and deposit requirements for 60 days for a residential customer who is a victim of domestic violence; during the winter shutoff period a residential customer may pay a required deposit in installments; and when a landlord fails to pay a landlord-paid utility, a tenant may have the bill put in the tenant's own name by meeting the utility's credit rules or paying a deposit under the Commission's rules. No Illinois statute governs a utility deposit that you collect yourself. If you take money to secure utility charges the tenant owes you under the lease, treat it as part of the security deposit: state it in the lease, and return any balance, with an itemized statement for any deduction, under the deposit return rules. Searched: the Illinois Compiled Statutes, the Illinois Constitution and the list of the 104th General Assembly's Public Acts. The Commission's deposit and landlord-arrangement rules were read; not searched: the rest of the Administrative Code, court rules, local ordinances and case law.

title: Late Fees for Subsidized Tenants
bodyText: Illinois statutes set no special late-fee rule for subsidized tenants; federal HUD rules do. Housing Choice Voucher: the family is not responsible for the part of the rent the housing authority's assistance payment covers, the authority's failure to pay is not a lease violation, and you may not end the tenancy for the authority's nonpayment. You may not demand or accept more from the tenant than the tenant's share. If you want the housing authority to pay a penalty when its payment is late, the payment contract provides one only where you charge the same late penalty to assisted and unassisted tenants and charge it against the tenant for late payment of the tenant's own share. HUD's tenancy addendum is added word for word to your lease and controls over anything else in it, and any lease change must be in writing with a copy to the housing authority. Public housing: the housing authority's lease may provide for late-payment penalties, but they are not due until two weeks after written notice. Cautious course for a voucher tenancy: charge a late fee only on the tenant's own share, only as your written lease provides, never because the housing authority paid late, and on the same terms you use for other tenants, because the Human Rights Act makes it a civil rights violation to alter the terms of a rental because of a tenant's source of income. The general late-fee rules (no statewide cap; collectible only if on the first page of the lease, for leases the rental fee law covers) also apply.

title: Security Deposits After a Domestic or Sexual Violence Move-Out
bodyText: Illinois has no special rule on when you must account for or return a security deposit after a tenant leaves because of domestic or sexual violence. The Safe Homes Act lets such a tenant, in the cases it describes, avoid liability for rent for the period after moving out, and no lease or separate agreement may waive or change that right, but the Act says nothing about the deposit. The ordinary Security Deposit Return Act rules apply: if you keep anything for damage, give the itemized statement with receipts within 30 days after the tenant vacates or the tenant's right of possession ends, whichever is later; otherwise return the whole deposit within 45 days after the tenant vacates. No statute says whether that clock starts when one co-tenant leaves while others stay, or waits until everyone has moved out. Cautious course: when one tenant leaves under the Safe Homes Act and others remain, agree in writing with the departing tenant and the remaining tenants how and when the departing tenant's share of the deposit will be handled, without asking anyone to give up a Safe Homes Act right; don't apply the deposit to rent for the period after the tenant left where the Act's defense may apply; and don't tell a prospective landlord that the tenant used the Act. Two related rules bind others, not you: a utility must defer its own initial credit and deposit requirements for 60 days for a qualifying victim of domestic violence, and the State's crime victims compensation program can pay the security deposit on the home a victim relocates to. Federal rules for federally assisted housing are not covered here.

title: Eviction Protection for Victims of Domestic or Sexual Violence
bodyText: In any Illinois eviction case, it is a defense if the court finds that your demand for possession is based solely on a tenant's or household member's status as a victim of domestic violence, sexual violence, dating violence or stalking; solely on an incident of actual or threatened violence of that kind against a tenant or household member; or solely on criminal activity directly relating to that violence committed against them by a household member, a guest or another person under their control. It is also a defense to an eviction for letting a barred person onto the property if the victim didn't knowingly consent to the person's entry or a valid court order allowed it. A tenant raising the defense must provide at least one of these: medical, court or police records documenting the violence, or a statement from an employee of a victim service organization or a medical professional the tenant or household member sought services from. The defense doesn't stop you from seeking possession only against the tenant or household member who committed the violence; against the whole household, victim included, if the victim's continued tenancy would pose an actual and imminent threat to other tenants, household members, you or your agents at the property; or against a victim who committed the criminal activity your demand rests on. It applies to every eviction under the eviction statute, including one after you void a lease for criminal activity on the premises. Related rules: the Human Rights Act bars discrimination in renting because a person is protected by an order of protection, a civil no contact order or a stalking no contact order (including an out-of-state order); no city or county may penalize a tenant or landlord, including by requiring the lease to be ended or not renewed, because of a domestic or sexual violence police call, incident or related crime, though the perpetrator may still be evicted; and a tenant who leaves under the Safe Homes Act may avoid rent for the period after leaving, a right no lease can waive. Rent owed before the tenant gave notice and left stays owed. Federal rules for federally assisted housing, and local ordinances such as Chicago's and Cook County's, may add more and are not covered here.

title: Protection-Order Citations in Illinois Tenant Law
bodyText: Illinois tenant protections for victims of domestic and sexual violence refer to the protection-order laws in several places, and one of those references is out of date. The Safe Homes Act lock-change section, for a threat from a person who is also on the lease, accepts a plenary order of protection under the Illinois Domestic Violence Act of 1986 or under a section of the Code of Criminal Procedure that was repealed effective January 1, 2018. Protective orders entered in criminal cases now come under a rewritten part of that Code, which calls them domestic violence orders of protection, civil no contact orders and stalking no contact orders, and calls the order entered after a hearing a final order rather than a plenary order. Cautious course: if a tenant asking for a lock change gives you a final domestic violence order of protection from a criminal case that grants the tenant exclusive possession of the home, treat it as the order the Safe Homes Act describes and change the locks (or allow the change) within 48 hours; don't refuse because the order's name or section number doesn't match the statute. The other references are current: the Safe Homes Act and the summary-of-rights law define domestic violence by the Domestic Violence Act's definitions section, which is in force; the plenary order sections of the Domestic Violence Act and the Civil No Contact Order Act are in force; and the eviction defense's barred-person rule points to an order-of-protection definition and an exclusive-possession remedy that both still exist in the criminal-case protective-order law, though the definition now sits in a renumbered paragraph. The Human Rights Act protects people protected by an order under the Domestic Violence Act, the criminal-case protective-order law, the Stalking No Contact Order Act, the Civil No Contact Order Act or another state's law. None of the library's other Illinois rows relies on the repealed section.

title: Documents That Support Domestic or Sexual Violence Protections
bodyText: Illinois has three tenant protections for victims of domestic or sexual violence, and each has its own document rule; they are not the same. (1) Leaving and stopping rent (Safe Homes Act): where a tenant or household member was under a credible imminent threat of domestic or sexual violence at the property, the statute requires only a written notice of that reason, given before or within 3 days after leaving; no document is listed, and a court decides whether the threat was real. Where a tenant or household member was a victim of sexual violence on property you own or control, the written notice (also within 3 days of leaving) must state the reason and the date of the violence and say the tenant gave you at least one of: medical, court or police evidence of the sexual violence, or a statement from an employee of a victim services or rape crisis organization the tenant or household member sought services from; and the violence must have happened no more than 60 days before the notice, unless hospitalization, shelter or counseling made earlier notice impossible. (2) Lock changes (Safe Homes Act): if the threat comes from someone not on the lease, the request must come with at least one of: medical, court or police evidence of domestic or sexual violence, or a statement from an employee of a victim services, domestic violence or rape crisis organization; if the threat comes from someone on the lease, or the lease is oral, the request must come with a plenary order of protection or plenary civil no contact order granting the tenant exclusive possession (a final order of protection entered in a criminal case should be treated the same way). No time limit applies. (3) Eviction defense: the tenant must provide at least one of: medical, court or police records documenting the violence, or a statement from an employee of a victim service organization or from a medical professional the tenant or household member sought services from; no time limit applies. Handing you this evidence does not waive the victim's privilege with the third party, and you may not pass it, or the fact that the tenant used the Safe Homes Act, to a prospective landlord without written consent unless the law requires it. Don't demand more than the statute lists. Utilities use their own list (an order of protection, or a letter on letterhead from treating medical personnel, law enforcement, a prosecutor, the Attorney General or a shelter), which doesn't govern your lease.

title: Screening Rental Applicants
bodyText: Illinois regulates tenant screening mainly through the Human Rights Act and the rental-fee law. Records you may not use: an arrest that did not lead to a conviction, a juvenile record, and any criminal record a court ordered expunged, sealed or impounded all count as an arrest record, and refusing to rent, changing terms, or asking about them in an application or inquiry is a civil rights violation unless State or federal law authorizes the inquiry or use. You may still screen for convictions that are not sealed or expunged, but any criterion (criminal history, income, credit) that has a discriminatory effect on a protected group, including people with a lawful source of income such as a housing voucher, is unlawful unless it is necessary to a substantial, legitimate, nondiscriminatory interest that a less discriminatory practice couldn't serve. You may forbid tenants, household members and guests from engaging in unlawful activity on the property. Fees: an application fee, including background checks, may not exceed $50 (with a narrow exception for a third-party background check that costs more), and you may not charge a second fee duplicating screening costs. If an applicant gives you a qualifying reusable screening report prepared within the last 30 days and free for you to use, you may not charge a screening fee or a fee to access it. A certificate of good conduct from a court relieves an applicant of State housing bars but does not limit your access to background information or your full discretion to accept or deny the application; the related liability shield protects only employers. No Illinois statute requires private landlords to wait until a conditional offer before checking criminal history, sets a look-back period, limits income tests to the tenant's share of the rent, shields you from negligent-leasing claims for renting to someone with a record, or requires a notice on applications about sealed records; public housing authorities follow their own stricter statutory rules. Local ordinances, such as Cook County's, may add more, and the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act governs adverse-action notices and the use of consumer reports.

title: Background Checks on Your Building Employees
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires you to run background checks on maintenance staff, resident managers or other employees who work in your rental buildings or hold keys to tenants' units. A maintenance employee of a property management company who services, installs, repairs or opens locks for tenants in a multi-family building doesn't need a locksmith license, and an owner's regular employees and on-site resident managers who lease units of that property don't need a real estate leasing license, so neither group passes a State licensing background review. People who lease units for others as a business must hold a residential leasing agent or broker license, and the State weighs their criminal history when licensing them. If you do screen employees, Illinois employment law limits how: an employer with 15 or more employees may not ask about or consider criminal history until the applicant has been found qualified and chosen for an interview (or, with no interview, until a conditional offer), unless a law requires excluding certain convictions or a fidelity bond is needed; no employer may use an arrest that did not lead to a conviction, a juvenile record or a sealed or expunged record, or ask whether records were sealed or expunged; and you may act on a conviction only if it is substantially related to the job or hiring would pose an unreasonable risk to property or to people's safety, after weighing listed factors, sending a written preliminary notice with the reasons and the report, and giving the applicant at least 5 business days to respond. An employer is not liable for an employee's acts just because the employee holds a court certificate of good conduct or relief from disabilities, except for a willful or wanton hiring decision. Federal rules on employment background reports, and local ordinances, may add more.

title: Tenant Records and Data Security
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires a residential landlord to keep a rent ledger, to give a tenant a payment history on request, to include a ledger with a notice for unpaid rent, or to keep tenant files for a set time. The rules that do reach your records are general business laws. Personal information: if you hold applicants' or tenants' names together with Social Security numbers, driver's license or State ID numbers, bank or card account numbers, medical or health insurance information, or biometric data, you must use reasonable security measures to protect those records; any contract under which you share them (for example with a screening company or property manager) must require the recipient to do the same; if the data is breached you must notify the affected residents as quickly as possible and without unreasonable delay, and the Attorney General as well if more than 500 Illinois residents are affected; and when you throw records away you must shred, burn, redact or erase them so they can't be read. A violation is an unlawful practice under the Consumer Fraud Act, and no lease waiver is valid. Social Security numbers: don't post or display them publicly, don't require tenants to send them over an unsecured internet connection, and don't print them on mailings other than applications and similar forms. Biometrics: if you use fingerprint, hand or face scanning for building entry or anything else, you must first tell the person in writing what is collected, why and for how long, get a written release, publish a retention and destruction policy (destroying the data when its purpose is met or within 3 years of the person's last interaction with you, whichever is first), never sell it, and protect it at least as well as other sensitive information; each violation can cost $1,000, or $5,000 if intentional or reckless, plus attorney's fees. Some records carry their own confidentiality rules: what a tenant gives you under the Safe Homes Act, and information about immigration status. Federal rules on disposing of consumer reports may apply instead of the Illinois disposal rule.

title: Keeping Tenant Information Confidential
bodyText: Illinois has no general statute barring a landlord from sharing what it knows about a tenant, and none sets a general consent rule. Several specific statutes do limit disclosure. Safe Homes Act: you may not tell a prospective landlord that a tenant or household member used the Act's rights (leaving because of domestic or sexual violence, or a lock change), or pass on any information they gave you in doing so, unless the law requires it or it is in a court case under the Act; the victim (or the victim's parent or guardian) may consent in writing. A violation can cost actual damages up to $2,000 plus the tenant's attorney's fees. Immigration status: unless a law or court order requires it, you may not disclose or threaten to disclose information about a tenant's immigration or citizenship status to anyone, including immigration or police authorities, to harass or intimidate the tenant, to retaliate for the tenant's exercise of rights, or to pressure the tenant to move out; the tenant can recover actual damages, a civil penalty up to $2,000 per violation and attorney's fees, and no waiver is valid. Threatening to disclose anyone's immigration status to keep them from testifying is a crime. Data: personal information such as Social Security, driver's license and account numbers must be protected with reasonable security, and any contract sharing it must require the recipient to protect it too; Social Security numbers may not be posted or displayed publicly; and biometric data (fingerprint or face scans) may not be disclosed without the person's consent or a legal requirement, warrant or subpoena. Cautious course: share tenant information only with the tenant's written consent, as the law requires, or with your own agents who need it, and never give a reference that mentions domestic violence, a protection order or immigration status.

title: Reporting Rent Payments to Credit Bureaus
bodyText: Illinois has no rent-reporting statute. No Illinois law creates a State rent-reporting program, requires you to offer tenants positive rent reporting, bars you from requiring it, or requires you to notify a tenant before reporting late rent to a credit bureau. If you report, federal credit-reporting law governs what you furnish. Three Illinois rules touch the subject. First, if a lease has a cosigner, a separate statute bars reporting adverse information about a cosigner of an obligation to a credit bureau, sending it to a collection agency or taking other collection action until you have mailed the cosigner a first-class notice that the primary obligor is delinquent, that the cosigner is responsible, and that the cosigner has 15 days to pay or make arrangements; if the cosigner does, nothing adverse may be reported. The statute speaks of a loan, and no statute says whether a lease cosigner or guarantor is covered, so the cautious course is to send that notice before reporting or referring a cosigner. Second, any fee you charge for a rent-reporting service that tenants must take is a non-optional fee that must appear on the first page of the lease, or the tenant doesn't owe it.
