Third, once a lease has begun and the tenant has moved in, it is a defense to an eviction if your demand rests even in part on the tenant's failure to give a Social Security number or the information needed to get a credit report.

title: Rent-Setting Software and Algorithms
bodyText: No Illinois statute bans or regulates setting rents with algorithmic pricing software, revenue-management tools or services that pool competing landlords' data. The general Illinois Antitrust Act still applies: it is a violation for competitors to agree, or combine or conspire, to fix, control or maintain the price or rate they charge, or otherwise to unreasonably restrain trade, and the Act defines a commodity as any kind of real or personal property. Whether using a shared pricing service that relies on competitors' nonpublic rent and occupancy data amounts to such an agreement is decided case by case under that Act and federal antitrust law; this library has not reviewed the cases. Cautious course: set your rents yourself; don't share nonpublic rent, occupancy or lease-term data with competing landlords or with a vendor that pools it for them; don't agree to follow a vendor's recommended rents automatically; and keep records of how you set each rent. Local ordinances may add rules.

title: Children in Rental Housing
bodyText: Illinois doesn't require a lease to say anything about children who will live in the home, and it has no landlord-tenant statute of its own on a child who is born or moves in during the tenancy. The Human Rights Act does the work. Familial status (a person under 18 living with a parent, legal custodian or their written designee, and anyone pregnant or in the process of getting legal custody of a child) is protected: you may not refuse to rent, change the terms or privileges of the tenancy, refuse to negotiate, misstate availability, or use criteria with a discriminatory effect because of it, and you may not use an application, advertisement, notice or inquiry that shows a preference against families with children. That covers ending, refusing to renew or changing a tenancy because a tenant has a baby or a child joins the household. Exemptions: a building of 4 or fewer units where you live in one, rooms in your own home, housing for older persons (for familial status only), and a child sex offender who owns and lives in the building may refuse to rent another unit in it to a parent or guardian of a minor; the first two never excuse discriminatory advertising or inquiries. Occupancy limits: only reasonable local, State or federal limits on the number of occupants are exempt, so a stricter limit you set yourself that keeps out families is exposed. A minor may not be named as a defendant in an eviction. Listing every occupant in the lease is lawful as long as you apply the rule to everyone and don't use it to exclude children. Local ordinances may add more.

title: Incentives for Renting to Veterans
bodyText: No Illinois statute offers landlords vacancy payments, damage reimbursement, tax credits or other incentives for renting to veterans (for example to veterans holding federal HUD-VASH vouchers), and none requires or regulates a veterans' rent discount or preference in private housing. The Illinois veteran tax credits are for employers who hire veterans, not for landlords. What Illinois law does say: military status (active duty, veteran status, reserve or National Guard service) and an unfavorable military discharge are protected classes under the Human Rights Act, so you may not refuse to rent, set different terms, or advertise or inquire in a way that shows a preference against applicants because of them; and a housing voucher is a protected source of income. A preference in favor of veterans isn't addressed by any Illinois statute; apply any such program consistently and make sure it doesn't have a discriminatory effect on another protected group. Federal and local programs may offer incentives; check with the local housing authority or veterans' service office.

title: Religious and Cultural Displays
bodyText: No Illinois statute gives a tenant a right to display religious or cultural items (for example a mezuzah on the doorpost, a wreath or a holiday decoration) that a lease may not restrict, and none limits a landlord's own display rules. One statute reaches condominiums: a condominium association's rules may not impair the free exercise of religion and may not prohibit any reasonable accommodation for religious practices, including attaching religiously mandated objects to the front-door area of a unit. If you rent out a condominium unit, your tenant lives under those association rules, so the association can't bar such an object, and a lease rule of yours that does is risky. Two broader rules shape any display limit you set. The Human Rights Act bars altering the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental because of religion or national origin, and the Illinois Constitution gives everyone the right to be free from discrimination based on creed or national ancestry in the rental of property; a rule that allows some displays but not those of a particular faith or culture, or is enforced that way, is exposed. Cautious course: if you limit displays (for safety, fire code or damage reasons), write a neutral rule about size, placement and attachment method, apply it the same way to every faith and culture, and grant reasonable requests for small door-area religious objects. Local ordinances may add more.

title: Political Canvassing in Your Buildings
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires you to let political candidates, campaign workers, petition circulators or voter-registration workers into an apartment building or other multi-unit property to reach tenants' doors, and none requires you to set aside space for campaign literature. The free speech and assembly guarantees of the Illinois Constitution limit government, not private landlords, so access by outsiders is your decision, subject to your tenants' right to invite their own guests. In a condominium, association rules may not impair speech rights under the First Amendment or the Illinois Constitution. Two related rules: in cities and counties with a board of election commissioners, owners and managers of hotels, lodging houses, rooming houses and furnished apartments housing 4 or more people outside the owner's family must file a sworn report of the lodgers claiming a voting residence there 28 to 30 days before each election; and retail electricity sellers must get consent before entering multi-unit residential buildings to solicit. Cautious course: if you adopt a no-soliciting or access rule, apply it the same way to every campaign, cause and religion, and don't restrict tenants' own political signs or activity in a way that singles out a protected group or punishes a tenant for organizing or complaining. Local ordinances may add rules.

title: Tenant Unions and Associations
bodyText: Illinois protects tenant organizing mainly through the Landlord Retaliation Act. You may not knowingly end a tenancy, raise rent, cut services, sue or threaten to sue for possession, or refuse to renew because a tenant in good faith organized or joined a tenants' union or similar organization, or complained to or sought help from a community organization about code violations or illegal landlord practices. If the protected activity happened within a year before your action, the law presumes retaliation unless you prove a legitimate, non-retaliatory reason or that your action began first; a tenant who proves retaliation can end the lease, get back the deposit, interest and prepaid rent, recover possession, and recover the greater of 2 months' rent or twice the damages, plus attorney's fees. No Illinois statute gives tenants of private housing an affirmative right to meet in common areas, distribute literature, or have you recognize or bargain with their association. Tenant associations do have statutory rights in assisted housing: before selling, prepaying or ending the subsidy on federally assisted or tax-credit housing, the owner must give tenants 12 months' notice, and a tenant association representing a majority of the tenants that forms within 60 days must receive a bona fide offer to buy; a violating owner owes each tenant a $500 civil penalty plus attorney's fees. A similar first right to purchase applies when an owner prepays certain Illinois Housing Development Authority mortgage loans. Housing authority boards include residents chosen from lists presented by official tenants' associations. The Human Rights Act also bars coercing, intimidating or interfering with anyone who helps others exercise fair housing rights. Cautious course: treat a tenant group's meetings, flyers and complaints as protected, apply any rule on common-area use neutrally, and document the legitimate reason for any action you take against an organizing tenant. Local ordinances, such as Chicago's, may add more.

title: Tenants' Guests and Visitors
bodyText:
No Illinois statute gives tenants a statutory right to receive guests, visitors or suppliers, bars a guest fee, or makes any guest right non-waivable, in any size of building. Guest stays are a matter for the lease; a reasonable written guest policy and a limit on how long a guest may stay before becoming an occupant are lawful.

Illinois law gives you two tools and sets two limits. Tools: you may bar a person who isn't a tenant or household member by written notice to the tenant saying the person is no longer allowed on the property and that inviting them back may be treated as a lease breach, whether or not the lease says so; and you may forbid tenants, household members and guests from engaging in unlawful activity on the property. Nothing in the cannabis law requires you to let a guest use cannabis on your property.

Limits: it is a defense to an eviction for letting a barred person in if the tenant or household member who was a victim of domestic violence, sexual violence, stalking or dating violence did not knowingly consent to the entry, or a valid court order allowed it; and the Human Rights Act may require a reasonable accommodation in guest rules for a tenant with a disability, for example a live-in or visiting caregiver.

A guest fee or guest-parking charge that every tenant must pay is a non-optional fee that must appear on the first page of the lease. In a condominium, the association may enforce its rules against a unit owner's tenants, invitees and guests.

Cautious course: don't bar ordinary visits or charge a fee merely for having a guest, apply guest limits evenly, and use the written barring notice for a specific person who causes problems.

title: Working With Police: Criminal Activity and Crime-Free Terms
bodyText: Illinois has no statute that creates, requires or regulates a crime-free lease addendum as such, requires you to let police into a tenant's unit, or makes you report crimes on your property. Its criminal-activity rules work through the lease and the eviction statute instead. A written lease must tell the tenant that if any lessee or occupant uses or permits the use of the premises for a felony or Class A misdemeanor, you may void the lease and recover the premises (the right exists even if the lease leaves this out). You may then file an eviction yourself or, if the State's Attorney or corporation counsel agrees, assign them the right to file on a form they prepare, while you stay liable for the costs; an eviction order in such a case may be stayed no more than 7 days unless everyone agrees. Separate rules cover drug activity (the lease is voidable at your option, with a 5-day posted notice) and Class X felony charges (only if you and the tenant signed the federal drug-free housing addendum). There is also an emergency eviction procedure for serious violent or drug crimes. Limits: no city or county may penalize you or a tenant, or force a lease to end, because of police calls made to prevent or respond to domestic or sexual violence or by or for a person with a disability, or because of domestic or sexual violence against a tenant, household member or guest; and it is a defense to an eviction that your demand rests solely on a tenant's status as a victim of domestic violence, sexual violence, dating violence or stalking, or on violence against them. You may bar a non-tenant from the property by written notice. Cautious course: use the required criminal-activity notice, don't add penalties for calling the police, and base any action on the criminal conduct itself, not on the number of police calls. Local ordinances may add more.

title: Registered Sex Offenders and Your Rental
bodyText: Illinois doesn't require you to tell applicants or tenants that a registered sex offender lives in the building or nearby, and no statute requires a sex offender registry notice in a lease. The State Police keep a public Statewide Sex Offender Database online, searchable by map for registered sex offenders within 5 miles of an address, and local police departments and sheriffs must let anyone inspect registrants' information. Anyone who provides or fails to provide information under the community notification law is immune from civil and criminal liability, and the immunity covers passing on information legally obtained under it. Special rules apply if you are a child sex offender who owns and lives in the building: it is a Class 4 felony to knowingly rent another unit in that building to a parent or guardian of a child under 18 (for leases or other rental arrangements entered into after January 1, 2009); refusing to rent to such a person doesn't violate the Human Rights Act; and a tenant who didn't tell you they were a parent or guardian may not end the lease on later learning your status. A tenant who is a child sex offender may not knowingly live within 500 feet of a school, playground, child care facility or program for children, or the victim (with exceptions for homes the offender owned before set dates); that duty is the offender's, not yours. A conviction is not a protected class under the Human Rights Act, but an arrest without conviction, a juvenile record and a sealed or expunged record are. Cautious course: if you mention the registry, do it the same way for every applicant (for example a neutral sentence pointing to the State Police database), and base any screening decision on an actual conviction applied consistently, not on an arrest or a sealed record.

title: Staff in 55-and-Older Rental Housing
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires a work card, license or background check for staff of ordinary 55-and-older or 62-and-older rental housing, or of any other ordinary rental housing. The State's mandatory background checks for workers apply to health care employers, which include assisted living and shared housing establishments, supportive living programs, nursing homes, home health agencies and similar licensed providers, not to an apartment community that simply limits occupancy by age. If you add licensed care or services, check whether the Health Care Worker Background Check Act then covers your staff. What Illinois does require of 55-and-older rental housing is heating and cooling: where the building has a system serving the units, cooling must run from June 1 to September 30 when the heat index exceeds 80 degrees, and heat must reach at least 68 degrees from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. and 62 degrees overnight from October 1 to May 31 when it is below 55 degrees outside; without a building-wide cooling system you must provide a cooled common gathering space if you have one. To keep the familial-status exemption for housing for older persons, the housing must qualify (for example, intended for and solely occupied by people 62 or older, or operated for people 55 or older with at least 80% of occupied units having someone 55 or older and published age policies). If you do screen employees, Illinois employment law limits how.

title: Penalties for Refusing a Service or Assistance Animal
bodyText: No Illinois statute makes it a crime for a landlord to refuse a tenant's assistance or service animal in a home; in housing, refusal is a civil rights violation under the Human Rights Act, which also bars refusing to rent, setting different terms, or adding an extra lease charge (other than for actual damage) because a person has a guide, hearing or support dog, and the Assistance Animal Integrity Act bars pet deposits, pet fees and special insurance for an assistance animal. Two criminal statutes protect access to public places and may reach parts of a rental property. The White Cane Law gives people who are blind, have a visual or hearing disability, epilepsy or another physical disability, and trainers, the right to be accompanied by a guide, support, hearing or seizure dog without an extra charge in hotels, lodging places, places of public accommodation and other places to which the general public is invited; denying or interfering with that right is a Class A misdemeanor. Separately, knowingly denying a person with a disability and a service animal (a dog or miniature horse) entry to a public place of accommodation is a Class C misdemeanor; that definition includes hotels and other places of lodging (except an owner-occupied building of 5 or fewer rental units) and rental establishments. No statute says whether these reach a private apartment, a building's common halls or a leasing office, and the library has not reviewed the cases. Cautious course: never turn away a person with a service animal from a leasing office, model unit, open house or any area open to the public, and handle a resident's animal request through the reasonable-accommodation process. No Illinois guide-dog statute separately requires you to waive lease restrictions under threat of a criminal penalty.

title: Tenant Animals Left Without Care
bodyText:
No Illinois statute lets you enter a rental to feed, care for or remove a tenant's animal when the tenant is away, hospitalized, detained or has died, and Illinois has no general landlord-entry statute. Entering a residence without authority is criminal trespass, so plan ahead in the lease: the optional animal-care clause has the tenant list every animal and name a caregiver whom you may let in for that purpose if the tenant can't care for the animal, with animal control, the police, a humane society or a shelter as the fallback.

The animal-welfare law puts the duties on the owner, meaning anyone who owns, keeps, harbors or has custody of the animal: provide enough wholesome food and water, adequate shelter, needed veterinary care and humane treatment, and never abandon an animal where it may become a public charge or suffer injury, hunger or exposure.

Public officers act through that law: on a complaint, a State Department of Agriculture investigator, police or an approved humane investigator may investigate, and county animal control wardens may investigate neglect and cruelty of companion animals, but none may enter a building that is a person's residence except with a search warrant or court order; animals can be impounded, including in an emergency.

If you or a caregiver give emergency care without charge to an injured animal or one separated from its owner by an emergency or disaster, you are not liable for civil damages except for willful or wanton misconduct.

Cautious course: use the optional clause, call animal control or the police if an animal inside a unit appears to be in distress and no caregiver can be reached, and don't enter on your own without the tenant's consent.

title: Pet Information Sheets
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires a landlord to give tenants a government fact sheet about pets and eviction, or any pet-related information sheet, whether or not you know the tenant has a dog or cat, and Illinois's eviction statute has no rule on what happens to a tenant's pets when an eviction order is carried out. The handouts Illinois does require with a lease are different: the Department of Human Rights summary of rights for survivors of domestic and sexual violence, attached as the lease's first pages, and, for housing built before 1978, the Department of Public Health lead information brochure (in addition to the federal lead pamphlet). If a tenant leaves an animal behind, the animal-welfare law's duties fall on whoever owns or keeps it, and animal control or the police can step in (see the animal-care row). One pet rule applies to some affordable housing: in multifamily units of 500 square feet or more acquired, built or rehabilitated with Illinois Affordable Housing Trust Fund money after January 1, 2022 and designated for low- and very low-income families, the tenant must be allowed at least 2 cats or one dog under 50 pounds (not counting service animals, and not for elderly housing or supportive living), subject to reasonable pet rules on noise, sanitation, registration, restraint in common areas, waste removal and vaccination. What to do: nothing is required for pets; put your pet rules, any pet deposit and pet rent (on the lease's first page), and the optional animal-care clause in the lease so the tenant has them in writing.

title: Government Inspections of Rentals
bodyText:
Illinois has no statewide rental inspection, rental licensing or certificate program for houses and apartments, and no statute lets a lease authorize a government inspector to enter so that the tenant must let the inspector in.

Inspections come from the inspector's own authority. Fire officials may inspect premises at reasonable hours and order fire hazards corrected (in a home rule city with its own fire code, under that local code). When a child or other occupant has an elevated blood lead level, the Department of Public Health or its local delegate inspects the home after showing credentials, and if the occupant refuses, it may get a search warrant. Inspectors checking for fake smoke detectors, sprinkler heads and similar devices may not inspect inside a living unit.

Cities and counties, especially home rule units such as Chicago, may run their own rental inspection or licensing programs; check local law.

Two Illinois rules make access matter to you: in a city that uses an administrative code hearing, it is a defense that the occupant refused you entry to correct the violation; and in subsidized housing, a lease can make repeated refusal of an inspection a ground for an emergency eviction (see the subsidized-housing inspection clause).

Cautious course: a lease clause can ask the tenant to cooperate with an inspection and to tell you promptly about an inspector's request, but it should not claim to be the tenant's consent to a government entry, and it must never discourage the tenant from asking for an inspection; a tenant's good-faith complaint to a government body is protected from retaliation.

title: Health Department Rules for Rentals
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires a landlord to give tenants a copy of county health department or public health district rules on request, or to refer tenants to a health authority. County boards of health and public health districts enforce state health laws and local ordinances and make sanitary inspections, and local governments may adopt housing and health codes that reach rentals; check the rules where your property is. One state rule limits health regulators for rentals: outside Chicago, no state or local health authority may regulate food that tenants prepare in a shared kitchen of a private, leased residential building for themselves and their guests. Separately, when a lead hazard is found, the state's lead law has its own notices for tenants (see the Illinois lead rows).

title: Renting a House in a Single-Family Zone
bodyText: No Illinois statute limits renting a house in a single-family zone, requires the owner to live on the lot, or sets owner-occupancy, short-term-letting or tenant-history conditions for a lot split or a two-unit conversion. Zoning is local: cities and villages zone under state enabling law, which lets them classify and restrict the use of property on the basis of family relationship, and home rule units have broad powers of their own. A local ordinance may therefore regulate who may live in a single-family home or whether it may be rented, short-term or long-term, and some owner-occupancy conditions appear in property-tax programs, which affect the owner's tax bill, not the right to rent. Check your city's or county's zoning code before renting a house, a room or part of a house.

title: Accessory Dwelling Units
bodyText: Illinois has no state accessory dwelling unit law: no statute makes a coach house, basement apartment, in-law unit or backyard home a use that cities must allow, bars owner-occupancy requirements, or sets a minimum rental term for such a unit. Whether you may build, convert or rent an accessory unit, and on what conditions (owner occupancy, parking, size, short-term rental limits), is decided by local zoning and building codes, including home rule ordinances; check them before you rent one. A rented accessory unit is a dwelling like any other: the Illinois landlord-tenant statutes, the smoke and carbon monoxide alarm rules and the lead rules for pre-1978 housing apply to it.

title: Good-Cause Eviction Notice
bodyText: Illinois has no statewide good-cause or just-cause eviction law for private rentals, so there is no good-cause notice to put in or attach to a lease. A fixed-term lease ends when its term expires, and a periodic tenancy ends on the statutory notice, as long as your reason is not unlawful (retaliation, discrimination, or a reason tied to domestic or sexual violence, immigration status or a call for police or emergency help). One state-law exception: multi-family housing assisted by the Illinois Affordable Housing Trust Fund may not evict tenants without good cause, and federally assisted housing has its own federal good-cause rules. Some local ordinances may add protections; check local law.

title: State Rights and Responsibilities Guide
bodyText: Illinois has no general state-published guide to landlord and tenant rights and responsibilities that you must hand a tenant before signing or at renewal. Three narrower state documents do go to tenants. From January 1, 2026, the Illinois Department of Human Rights summary of housing protections for survivors of domestic and sexual violence must be attached as the first page of every written residential lease, new or renewal, and each tenant signs the acknowledgment at the bottom of each page (see the summary-of-rights clause). For housing built before 1978, the Department of Public Health lead brochure goes to a prospective tenant before the lease. The radon rules require the state radon pamphlet in the cases they cover (see the radon rows). The state pamphlet on rights and obligations under the mobile home act is for mobile home parks, which these rows do not cover. Some local ordinances, including Chicago's and Cook County's, require their own summaries; check local law.

title: Changing Lease Terms
bodyText: No Illinois statute sets a notice period for changing the terms of a residential tenancy, and none says whether a change needs a full termination notice. During a fixed term, terms change only as the lease allows or by written agreement. In a month-to-month tenancy you may end the tenancy with 30 days' written notice (7 days for week-to-week) and offer new terms; whether a tenant who stays after a notice of new terms is bound by them is a question of case law. Three statutes limit changes. First, you may not switch a tenant from landlord-paid to tenant-paid utilities, or from master-metered to individually metered tenant-paid utilities, during a lease term; you must give at least 30 days' notice, and a tenant under a lease must get it at least 30 days before the lease ends, unless you both sign a written amendment. Second, for leases covered by the rental fee law (entered into on or after July 1, 2026 under the cautious reading), a tenant is not liable for a non-optional fee that is not on the first page of the lease, so a new or raised recurring fee should go into a new or amended first page that the tenant signs, and you may not charge a fee for modifying or renewing a lease. Third, a rent increase or other change made because the tenant complained or used a legal right in good faith is retaliation. Cautious course: make term changes at renewal or by a written amendment signed by both parties, and for a month-to-month tenancy give at least the 30-day termination notice with the new terms and a new first page.

title: Code Enforcement, Repair Orders and Receivership
bodyText: If your building does not meet a city's minimum health and safety standards and you fail to fix it after notice, the city may go to court for an injunction or other order, and the court may appoint a receiver to bring the building into compliance. A receiver may use the rents toward maintenance, repair and rehabilitation, ahead of any assignment of rents, and may borrow through receiver's notes or certificates that become a first lien on the property, ahead of earlier mortgages and liens except taxes. A receiver may also bring eviction cases. Cities, and counties outside city limits, may also demolish, repair or enclose dangerous and unsafe buildings after notice and recover the cost as a lien; in Chicago an owner or tenant within 1,200 feet of a dangerous building can ask the city to act, and sue if it does not. Cities that adopt administrative code hearings can fine you and order repairs; those orders bind the property, so a buyer takes subject to them, and no tenant may be evicted or threatened with eviction solely for testifying at a code hearing. A city may also seek a receiver for a distressed condominium building. In counties over 100,000 people, an owner who collects rent while a building has more apartments than the local ordinance allows can owe each affected occupant up to three times the rent paid, once 30 days have passed after written notice of the violation. The newer Illinois Receivership Act does not apply to small owner-occupied residential property, and under it a receiver may not reject an unexpired lease where the tenant lives in the unit as a primary residence. Cautious course: answer code notices promptly, keep repair records, and know that a code case can end in a receiver controlling your rents.

title: Lead Certificate of Compliance
bodyText: Illinois has no general lead-safe certificate for rentals and no rule that a lead certificate be attached to the lease. The certificate Illinois law does use is the certificate of compliance: when the Department of Public Health or its local delegate finds a lead hazard (usually after a child's elevated blood lead test), it serves a mitigation notice on the owner, and after a follow-up inspection confirms the hazard was mitigated it issues a certificate of compliance. If you have received a mitigation notice for a unit, or bought the building from an owner who did and were told so, you may not enter into a new lease for that unit until you have mitigated the hazard and obtained the certificate of compliance. Before renewing a lease of that unit, you must give the current tenants written notice that a lead hazard was identified, by giving them copies of the mitigation notice and inspection report, unless you already have the certificate. Once you have the certificate, the Department's rules still require you to tell each new tenant of that unit in writing, before the lease is signed, that a lead hazard was identified there; a copy of the inspection report, mitigation notice and certificate does this. Keep the certificate with your lease records; the Illinois lead information clause lets you record it. We read the Department of Public Health's lead rules.

title: Illinois Lead Notices
bodyText:
Beyond the federal lead disclosure and EPA pamphlet, Illinois's Lead Poisoning Prevention Act adds its own notices.

Before entering into a lease of a unit in a building with dwelling units built before 1978, give the prospective tenant the Illinois Department of Public Health's lead information brochure. If you have received a lead mitigation notice for a unit:
- before renewing its lease, give the current tenants copies of the mitigation notice and inspection report unless you have a certificate of compliance
- do not enter into a new lease of the unit until you have mitigated and obtained the certificate
- post the Department's notices at all entrances to the building until you have complied.

Even after mitigation, the Department's rules require you to tell each prospective tenant of that unit in writing, before the lease is signed, that a lead hazard was identified there; giving copies of the inspection report, mitigation notice and certificate of compliance satisfies this.

Before lead abatement or mitigation work starts in an occupied building, tell the occupants 7 to 30 days ahead of the work area, the start date, the licensed contractor's name and phone number, and that they must move personal items out of the work area.

If you do not mitigate as ordered, the State's Attorney may charge you and must take measures to have the tenants of the affected units withhold rent until you comply, and no tenant may be evicted because rent is withheld under the Act or because of action the Act requires of you.

Water suppliers notify building owners and occupants directly when they find a lead service line, and since July 10, 2026 a legal occupant may consent to a free service-line replacement if the owner is unavailable or unwilling. The Illinois lead information clause records delivery of the state documents. We read the Department of Public Health's lead rules.

title: Landlord Registration and Rental Licensing
bodyText: Illinois has no statewide landlord or rental registration or licensing law, and no state rule that an out-of-state owner must hire an in-state broker or manager. Many cities and some counties, especially home rule units, require owners to register rental buildings or get rental licenses, and state law builds on those ordinances: where a city has an owner registration ordinance, code-enforcement and receivership notices may be mailed to the address you registered, and notice is treated as given 4 days after mailing. Keep your registered address current. State law also reaches owners through disclosure duties. If title is held by a land trust or the building is run by a managing agent, the trustee or agent must disclose every owner and beneficiary to the enforcing agency within 10 days after receiving the first written notice of a health or safety code violation, and for residential buildings the names go on a public register if the violation is not corrected within 180 days. An owner of a building with more than 4 units who neither lives nor keeps an office there and has no resident or on-site manager or agent must post the manager's and the fire insurer's names, addresses and phone numbers, or put that notice in the lease (see the building manager and insurer notice clause).

title: Recording a Lease
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires a residential lease to be recorded or registered, and recording changes none of the landlord-tenant rules. Under the general recording law, an instrument relating to real estate that is recorded is notice to later buyers and creditors, and one that is authorized to be recorded but is not filed does not take effect against creditors and later buyers who had no notice. Whether an unrecorded lease binds a buyer or lender turns on notice, including the tenant's possession, which is case law. Illinois law also voids any provision prohibiting the recording of a deed, mortgage or other instrument relating to or affecting the title to real estate, in instruments signed after July 19, 1995. Whether a residential lease is such an instrument has not been reviewed here, so the cautious course is not to put a no-recording clause in your lease. If you rent out a condominium unit, the condominium law requires you to deliver a copy of the signed lease (or, for an oral lease, a memorandum of it) to the association's board by the date of occupancy or 10 days after signing, whichever comes first, and the association can bring an eviction case to enforce its leasing requirements (see the condominium leasing row).

title: Certificate of Occupancy
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires a landlord to hold, show, post or disclose a certificate of occupancy to a tenant, or to state a unit's legal occupancy in the lease. Certificates of occupancy and occupancy permits are local: cities issue them under their building codes, and a county board may require an occupancy permit for a newly built home outside city limits (one per new dwelling, generally without a fee). Where your city or county requires one for a rental, a lease does not cure its absence, and renting more units than the local ordinance allows can make you liable to each affected occupant for up to three times the rent paid, once 30 days have passed after written notice of the violation, in counties over 100,000 people. Check local rules before renting a new, converted or added unit.

title: Code Violations and Condemnation Orders
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires a landlord to tell a prospective or current tenant about outstanding building, housing or health code violations, inspection orders or condemnation proceedings, as a general rule. Notices reach tenants in other ways. When a city's or county's building department finds a building code violation, it must post a "Notice of Violation" near the building's main entrance, and anyone else who removes or defaces it commits a petty offense. A city may also post a 2-by-2-foot notice on an open, vacant building it plans to demolish, repair or enclose. Under the lead law, an owner who receives a mitigation notice must post the Department's notices at every entrance, and before renewing the lease of that unit must give the tenants copies of the mitigation notice and inspection report unless the hazard has been certified as mitigated (see the Illinois lead rows). If you offer a lease with an option to purchase, the Residential Real Property Disclosure Act applies, and its form asks whether you have received an uncorrected notice of violation of local, state or federal law relating to the property. If the property is in a land trust or run by a managing agent, owners' names must be disclosed to the enforcing agency after a violation notice and become public for residential buildings if the violation stays uncorrected for 180 days. Code orders bind the property after a sale, and a tenant may not be evicted or threatened with eviction solely for testifying at a code hearing. Cautious course: misrepresenting known conditions can expose you under general fraud law; disclose known orders that affect the unit.

title: No Penalty for Skipping a Condition Inspection
bodyText: Illinois has no statute requiring a move-in or move-out inspection, a condition checklist, or a notice telling the tenant of a right to an inspection, so there is no penalty, such as losing the right to keep part of the deposit or paying double damages, for skipping one. The deposit penalties that do exist are in the Security Deposit Return Act: to keep any part of a deposit for damage you must give the itemized statement with receipts within 30 days, or return the whole deposit within 45 days, and a landlord who refuses to give the statement or gives it in bad faith and fails to return the deposit on time owes twice the deposit due plus court costs and attorney's fees. Under the rental fee law, you may not charge a fee for an in-person walk-through at move-in or move-out. A dated, signed condition record at move-in and move-out remains the best evidence for any deduction.

title: Rent After Condemnation or a Vacate Order
bodyText: No Illinois statute generally bars a landlord from collecting rent after a building or unit is condemned, ordered vacated or found unfit, and none sets an automatic rent abatement for those events. Whether rent is owed for premises the tenant cannot lawfully occupy, and whether the tenant may end the lease, turn on the lease and on case law (implied warranty of habitability, constructive eviction). Three statutes do cut off or redirect rent. Under the lead law, if you do not mitigate a lead hazard as ordered, the State's Attorney must take measures to have the tenants of the affected units withhold rent until you comply, and no tenant may be evicted for that withholding. In counties over 100,000 people, if you collect rent while a building has more apartments than the local ordinance allows, you can owe each affected occupant (or the public aid agency that paid the rent) up to three times the rent paid, once 30 days have passed after written notice of the violation. If a court appoints a receiver for a building that fails the city's health and safety standards, the receiver collects the rents and uses them for repairs. Cautious course: do not demand rent for a unit under a vacate order; check your lease's casualty and condemnation terms and local ordinances, which may set their own rules.

title: Housing Code Variances
bodyText: Illinois has no state housing or sanitary code for rentals, and no statute requires you to tell tenants about, or attach to the lease, a variance, exception or waiver from a housing, sanitary or health code. Housing and health codes, and any variances from them, are local; a city or county that grants one may set its own notice conditions, so follow any condition attached to a variance you receive. The lead law has its own waiver: the Department of Public Health may, case by case, waive the use of licensed lead abatement workers if the waiver does not endanger health or safety; it carries no tenant-notice rule.

title: Fire Sprinklers in Rentals
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires you to install or retrofit fire sprinklers in a rented house or apartment building as such. Two state laws require sprinklers in student housing. Dormitories of colleges and universities that provide on-campus housing had to have fire sprinkler systems by 2013 (or September 1, 2014 under an approved compliance plan), with fines of up to $1,000 a day. Greek housing (housing for members of a tax-exempt fraternity or sorority whose active members are mainly students) begun on or after January 1, 2011 must be built with automatic sprinklers, older Greek housing had to have them by January 1, 2019, and it is unlawful to occupy a noncomplying structure as Greek housing, so if you rent a building to a fraternity or sorority for member housing, it must be sprinklered; a stricter local ordinance controls. Otherwise, sprinkler requirements come from local building and fire codes and the State Fire Marshal's fire safety rules, which can require sprinklers in new construction, high-rises or major renovations. Only licensed fire sprinkler contractors may install, inspect and service fire sprinkler systems, and a water connection or usage charge for an automatic sprinkler system may not exceed its actual cost.

title: Sprinkler Notices
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires a landlord to tell a tenant whether the building has fire sprinklers, to give a sprinkler notice with the lease, or to report on sprinkler maintenance to tenants. The only statewide form that mentions sprinkler systems is the seller's disclosure report, which applies when you sell or grant a lease with an option to purchase; it asks about known material defects in the plumbing system, including a sprinkler system. Fire protection districts may offer grants to owners of single-family homes that install and maintain approved sprinkler systems, and Illinois has no state tax credit for sprinkler retrofits in rentals. Local ordinances, including Chicago's, may require sprinkler notices; check local law.

title: Fire Code and Fire Safety Duties
bodyText: Illinois has no statute that names a fire code edition for existing rental housing. The State Fire Marshal adopts fire prevention and life safety rules, which local fire officials enforce except where a locality has standards the Fire Marshal finds equal or higher; in home rule units that have their own fire prevention and life safety ordinances, the local code governs instead (except for State-owned buildings and State-licensed facilities). Several statutes set fire-safety duties for rentals directly. Smoke detectors and carbon monoxide alarms must be installed and maintained (see the alarms clause). Owners of buildings with 6 or more living units, other than hotels, motels and condominiums, and of apartment buildings with more than 3 levels above street level must permanently post fire-procedure instructions with a diagram of all fire exits inside each dwelling unit (units on the ground floor with a direct exit outside are excluded), meeting the local fire department's standards; failing to do so is a petty offense. Outside municipalities with their own fire escape ordinances, buildings of 4 or more stories, including flats and apartment buildings, need approved fire escapes. Dormitories and fraternity and sorority housing must have sprinklers (see the sprinkler row). No person may keep combustible or explosive conditions that endanger a building, or let a building become especially liable to fire through faulty construction, age or lack of repair.

title: Which Code Edition Applies
bodyText: Illinois uses both fixed and moving code editions, so which version governs your building depends on the code and who adopted it. Cities, counties and fire protection districts adopt building, plumbing, electrical and fire codes by reference by ordinance, with copies filed for public inspection before adoption; a later edition or amendment applies only when the local body adopts it the same way. Counties and cities must report the title and edition of a new building code to the Capital Development Board, which lists them publicly. Ask your building department which editions it has adopted. Some state statutes float with new editions: the state energy code is the latest published International Energy Conservation Code as the Capital Development Board adopts it (reviewed and adopted within a year of publication); for new one- and two-family homes in places with no local building code, the International Residential Code means the current or most recent preceding edition; carbon monoxide alarms must meet the most recent Underwriters Laboratories or Canadian Standards Association standards; and since 2025 local building codes must regulate structural design at least as strictly as the least restrictive model-code edition published in the past ten years. Some are fixed: elevator safety upgrades follow the 2007 and 2005 editions of the ASME elevator codes, and for commercial buildings (including those with 3 or more units) in places with no building code, the requirements in effect on January 1 of the year the permit was applied for apply for the whole job. New work generally must meet the code in force when it is permitted; existing buildings are governed by local property maintenance and fire codes and the State Fire Marshal's rules, not reviewed here.

title: Home Child Care in a Rental
bodyText:
Illinois has no statute that gives a tenant a right to run a home child care in a rental, and none that limits what a lease may say about it, so your lease decides (Illinois's residential-use clause bars business use unless you consent).

State law regulates the child care itself. Since July 1, 2026, licensed home child care is called an early care and education home (more than 3 and up to 12 children, counting the provider's own children under 12) or a group early care and education home (up to 16), licensed by the Department of Early Childhood; care for no more than 3 children under 12 (or up to 6 from one household) is exempt. While a home is used for child care, smoking is banned there under the Smoke Free Illinois Act. A licensed child care home is a regulated facility under the lead law. An insurer may not cancel or refuse to renew a policy on a licensed early care and education home solely because the child care operates there. Local zoning may limit home child care.

If you are willing to allow child care, the optional child care clause lets you consent on conditions (license, insurance, no smoking, responsibility for damage).

title: Home Businesses in a Rental
bodyText:
No Illinois statute makes a home-based business a permitted use of a dwelling, gives a tenant a right to run one, or limits what a lease may say about business use, so the lease decides; Illinois's residential-use clause bars business use without your consent. Zoning of home occupations is local.

Two food laws let people make food for sale in their own homes. A cottage food operation may produce food in a kitchen in the operator's primary domestic residence, must register each year with the local health department (fee up to $50), and in Chicago must also follow any city law that applies equally to all home-based businesses; home rule units may not regulate cottage food inconsistently with the state law. A home kitchen operation may sell non-potentially hazardous baked goods made in the operator's primary domestic residence, up to $1,000 a month.

Neither law says anything about a landlord's consent, so a tenant who wants to run one still needs your consent if the lease bars business use. Smoking is banned in a home while it is used as a business open to the public, and a person doing business under an assumed name at home may list the county clerk as agent for service.

If you allow a home business, consider conditions in writing: no customer traffic or signs beyond what local law allows, compliance with licenses and zoning, insurance, and responsibility for damage.

title: Student Housing
bodyText: Illinois has no student-housing statute that changes a private landlord's duties to student tenants, and its landlord-tenant statutes have no student or dormitory exemption, so a lease to students of a privately owned apartment or house follows the ordinary rules, including the rental fee law, deposit return and the notices to end a tenancy. A few statutes do single out student housing. College and university dormitories must have fire sprinklers, and so must fraternity and sorority (Greek) housing for students, which may not be occupied as Greek housing without them, whoever owns the building. Smoking is banned throughout the living quarters of any building used in whole or in part as a student dormitory that a college or university owns and operates or otherwise uses, which can reach a private building a school master-leases. Some statutes exclude dormitories: the peephole requirement for buildings of 5 or more rental units does not apply to dormitories, and the installment-contract laws exclude school dormitories and fraternity houses. Colleges must give homeless students and students in care priority for on-campus housing, and a student called to military service is charged for school housing only for the time occupied. Local ordinances, including those of college towns, may add rules for student rentals or occupancy; check local law.

title: Renting a Single-Family Home
bodyText: Illinois has no special disclosure for renting a single-family house: no required statement of the home's permitted occupancy, and no type-size or first-page rule tied to single-family rentals. Two first-page rules apply to every written residential lease regardless of building type: all non-optional fees must appear on the first page or the tenant does not owe them (for leases covered by the rental fee law), and the domestic and sexual violence summary must be attached as the first page with each tenant's signed acknowledgment. Single-family homes do appear in the Human Rights Act, which exempts certain sales and rentals of single-family homes by owners from parts of its housing provisions (never from its advertising ban); see the fair housing row. Occupancy limits for houses are local (zoning and property maintenance codes).

title: No Required Habitability Statement
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires your lease to state that the home is, or will be delivered, fit to live in, in good repair or habitable, and no statute prescribes wording for such a statement. Illinois has no general habitability statute for houses and apartments; Illinois courts recognize an implied warranty of habitability in residential leases, which applies whether or not the lease mentions it. Separately, it is a crime (criminal housing management) for an owner or manager to recklessly let a residential property's condition endanger anyone's health or safety, whatever the lease says. What your lease says still matters: the tenant's repair-and-deduct right reaches repairs the lease requires as well as repairs a law or local ordinance requires, so a repair promise in the lease widens it, and a lease term excusing you from liability for your own negligence in operating or maintaining the property is void. The library's shared clauses cover the subject without a separate statement: the existing-condition clause records the condition the tenant accepts at move-in, and the maintenance clause states your repair duty. A "fit for human habitation" standard appears in Illinois law only as a funding condition for housing financed under the Illinois Affordable Housing Program; if your property has that financing, follow the program's standards. Local codes and ordinances, including Chicago's and Cook County's, may require more.

title: Stoves and Refrigerators
bodyText:
No Illinois statute requires you to supply a stove, oven, refrigerator or other kitchen appliance in a rented house or apartment, or says who must repair one you do supply. The lease decides: list the appliances you provide and maintain (the shared appliances clause does this), and if the tenant is to bring a stove or refrigerator, or you leave one you will not maintain, say so in the optional excluded-items clause.

If you do supply an appliance, the tenant's repair-and-deduct right reaches repairs the lease requires, and a lease term excusing you from liability for your own negligence in maintaining the property is void.

One criminal rule matters when an appliance is replaced: leaving a discarded refrigerator, icebox or ice chest of one and one-half cubic feet or more with a latching lid or door where children can reach it, or knowingly letting one stay on premises you own, lease or manage, is a Class C misdemeanor, so remove the door or latch or haul it away.

If your housing is financed under the Illinois Affordable Housing Program, the program requires prompt response to tenant requests, including appliance requests, as a funding condition. Local building and housing codes may require cooking and refrigeration equipment.

title: Appliances You Leave but Will Not Maintain
bodyText:
No Illinois statute presumes that an appliance left in a rented house or apartment is one you supply, lists appliances you must supply, or bars a lease from excluding an appliance from your repair duty. The lease decides, so list what you include (the shared appliances clause) and, if you leave an item you won't maintain or the tenant brings their own, use the optional excluded-items clause.

Two statutes limit how far that clause can go. A lease term excusing you from liability for injury to a person or property caused by your own negligence in operating or maintaining the property is void, so the clause can say you won't repair an item but can't disclaim negligence. And the tenant's repair-and-deduct right reaches repairs a law, rule or local ordinance requires as well as those the lease requires, so a code-required repair stays yours whatever the lease says.

You must also supply and install required smoke detectors and carbon monoxide alarms, and in 55-and-older housing with a building-wide system you must run heating and cooling to statutory standards; never list those.

Illinois courts recognize an implied warranty of habitability, so the cautious course is never to exclude anything whose failure would affect health, safety or habitability, and to repair or remove such an item before the tenancy starts.

Charge nothing for an excluded item; for leases the rental fee law covers, a fee for routine maintenance and upkeep of the unit is barred. Local ordinances, including Chicago's and Cook County's, may require you to supply or maintain particular appliances.

title: Furnished Rentals
bodyText:
No Illinois statute sets special rules for renting a house or apartment furnished: there is no required furniture inventory, no separate furniture deposit rule and no rule on who repairs furniture you supply. Use the optional furnishings clause to list each item and its condition, and record the furniture in your move-in condition report.

Damage to furniture you supply is handled like other damage under the security deposit law: if you keep any of the deposit for it, give the tenant an itemized statement of the damage and the cost within 30 days after the later of the move-out date and the end of the tenant's right of possession, with paid receipts.

The Bedbug Inspection Act requires a merchant who regularly rents or leases furniture to customers to inspect previously rented furniture, and treat any pests, before renting it again; it is written for furniture-rental businesses, and no statute or reviewed decision says it reaches a landlord who rents a furnished home, but the cautious course is to inspect and treat furnished items between tenants anyway.

If you rent furnished apartments in a city or county with a board of election commissioners and house 4 or more people outside your family, the Election Code requires a sworn report of residents claiming a voting residence before each election. Renting furnished rooms short-term may bring a property under hotel tax rules (see the rent tax row).

title: Shifting Maintenance Duties to the Tenant
bodyText: Illinois has no general statute on whether a lease may shift your repair or maintenance duties to the tenant, and no statute lists particular duties, such as common-area garbage removal, that may be shifted on conditions. That is because Illinois has no general habitability or repair statute for houses and apartments; your baseline duty comes from the implied warranty of habitability recognized by Illinois courts and from local codes. Two statutes do let a written agreement move a specific duty. In Cook County, your duty to change or rekey the lock between tenants does not apply if the tenant has obtained the right to change or rekey the lock under a written lease. And you may not switch a tenant from landlord-paid to tenant-paid utilities during a lease, but you and the tenant may agree to amend the lease to make that change if the amendment is in writing and signed by both of you; a lease term that conflicts with the shared-meter rules is void. Some duties can't be moved: you must supply and install required smoke detectors and carbon monoxide alarms (the tenant tests them, replaces batteries and reports problems in writing), and in 55-and-older housing with a building-wide system you must run heating and cooling to the statutory standards. Cautious course: a lease may give the tenant routine upkeep such as yard care, snow removal or changing light bulbs and filters, ideally with a stated rent credit, but keep structural, heating, plumbing, electrical, water and safety items yours, and never write a clause excusing you from liability for your own negligence in maintaining the property, which is void. For leases the rental fee law covers, you may not charge the tenant a fee or fine for routine maintenance and upkeep of the unit, so assign the task itself rather than billing for it.

title: Promises to Repair
bodyText:
No Illinois statute requires your promise to clean, repair or improve a rental to be in writing, to carry a completion date, or to be made before the lease is signed. Whether an oral or pre-lease promise binds you is a question of contract law; a lease for more than one year must itself be in a signed writing.

Two statutes make writing the promise down the safer course. A repair the lease requires is one the tenant can enforce through repair and deduct: if it costs no more than the lesser of $500 or half a month's rent and you don't make it within 14 days after the tenant's written notice by certified or registered mail (or sooner in an emergency), the tenant may have it done and deduct the paid bill from rent, so be precise about what you promise and when.

And the Consumer Fraud Act bars misrepresenting a material fact in trade or commerce; whether it reaches a residential lease is for the courts, but the cautious course treats a promise used to win a tenant and then not kept as exposed.

What to do: list every promised cleaning, repair or improvement, with a completion date, in the lease or a signed addendum (the optional promised-work clause does this), say that the listed items are one-time work, and don't make oral promises you don't intend to keep.

If your housing is financed under the Illinois Affordable Housing Program, the program requires the property manager to respond to tenant requests within a reasonable time (1-2 days) as a funding condition.

title: Repair Requests and Notice
bodyText:
Illinois has no general statute on how a tenant must ask for repairs, and none says that a lease allowing verbal requests waives a right to written notice. Three statutes set the rules that do exist.
- Repair and deduct: before a tenant may have a small repair made and deduct the cost, the tenant must notify you in writing by registered or certified mail or other restricted delivery service, at the address for you or your agent shown in the lease (or your last known address if none is listed), and wait 14 days, or less in an emergency; a lease can't change that method, and putting your notice address in the lease decides where the notice goes.
- Alarms: the tenant must notify you or your agent in writing of any smoke detector or carbon monoxide alarm deficiency the tenant can't correct, and must give you access to fix it.
- Retaliation: you may not end a tenancy, raise rent, cut services, sue or threaten to sue for possession, or refuse to renew because a tenant in good faith complained or asked you to make repairs the lease or a code requires; the protection turns on the complaint or request, not on whether it was written, so a lease term requiring written requests doesn't narrow it.

For leases the rental fee law covers, you may not charge a fee or fine for contacting you or your manager for maintenance or service requests, for after-hours maintenance requests, for calls to a maintenance hotline, or for travel to complete needed repairs.

Cautious course: ask for repair requests in writing (the optional repair-requests clause does this), give an emergency phone number, and act on and keep a record of every request however it arrives.

title: No Termination Because Repairs Cost Too Much
bodyText: No Illinois statute lets you end a residential lease, or refuse a repair, because the repair would cost too much compared with the rent or the property's value, and none gives the tenant that right. Illinois also has no statute on a house or apartment that becomes unlivable after a fire or other casualty, so what happens then depends on the lease and on case law; the library's optional casualty clause sets a lease rule for it. Your repair duties come from the lease, local codes and the implied warranty of habitability recognized by Illinois courts, and a tenant may use repair and deduct for small repairs the lease or a code requires whatever their cost relative to rent, up to the statutory limit. The statutes that do let a tenant end a lease turn on other facts: your failure to pay a landlord-paid utility, an undisclosed flood risk or flooding, an unmitigated radon hazard, Safe Homes Act violence, military orders and retaliation remedies, each covered in its own row. If a building is too costly to repair, ending a tenancy early still requires either a lease term that allows it or the ordinary termination notices and an eviction case; never cut off services or remove a tenant yourself. Local governments may order dangerous buildings repaired, closed or demolished under their own powers and ordinances.

title: No Repair Escrow or Exemption Notice
bodyText: Illinois has no statute letting a tenant pay rent into an escrow account while repairs are outstanding, so there is no exemption from such a remedy for small landlords and no exemption notice for you to give. Rent can still be diverted from you by a court or a prosecutor in three cases. If the property is in a condition that endangers anyone's health or safety, the State's Attorney may get an order barring you from collecting rents and directing rents into an escrow account at the circuit clerk, used only for necessary repairs, delinquent taxes and other property debts; the order doesn't let tenants stop paying rent. Recklessly letting a residential property stay in such a condition is itself the crime of criminal housing management. After a lead mitigation violation, the State's Attorney must take measures so that tenants of the affected units withhold rent from you until the mitigation is done, and no tenant may be evicted for withholding it. And a court may appoint a receiver to collect rents and use them for repairs when a municipality sues over a building that fails its health and safety ordinances, or to pay utilities when you fail to pay a landlord-paid utility bill. The repair-and-deduct statute doesn't apply to owner-occupied buildings of 6 or fewer units, public housing, condominiums or housing cooperatives; that exclusion applies automatically, with no notice.

title: No Rent-into-Court Rule
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires a tenant to pay rent into court, or into escrow, to defend an eviction case, to demand a jury, to get a continuance or to raise a counterclaim, and none makes a tenant's counterclaim mandatory. In an eviction case the tenant may offer any defense under a general denial, but matters not germane to the purpose of the case can't be brought in by joinder, counterclaim or otherwise; you may join your claim for rent and get judgment for the rent found due. Some statutes expressly let a tenant bring a claim in your case: a tenant billed for utility service outside the unit on a shared meter may recover those damages by counterclaim in any action you bring, and in a distress-for-rent proceeding the tenant may counterclaim as in other civil actions. Either party may demand a jury in any case about residential premises, whatever the lease says, with no rent deposit required by statute. A tenant who withheld rent for repairs can't use that as a defense unless the tenant met every requirement of the repair-and-deduct statute, and tenants withholding rent under a lead-mitigation order can't be evicted for it. If you appeal an eviction judgment, you may keep enforcing and accepting the tenant's lease obligations while the appeal is pending. Supreme Court rules on appeal bonds and stays are court rules not reviewed here.

title: No Statutory Right to Fix a Tenant's Breach and Bill It
bodyText:
No Illinois statute lets you fix a tenant's breach (damage, removal of items, cleanup) and bill the cost, as rent or otherwise, and none forbids a lease term that does. The right comes only from the lease; the optional clause sets it up.

Several rules limit how you use it. Illinois law bars entering land or buildings except where entry is allowed by law, and then only peaceably, and Illinois has no general entry statute, so enter only as your lease allows; never change locks, remove belongings or cut off utilities to force a cure. Charge only the actual, reasonable cost with an itemized bill. Don't call the cost rent: no statute makes a lease charge rent, and the 5-day rent demand should carry only rent.

For leases the rental fee law covers, list the charge among the conditional charges on the first page of the lease, since a non-optional fee not on the first page can't be collected, and never charge for routine maintenance and upkeep of the unit or for pest abatement where the tenant in no way contributed to the infestation; renaming a fee doesn't avoid the law.

An unpaid bill can be recovered by written demand, as a material lease default supporting a 10-day notice, from the deposit for property damage with the statutory itemized statement after move-out, or in a separate money claim.

The Installment Sales Contract Act gives a seller a repair right on 72 hours' written notice, but it covers installment sales of homes, not leases.

Illinois sets no period for the tenant to fix the problem first; giving at least 7 days, or less in an emergency that threatens health, safety or the property, is the cautious choice.

title: Who Makes Repairs
bodyText:
No Illinois statute lets you designate the repairer a tenant must use, or sets up a list of approved repairers, for a house or apartment. The one statute on tenant-arranged repairs, the repair-and-deduct law, leaves the choice of repairer to the tenant, within limits: the work must be done in a workmanlike manner and to code, by a tradesperson or supplier unrelated to the tenant who holds any license or certificate the law requires and is adequately insured; the tenant is responsible for damage the repairer causes and loses the remedy without those safeguards.

That law has no sentence voiding lease terms that narrow it, but home rule units may not diminish it, and whether a lease may is case law not reviewed here, so the cautious course is not to require your own repairer for repair-and-deduct work.

A lease may still name your repair contact, say that your repairs are made by you or a repairer you choose, and bar the tenant from making or hiring repairs at your expense without your written consent except as the law allows; the optional clause does this and may list preferred repairers the tenant may use.

Repairs under the statute aren't treated as authorized by you for mechanics lien purposes. The Installment Sales Contract Act forbids a seller to require that only the seller or its agent make repairs, but it covers installment sales of homes, not leases.

title: No Shutdown Rent Protection
bodyText: No Illinois statute delays rent, waives late fees or pauses eviction cases for federal or State employees or contractors affected by a government shutdown or a lapse in appropriations. The lease's ordinary rent, late-fee and default terms apply, along with the usual statutory steps: a written 5-day demand for unpaid rent before an eviction case, and acceptance of a partial payment as the demand rules provide. Consider a written payment plan for an affected tenant. Servicemembers have separate rights (see the servicemember row), and federal programs or local ordinances may offer help that is not covered here.

title: No Rule on Prorating Subsidized Rent
bodyText: No Illinois statute sets a formula for reducing a subsidized tenant's share of rent, or the housing agency's share, when part of the unit is unfit. For a Housing Choice Voucher tenancy, federal rules and your contract with the housing agency govern. You must keep the unit up to the program's housing quality standards and fix a deficiency within 24 hours of notice if it is life-threatening, otherwise within 30 days or an approved extension. The agency may withhold its payment once it has told you in writing of a deficiency and must pay it back if you fix it in time; if you don't, it must abate its payment, does not pay you for the abated period, and must end the contract if the unit is not fixed within 60 days or a longer period it sets. You may not end the tenancy because the agency withheld or abated its payment, and during an abatement the tenant may end the tenancy. The federal rules do not prorate the tenant's share. If the tenant's household caused the deficiency, the agency may waive your duty to fix it and hold the tenant responsible. Illinois law has one statutory rent abatement for tenants generally: if you cause utility service to be cut off by not paying a landlord-paid bill or by tampering, the tenant gets a 100% abatement of rent for each month, prorated for part of a month, plus consequential damages. Otherwise, abatement for an unfit unit turns on the implied warranty of habitability recognized by Illinois courts. Two Illinois rules touch subsidized tenancies: a foreclosure receiver must accept rental assistance payments for an occupant, and housing funded by the Rental Housing Support Program must have tenants able to afford the tenant's share of the rent. Cautious course: if part of a subsidized unit is unusable through no fault of the tenant, don't charge the tenant's share for that part, and tell the housing agency in writing. We read the federal voucher maintenance and owner-breach rules.

title: Alternate Housing During Repairs
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires you to provide or pay for alternate housing, or to relocate a tenant, while a rented house or apartment is repaired or after a fire or other casualty, whether or not the tenant asks. If the home can't be lived in, what happens to the rent and the lease turns on the lease (the optional casualty clause covers it) and on the implied warranty of habitability recognized by Illinois courts; don't charge rent for a period the home is unusable through your fault. If you cause utility service to be cut off by not paying a landlord-paid bill or by tampering, the tenant is entitled to a full rent abatement for that period plus consequential damages. Relocation payments in Illinois law are a government duty, not a landlord's: a condemning authority must reimburse displaced persons' reasonable relocation costs when it takes property by eminent domain, and State agencies follow the federal relocation rules. A court in a domestic violence case may order the abuser, not the landlord, to provide alternate housing for the victim. Local ordinances, including Chicago's, may require relocation help when a building is closed for code violations.

title: Building Facilities With Their Own Rules
bodyText: Illinois has no landlord-tenant list of facilities you must supply, and no statute on automatic garage door openers in rentals, but several statewide laws put duties on you as the owner of particular building facilities, whatever the lease says. Pools: a pool at an apartment building, condominium or other group of 5 or more living units is a swimming facility that needs a license from the Department of Public Health or the local health department to operate. Elevators and lifts: outside cities of more than 500,000 people, the owner or lessee must register each elevator, platform lift, dumbwaiter or escalator, have required tests done by a licensed elevator contractor, and hold a certificate of operation renewed annually; conveyances in a private residence not open to the public are exempt. An unsupervised automatic passenger elevator open to the public must have tactile or braille control markings, and failing to keep them is a petty offense fined $100 a day. Alarms: you must supply and install required smoke detectors and carbon monoxide alarms. Water lines: if you replace part of a lead or connected galvanized service line, you must give the water supplier 45 days' notice, and after an emergency repair you must provide certified filters for each kitchen area. In 55-and-older housing, building-wide heating and cooling must meet statutory standards, or a cooled common room must be open to tenants. Housing financed under the Illinois Affordable Housing Program must, as a funding condition, provide working laundry machines where most residents are 65 or older or have a disability. List the amenities you provide in the lease and keep the right to set reasonable rules for them (the shared common-area clause does this). Local codes, including Chicago's, add their own facility rules.

title: Quiet Possession
bodyText: No Illinois statute writes a covenant of quiet possession or quiet enjoyment into a residential lease. The statutory covenants of quiet enjoyment and peaceable possession attach to warranty deeds and mortgages, not leases. Illinois courts generally imply a covenant of quiet enjoyment in a lease, so assume your tenant has it. Statutes protect the tenant's possession in other ways: no one may enter land or buildings except where entry is allowed by law, and then only peaceably; you recover possession only through an eviction case; you may not interrupt or cut off a tenant's utility service, except temporary shutoffs for emergencies or, on 7 days' written notice, for repairs; and you may not retaliate against a tenant for complaints or for exercising legal rights. Illinois has no general statute on when you may enter, so put your entry terms in the lease and follow them.

title: Tenant Duties Under Illinois Law
bodyText: Illinois has no landlord-tenant act listing a residential tenant's duties, but several statutes put duties on tenants whatever the lease says. (1) Alarms: the tenant must test and provide general maintenance for the smoke detectors and carbon monoxide alarms in the unit, replace required batteries (you make sure they work at move-in), notify you or your agent in writing of any deficiency the tenant can't correct, and give you access to correct it. (2) Holding over: a tenant who wilfully stays after the term ends and after your written demand for possession owes double the yearly value of the property for the time you are kept out; a tenant who gives notice of leaving on a date the lease allows and then doesn't leave owes double rent. (3) Radon: a tenant who tests for radon in the first 90 days must give you copies of the results within 10 days after receiving them. (4) Repair and deduct: a tenant using it must use a licensed, adequately insured tradesperson unrelated to the tenant, give you the paid bill and the repairer's contact details, and is responsible for damage the repairer causes. (5) Safe Homes Act lock changes: a tenant who changes the locks after you fail to act must use locks of similar or better quality, do it in a workmanlike manner and try in good faith to give you a key within 48 hours. (6) EV charging: a tenant installing a charger must agree in writing to your design specifications, use a licensed electrical contractor and provide insurance or reimburse your added premium within 14 days, and is responsible for damage from the system in shared areas unless you agree otherwise. (7) In subsidized housing, a tenant must allow lawful inspections or face emergency eviction proceedings. (8) If a condominium board takes over a unit owner's lease after the owner defaults, the tenant pays rent to the board. Criminal laws also apply: knowingly damaging property of another is criminal damage to property, and using or letting the premises be used for a felony or Class A misdemeanor lets you void the lease. Illinois has no general statute on waste by a residential tenant. Put the tenant's other duties in the lease.

title: Acts the Law Forbids Tenants
bodyText:
Illinois has no statute listing acts a residential tenant may not do, so the shared prohibited-acts clause (no damage, no interference with others' peaceful enjoyment, no unreasonable refusal of access for repairs, inspections or showings) is what puts them in the lease; use it as written.
