Several laws back it up: knowingly damaging property of another is criminal damage to property; a tenant who refuses lawful inspections in subsidized housing can face emergency eviction proceedings; using or allowing the premises to be used for a felony or Class A misdemeanor lets you void the lease and recover possession; and drug activity on the premises has its own remedies. A tenant who stays after the lease ends owes double rent or double the yearly value in the cases the statutes describe.

Don't treat lawful tenant conduct as a prohibited act: calling police or emergency services, a Safe Homes Act lock change, installing an EV charger on the statutory terms, and complaints about conditions are protected.

title: Tenant Repair Agreements
bodyText:
No Illinois statute authorizes, limits or sets formalities for an agreement that a residential tenant will do repairs, maintenance or minor remodeling: there is no separate-writing rule, no single-family limit and no required consideration. So you may use the optional tenant maintenance agreement, listing each task and what, if anything, you give in return, such as a stated rent credit.

Limits still apply. A lease term excusing you from liability for your own negligence in operating or maintaining the property is void. The tenant keeps the repair-and-deduct remedy for repairs a law, rule or local ordinance requires, so code-required repairs stay yours. You must supply and install required smoke detectors and carbon monoxide alarms (the tenant's statutory part is testing, general maintenance, batteries and reporting). Switching a tenant from landlord-paid to tenant-paid utilities during a lease needs a written amendment signed by both of you. For leases the rental fee law covers, you may not charge a fee or fine for routine maintenance and upkeep of the unit, so the tenant may do a task but you may not bill the tenant for upkeep you do.

Because Illinois courts recognize an implied warranty of habitability, the cautious course is to assign only routine tasks such as yard care, snow removal and replacing filters or light bulbs, keep structural, heating, plumbing, electrical and safety work yours, and say that parts the tenant installs become yours.

title: Move-In and Move-Out Inspections
bodyText:
No Illinois statute requires a move-in or move-out inspection, a written condition report, checklist or inventory, or a notice to the tenant about one, and none says a tenant who signs or fails to object to a damage list loses a claim. For leases the rental fee law covers, you may not charge any fee or fine for an in-person walk-through of the unit at move-in or move-out.

A condition report is still your best evidence for the deposit.

To keep any part of the deposit for damage, you must give the tenant, within 30 days after the later of the move-out date and the end of the tenant's right of possession, an itemized statement of the damage with the estimated or actual cost of each repair and paid receipts (or receipts within 30 days after an estimate); if the lease specifies a cost for a component, that cost must be for damage beyond normal wear and tear and reasonable to restore the premises to their condition when the lease began, which a signed, dated move-in report with photographs helps prove.

At move-in you must also make sure the smoke detector and carbon monoxide alarm batteries are working, which the report can record.

Use the optional move-in condition report clause, offer a joint walk-through at move-out without charge, and give the itemized statement on time. Voucher programs and local ordinances may add inspection rules not covered here.

title: Habitability: What Illinois Has and Lacks
bodyText: How Illinois compares on habitability features found elsewhere. Absent (we found no statute): a statewide warranty of habitability or housing code for private rentals; a required lease statement that the home is fit to live in; a list of required facilities such as a stove or refrigerator; a presumption that appliances left in a unit are yours; a statutory waiver, materiality or presumption rule for habitability; general repair deadlines; tenant rent withholding or rent escrow for repairs, and so no small-landlord exemption notice; a right to end the lease or refuse repairs because they cost too much; a statutory right to fix a tenant's breach and bill it; a designated-repairer rule; a duty to provide alternate housing; a statutory covenant of quiet possession; furnished-rental rules; move-in inspection or checklist rules; a shutdown rent protection; and a rule prorating subsidized rent. Present: repair and deduct for repairs up to the lesser of $500 or half a month's rent after 14 days' written notice (not in owner-occupied buildings of 6 or fewer units, public housing, condominiums or cooperatives); a void rule for lease terms excusing your negligence; smoke detector and carbon monoxide alarm duties; heating and cooling standards in 55-and-older housing; landlord-paid utility rules with lease termination, pay-and-deduct and full rent abatement for shutoffs you cause; shared-meter disclosures; Cook County rekeying between tenants; retaliation protection for repair requests and code complaints; the crime of criminal housing management, with a State's Attorney injunction that can send rents into a court escrow for repairs; lead mitigation, with rent withheld by tenants until it is done; radon testing and termination rights; flood disclosure and remedies; municipal receivers who use rents for code repairs; and owner duties for pools, elevators and lead service lines. Each is covered in its own row.

title: Water Heater Temperature
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires you to set a water heater to a maximum temperature before a new tenant moves in, to check its setting between tenancies, or to install anti-scald devices, and no statute puts a water-heater duty on a landlord at all. The only state statute on water heaters is an energy-efficiency rule for sellers: a new storage water heater bought for resale or installation in Illinois must be certified as meeting the national ASHRAE 90 efficiency standard. Illinois's plumbing rules, which are agency rules rather than statutes, and your local building or housing code may govern how a water heater is installed and how hot it may run; check them, especially in Chicago and Cook County. As a matter of care, a setting of about 120 degrees Fahrenheit at each turnover reduces scald risk, and you remain responsible for the safe operation of equipment you control.

title: Window Guards and Security Bars
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires you to install window guards or window stops where children live, to give a window-guard notice in or with the lease, or to fit security or burglar bars with a release mechanism or disclose one. There is one narrow exception: housing financed under the Illinois Affordable Housing Program must meet a funding standard that its windows open and close, have safety mechanisms installed and are inspected regularly. If your property has that financing, follow the program's standards and your funding documents. Separately, an old state fire-escape law requires buildings of four or more stories, including flats and apartment buildings, to have fire escapes reachable from windows or doors on each upper story, so never block an escape window with fixed bars. Local building, fire and housing codes, including Chicago's, may require window guards or regulate bars; check them before you install either.

title: Steam Radiator Covers
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires you to provide radiator covers on request, to attach a radiator-cover rider or notice to the lease, or otherwise to shield steam or hot-water radiators against burns. If your building has exposed steam radiators and young children live there, covers are a sensible precaution, and local housing codes, including Chicago's, may set their own heating-equipment rules.

title: Pools and Spas at Rental Properties
bodyText:
If your rental property has a pool at an apartment or condominium building, or at another group or association, with 5 or more living units, Illinois treats it as a swimming pool under the Swimming Facility Act. It is unlawful to open, maintain or operate it without a license from the Illinois Department of Public Health or, where a local health department has taken over the program by ordinance, from that local department, and building or majorly altering it needs a Department permit first.

Spas and hot tubs are covered too unless they are at an individual single-family home for the occupant and guests, and so are bathing beaches at buildings with 5 or more living units.

As a licensee you must display the license, give inspectors access, submit water samples and records, and follow the Department's rules. The Act lists as violations, among others, failing to post Patron Regulations and Bather Load signs, failing to provide a lifeguard or warning sign as the rules require, failing to secure the pool area, and failing to submit a Drowning and Injury Report within 24 hours; penalties run per day, and the Department can order a pool closed at once.

No one may prohibit a person from using a life jacket in a pool when a statement signed by a licensed physician shows a disability or condition that requires one. A licensed facility must allow a service animal trained to work in the water unless it poses a direct threat, and no other animal may use it.

A pool at a private single-family home used only by the owner and guests is outside the license; the Act does not say how it treats a pool at a single rented house, so ask your local health department.

Illinois has no statute requiring a fence or barrier for a residential pool, or a pool-safety notice when you sign a lease; local building codes usually set barrier rules. Letting a pool become a breeding ground for mosquitoes or other pests is a public nuisance.

If you charge a mandatory pool or amenity fee, it must be on the first page of the lease under the rental fee law. The optional pool-use clause sets household rules for a pool or spa.

title: Smart Locks and Electronic Entry
bodyText:
Illinois has no statute written for smart locks or app-based entry: nothing requires you to offer a physical key, to give notice before switching tenants to a smart system, or to limit entry logs. Several general laws still apply.

Biometric entry: if a lock or reader uses a fingerprint, face, hand, eye or voice scan, the Biometric Information Privacy Act applies to you. Before collecting a resident's biometric identifier you must tell the person in writing that it is being collected or stored, and for what specific purpose and how long, and you must get the person's signed written release.

You must have a public written policy for destroying the data when its purpose ends or within 3 years of the person's last interaction with you, whichever comes first; you must store, transmit and protect it using the reasonable standard of care in your industry and at least as carefully as your other confidential and sensitive information; you may not sell or profit from it, and you may disclose it only with consent or as the Act allows.

Each violation can cost $1,000 (negligent) or $5,000 (intentional or reckless), or actual damages if higher, plus attorney's fees; repeated scans of the same person by the same method, or repeated disclosures of the same person's data to the same recipient, count as a single violation. The simplest course is to offer a non-biometric credential and never require a scan.

Changing access between tenants: in Cook County, before a new tenant takes possession you must change or rekey the unit's lock, and for an electronic or digital lock that means changing the code or the method of unlocking from the prior tenant's; you are liable for a theft caused by failing to do so. Deactivating every prior occupant's codes and credentials is good practice everywhere.

Domestic or sexual violence: a tenant's Safe Homes Act lock-change request reaches a smart lock too. The Act speaks of changing locks, so the cautious course is to change the codes and deactivate the threatening person's credentials within 48 hours, and to change the physical lock as well if the tenant asks. Illinois has no statute letting a survivor ask an app or device account manager to cut off another person's access.

Fees and tampering: a mandatory technology, smart-home or access fee is a non-optional fee that must be on the first page of the lease, and renaming it does not avoid the rental fee law. Damaging or disabling digital locks, card readers, biometric access equipment or security cameras is a crime under the tampering statute. The optional smart-access clause sets these terms in the lease.

title: Key Control and Staff Screening
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires you to adopt a written key-control policy, to log who holds master keys, or to run background checks on employees who can enter tenants' units, whatever the size of the complex. Two related rules do apply. In Cook County you must change or rekey each unit's lock, including an electronic or digital lock's code, between tenants. And if you screen applicants, a rental application fee, including background checks, is capped at $50 unless the third-party check costs more and you follow the billing rules. Because you remain liable for your own negligence and a lease cannot excuse it, a written key-control practice (locked key storage, a sign-out log, prompt rekeying when a key is lost or an employee leaves) and screening of staff who hold keys are sensible protections, especially in larger buildings. Local ordinances may add rules.

title: Common-Area Lights on a Tenant's Meter
bodyText:
Illinois lets a tenant's own utility account carry common-area lighting (or other service outside the unit) only if you do four things before you offer the lease or a renewal, take a deposit or otherwise agree to rent:
- give a written statement of the specific areas and uses the tenant's meter serves, including uses that may arise later
- give copies of the unit's utility bills for the previous 12 months, unless the tenant waives them in writing
- never suggest or require that the tenant collect from neighbors
- state in writing the amount of any rent reduction you offer for the outside usage.

If you skip a step, the tenant can recover the utility bills for service outside the unit, trebled if the violation was knowing or intentional, and a lease term inconsistent with the rule is void.

You may not switch a tenant from landlord-paid to tenant-paid utilities during a lease term without a written amendment both of you sign, and you must give at least 30 days' notice before the change (for a tenant under a lease, at least 30 days before the lease ends).

If you pay a common meter that serves common-area lighting and fall behind, the tenants may end the lease or pay the bill and deduct it from rent.

No statute sets a common-area lighting standard for apartment buildings; local housing codes usually do. The optional common-area service clause records a compliant arrangement in the lease.

title: Balcony and Porch Inspections
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires you to have balconies, decks, porches, exterior stairways or other elevated exterior elements inspected on a schedule, to report the results, or to give tenants notice of an inspection. Local building and housing codes, such as Chicago's, may set porch and balcony standards or require inspections; check yours. Because a failing balcony or porch is a serious hazard and you remain liable for your own negligence, have elevated exterior structures checked regularly, repair rot, rust and loose railings promptly, and close a structure to use until it is repaired.

title: Asbestos in Rental Buildings
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires you to tell tenants about asbestos in the building, to survey for it, or to put an asbestos notice in the lease. What the law does regulate is work on asbestos. In an apartment building or condominium of 10 or more dwelling units, which Illinois treats as a commercial or public building for this purpose, anyone who removes, encapsulates or encloses asbestos must hold a Department of Public Health license, and you must hire a response action contractor from the Department's list; violations are misdemeanors with daily fines. Buildings of fewer than 10 units and detached single-family homes are outside that licensing Act. For a renovation or demolition covered by the federal asbestos air-emission rules, the owner or operator must file a 10-day notice with the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency and pay its fee, and your city or county must remind you of that when it issues the permit. Never let anyone spray or disturb asbestos so that fibers escape. If your lease gives the tenant an option to buy a property with 1 to 4 dwelling units, or a condominium or cooperative unit, the Residential Real Property Disclosure Act applies to that lease: you must give the tenant the statutory disclosure report, answered from your actual knowledge, before the contract is signed (the cautious course is before the lease is signed), and its questions include whether you are aware of unsafe concentrations of or unsafe conditions relating to asbestos. Before renovation work that could disturb old insulation, flooring, plaster or textured ceilings, have the material tested, and tell affected tenants about the work and any precautions.

title: Bed Bugs and Pests: Tenant Cooperation
bodyText:
No Illinois statute requires a tenant to report bed bugs or other pests, to prepare the unit for treatment, or to let a pest control operator in, and no statute sets your treatment duties or deadlines. Those duties come from your lease, so the optional pest-cooperation clause asks the tenant to report suspected pests promptly, allow inspection and treatment under the lease's entry terms, and follow written preparation instructions.

Charges are limited: for leases the rental-fee law covers, you may not charge any fee or fine for pest abatement or removal where the tenant in no way contributed to the infestation, so treatment you pay for is the default and the clause charges the tenant only for an infestation caused by the tenant's household or guests.

If your property is financed under the Illinois Affordable Housing Program, the property manager must provide pest control as a funding standard. Illinois's Bedbug Inspection Act binds merchants who rent furniture or electronics, not landlords. Chicago and some other cities have their own bed bug ordinances; check yours.

title: Pesticide Application Notices
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires you to give tenants notice before or after pest control treatment inside a building, or to attach a pest control notice to the lease. The notice rules that do reach rental property are outdoors and on the applicator. When lawn care products (fertilizers or pesticides) are applied to a lawn by an applicator for hire, which includes your own employee applying them to lawns you own or manage, the applicator must place a lawn marker reading "LAWN CARE APPLICATION - STAY OFF GRASS UNTIL DRY" at the usual points of entry, including at residential properties of two or more families; the owner or resident removes it the next day. The applicator must also give the customer the product information the Act lists, and must notify in advance any neighbor who has asked. A commercial applicator of a barrier mosquito treatment must post comparable signs on residential property it treats. Anyone you hire to treat a building for insects or rodents must be a licensed structural pest control business, and if your own staff use restricted-use pesticides in your buildings, that location must be registered. Telling tenants in advance of any treatment, with the product used and any preparation or re-entry instructions, is good practice and helps the tenant cooperate. Chicago and other cities may have their own notice rules.

title: Waterbeds
bodyText:
No Illinois statute gives a tenant a right to keep a waterbed or other liquid-filled furniture, bars a lease from prohibiting one, or sets insurance, deposit, floor-load or installation rules for them. Whether to allow one is your choice, and the optional waterbed clause makes it subject to your prior written consent.

If you consent on conditions, put them in writing; any extra money you hold against waterbed damage should be handled as part of the security deposit, and a mandatory charge the tenant cannot avoid would have to be listed on the first page of the lease under the rental fee law. Local codes may limit floor loads.

title: Window and Portable Air Conditioners
bodyText:
No Illinois statute gives tenants a right to install a portable, window or through-the-wall air conditioner, bars a lease from restricting one, or requires the lease to disclose a restriction. Whether to allow them is your choice, and the optional cooling-equipment clause sets the terms.

Three related rules apply. In rental housing limited to people 55 or older, a building-wide cooling system must run from June 1 through September 30 whenever the heat index exceeds 80 degrees, and if there is no building-wide system you must provide at least one cooled indoor common gathering space, free to all tenants, when the heat index exceeds 80 degrees (a property with no such space is exempt). Housing financed under the Illinois Affordable Housing Program must meet funding standards for cooling and dehumidification. And a utility may not cut off gas or electricity for nonpayment when it is the only source of cooling at a residence, including master-metered apartment buildings, on forecast days of 90 degrees or more or during an excessive heat warning.

A tenant with a disability may need a cooling unit as a reasonable accommodation or modification, so handle those requests individually. Local codes may regulate window units and emergency-escape windows.

title: Tenant Cameras and Video Doorbells
bodyText:
No Illinois statute gives tenants a right to install security cameras or video doorbells, bars a lease from requiring your consent, or sets rules written for rentals. Two criminal laws set the limits for everyone, you included.

First, it is a crime to make a video recording or transmit live video of another person in that person's residence without consent, including from outside the residence with a remote device, and a rented apartment or house counts as a residence; stairwells, corridors, laundry rooms and other areas the public can use do not. So a tenant's camera must not look into a neighbor's unit, and you must never place a camera inside a tenant's home.

Second, Illinois eavesdropping law makes it a crime to record a private conversation secretly without the consent of everyone in it, so a camera or doorbell that records sound should be disclosed or have audio turned off. Damaging or disabling security cameras or other parts of a security system is also a crime.

Your lease can require consent before a tenant attaches a device to the building and set aiming and audio limits; the optional tenant-camera clause does that.

title: Private Wells Serving Rentals
bodyText:
No Illinois statute requires you to test a private well before each tenancy or to give tenants test results with the lease. But a well that serves rental housing is regulated as more than a homeowner's well.

Illinois treats a private water system as one serving an owner-occupied single-family home; a water supply serving anyone else, such as a rented house or a small apartment building, is a semi-private water system, and as its owner or operator you are its supplier of water. Semi-private systems must be built under Department of Public Health rules, the Department may inspect, and you must give it access. The law lets the Department require water samples on a schedule, but its current rules set no routine testing schedule for a semi-private system; they apply sampling rules to public water systems and to newly built or modified wells.

If the water fails a drinking water standard at the tap, you must conspicuously post a notice of the failure for as long as it continues. A system with 15 or more service connections, or regularly serving an average of 25 or more people daily for at least 60 days a year, is a public water system with its own rules.

If the Environmental Protection Agency finds groundwater contamination threatening a private or semi-private system, it notifies the property owner; tell your tenants promptly. Owners or users of private wells within half a mile of a landfill or hazardous waste facility can ask the Agency for free annual testing.

If your lease gives the tenant an option to buy a property with 1 to 4 dwelling units, or a condominium or cooperative unit, the Residential Real Property Disclosure Act applies to that lease: you must give the tenant the statutory disclosure report, answered from your actual knowledge, before the contract is signed (the cautious course is before the lease is signed), and its questions include whether you are aware of material defects in the well or well equipment or unsafe conditions in the drinking water.

Testing at each turnover and sharing results is good practice; the optional water-supply clause records it. We read the Department of Public Health's water and well rules.

title: Contaminated Property and Environmental Covenants
bodyText:
No Illinois statute requires you to tell a tenant that the property is or was contaminated, is a brownfield, or carries a recorded environmental use limitation, and none requires a lease to incorporate those limitations. But the limitations still bind the property.

An environmental covenant made under the Illinois Uniform Environmental Covenants Act runs with the land, and the agency may direct that a copy go to each person in possession of the property, which includes tenants. A No Further Remediation Letter from the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency is recorded in the chain of title and bars uses inconsistent with its land use limitations; failing to maintain the required controls can void the letter. The covenant itself may require notice when a specified interest is transferred or the use changes, so read it before you lease.

If you own a contaminated 1-to-4-unit property through an entity, or you are an individual who owns more than 10 dwelling units in Illinois, you can be liable for cleanup as the owner, and a lease indemnity cannot shift that liability to a tenant.

If your lease gives the tenant an option to buy a property with 1 to 4 dwelling units, or a condominium or cooperative unit, the Residential Real Property Disclosure Act applies to that lease: you must give the tenant the statutory disclosure report, answered from your actual knowledge, before the contract is signed (the cautious course is before the lease is signed), and its questions include underground fuel storage tanks, unsafe conditions in the drinking water and uncorrected notices of violation.

The optional environmental-use clause gives the tenant a copy of the limitations and makes compliance a lease duty.

If it requires notice to the agency or the holder of a lease or a change in use, give that notice when you lease.

title: Defective Drywall
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires you to disclose defective, corrosive or imported drywall to a tenant, or sets rules for remediating it in a rental. If your lease gives the tenant an option to buy a property with 1 to 4 dwelling units, or a condominium or cooperative unit, the Residential Real Property Disclosure Act applies to that lease: you must give the tenant the statutory disclosure report, answered from your actual knowledge, before the contract is signed (the cautious course is before the lease is signed), and its questions include whether you are aware of material defects in the walls, so known defective drywall would belong there. If you know of corrosive drywall or the problems it causes (sulfur odors, corroded wiring or copper), tell tenants and remediate it; concealing a known defect that affects health or safety invites liability.

title: Chemical Exposure Warnings
bodyText: Illinois has no law like California's Proposition 65: no statute requires you to post or give tenants a warning that the property exposes them to chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm, and no statute requires a formaldehyde notice for rental housing. The chemical warnings Illinois does require reach landlords only in narrow ways. The radon disclosure for residential leases is its own rule, covered in the radon rows. If you employ maintenance staff, the Toxic Substances Disclosure to Employees Act requires labels and information for employees about toxic substances they work with; it protects workers, not tenants. Other specific hazards (lead, asbestos, radon) have their own rules, covered in their own rows.

title: Military Air Zones and Aircraft Noise
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires you to tell a tenant that a property lies in a military air installation's noise zone, clear zone or accident potential zone, or near a military base, and no statute gives a tenant a right to end the lease on learning it. Illinois addresses these zones through land use, not disclosure: a county with a U.S. Air Force installation whose runways are at least 7,500 feet long may control land use in the zones mapped in the Air Force's compatible-use study, and may acquire land or easements in clear zones, accident potential zones or the 65-decibel noise contour where a use is incompatible. Airports with permanent noise monitoring publish noise contour maps. If your property is near Scott Air Force Base or a busy airport, telling applicants about aircraft noise avoids disputes, and you should check county zoning before changing the property's use.

title: Ordnance, Demolition and Shared-Meter Disclosures
bodyText: Of the three disclosures some states require before a lease is signed, Illinois requires only one. Shared utility meters: if a tenant's own utility account will also pay for service to common areas or other units, you must give a written statement of the areas and uses it serves, 12 months of the unit's bills (unless the tenant waives them in writing) and any rent reduction in writing before you offer the lease, take a deposit or otherwise agree to rent; see the shared-meter and common-area lighting rows. Former military ordnance sites: no Illinois statute requires you to disclose that the property is near one. Demolition: no Illinois statute requires you to tell applicants or tenants that you have applied for a demolition permit or plan to demolish the building; when a city or county issues a demolition or renovation permit for a building covered by federal asbestos rules, it must remind you of the federal asbestos notice, which goes to the Environmental Protection Agency, not tenants. Ending tenancies for a demolition still follows the ordinary notice rules, and local ordinances, including Chicago's, may add relocation or notice duties.

title: Shoreline and Lake Access
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires you to tell tenants about public rights of access along a shoreline, rights-of-way to the water, or public trust rights at a lakefront or riverfront rental. One shoreline rule can reach a property owner: if you own a pier, or a drop-off (a shoreline area intended for direct public access to the water), on Lake Michigan, you must install and maintain public rescue equipment, including ring life buoys in high-visibility stations with warning signage, and if the area becomes a high-incident drowning area you must update and share a water safety plan and upgrade the equipment within a year. If your rental includes private water frontage, a dock or a beach, setting use rules in the lease (guests, children, alcohol, swimming at one's own risk without releasing your own negligence) is your choice; a beach at an apartment or condominium building or association of 5 or more units is a licensed bathing beach under the swimming facility law.

title: Release of Tenants' Energy Usage Data
bodyText:
Illinois's Utility Data Access Act lets you get electric and gas usage data for your building from a large utility (one with more than 100,000 Illinois customers), at no charge, to use with the ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager benchmarking tool.

If the building has at least 5 utility accounts (residential and nonresidential combined), you can request whole-building data aggregated across tenant and owner meters without each tenant's consent. In a smaller building, the utility releases data from a tenant's own account only with the tenant's authorization, and the Act says that authorization may be given in a lease provision; it stays valid until the tenant revokes it.

The Illinois Commerce Commission must adopt the request procedures and a standard authorization form, so until those are in place the utility may ask for its own consent form. The optional energy-data clause provides the authorization and the tenant's promise to sign the utility's form; because the law lets a tenant revoke at any time, the clause does not treat revocation as a breach.

No Illinois statute requires you to benchmark a residential building; Chicago and some other cities may, by ordinance.

title: Recycling at Rental Properties
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires you to provide recycling at a rental property or to tell tenants where and how to recycle. Recycling is organized locally: each county's waste management plan must include a recycling program, and the plan may require residents to separate recyclable materials when they put out trash, so a county or city ordinance may set rules for your building and its collection service. A statewide recycling needs assessment has noted that many multifamily residences lack adequate recycling access, but it creates no duty for owners. If your building has recycling, say in the lease or house rules where the containers are and what goes in them, and keep any separation rules your local program requires. Any mandatory trash or recycling fee you charge must be listed on the first page of the lease under the rental fee law.

title: Notice and Cure Before Eviction
bodyText:
Illinois has two notice tracks before an eviction, plus a few special grounds.

Unpaid rent: a written demand giving at least 5 days to pay; full payment of the amount demanded within that time keeps the lease in force (see "Notice for Unpaid Rent").

Breach of any other lease term: when the tenant defaults in any of the terms of the lease, you may end the tenancy with a written notice to quit giving 10 days, in the form the statute suggests. The statute doesn't require that notice to offer a chance to fix the breach, and it doesn't limit this ground to a "material" breach: it reaches a default in any of the lease's terms.

No Illinois statute lets the lease set its own cure period or its own way of serving the notice in place of the statute's, and none lets the lease decide which terms are material. Whether a court will end a tenancy for a trivial breach, or enforce a lease clause that shortens the notice or adds a service method, is for the courts.

Cautious course: give the full 10 days, describe the breach in the notice, and serve it by a statutory method (handing it to the tenant, leaving it with a person 13 or older residing on or in possession of the premises, certified or registered mail with a returned receipt, or posting it if no one is in actual possession). You may give a longer period or a chance to fix the breach if you choose; the library's Illinois default clause says you need not where the law lets you proceed without one.

Special grounds: if the premises are used for a felony or Class A misdemeanor, or for drug activity, you may void the lease and give 5 days' written notice to vacate; if a tenant invites onto the premises a person you have barred by written notice, you may treat it as a breach of the lease even if the lease doesn't say so; and in subsidized housing, repeated refusals of inspection support an emergency eviction where the lease says so.

Limits: a tenant has a defense where the eviction is based solely on the tenant's or a household member's status as a victim of domestic or sexual violence, or on the tenant's immigration status, and retaliation is barred. No tenant may be evicted because rent is withheld under the Lead Poisoning Prevention Act, and multi-family housing assisted by the Illinois Affordable Housing Trust Fund may not evict without good cause.

Attach the notice and proof of service to the eviction complaint (and, for a breach case, the lease or its relevant parts).

For a property with a federally backed mortgage or in a covered federal housing program, federal law may also require at least 30 days' notice to vacate before you file (see "Federal 30-Day Notice to Vacate for Federally Backed Properties").

title: Your Remedies When a Tenant Defaults
bodyText: When a tenant defaults, Illinois gives you several remedies, and you can use them together. Possession: an eviction case filed in the circuit court for the county where the property is, after the demand or notice the default calls for. Rent with possession: you may join a claim for rent in the eviction complaint, including the pro rata rent for any period the eviction order is stayed, and the court may enter judgment for the rent found due. Other money claims, such as damage to the unit, can't be joined. If the tenant was notified only by posting or publication and doesn't appear, the court may decide possession only, and the rent claim waits until the tenant appears or is served. Money alone, with or without ending the lease: you may sue for unpaid rent or damages in an ordinary civil case. Illinois's circuit courts hear every such claim; there is no separate lower court. A claim of $10,000 or less, not counting interest and costs, can be brought as a small claim, but a corporation can bring one only through a lawyer (see "Entity Landlords in Court"). Other statutory remedies: double the yearly value against a tenant who willfully holds over after the term and after your written demand for possession, or double rent against a tenant who gives notice to leave and stays; distress for rent; and ejectment, without a formal demand, where half a year's rent is in arrears (the tenant can end that case by paying the arrears and costs before judgment). Your recovery is limited by your duty to take reasonable measures to mitigate your damages, such as trying to re-rent. No Illinois statute authorizes or bars a lease clause that makes all the rent for the rest of the term due at once on default ("acceleration"); whether one is enforceable, and how it fits with the mitigation duty and the rule against penalties, is case law. Cautious course: claim rent as it falls due, or for the period until the unit is re-let, and credit what re-renting brings in.

title: Keeping the Tenancy After a Rent Default
bodyText: Illinois gives a tenant who falls behind on rent a few statutory chances to keep the tenancy, and no general right to undo the forfeiture later. During the rent demand: if the tenant pays the full rent demanded within the time in your written demand (at least 5 days), the lease isn't terminated. Partial payments don't cancel the demand if it prominently carries the statutory statement, and you may agree in writing to continue the lease for a partial payment. Ejectment: where half a year's rent is in arrears you may bring an action of ejectment without a formal demand; the tenant may end it by paying or tendering the arrears and costs at any time before final judgment, and after judgment the lease ends unless the tenant wins an appeal or obtains relief by a petition filed within 6 months. After an eviction order: the order can't be enforced more than 120 days after entry unless you obtain an extension, and the court won't extend it if the tenant shows the tenancy was reinstated, the breach was cured or waived, or the tenant has kept a post-judgment agreement with you. We found no Illinois statute that lets a tenant reinstate the lease by paying the arrears after the demand period has run, before trial, after judgment or before the sheriff acts, and none that makes you accept such a payment. Collecting past-due rent after you file doesn't invalidate the case. The cure and stay rules for condominium owners and installment buyers don't apply to tenants. Whether a court could still relieve a tenant from forfeiture on equitable grounds is case law. Cautious course: decide before you take money after the demand period whether you are reinstating the tenancy, and if you aren't, say so in writing when you accept it, or return it. For a property with a federally backed mortgage or in a covered federal housing program, federal law may also require at least 30 days' notice to vacate before you file (see "Federal 30-Day Notice to Vacate for Federally Backed Properties").

title: Paying to Stop an Eviction
bodyText: Partial payments: after you serve a written demand for unpaid rent, partial payments that don't add up to the full amount demanded by the end of the notice period don't cancel the demand, but only if the demand prominently states: "Only FULL PAYMENT of the rent demanded in this notice will waive the landlord's right to terminate the lease under this notice, unless the landlord agrees in writing to continue the lease in exchange for receiving partial payment." You may agree in writing to continue the lease for a partial payment. Redemption: the tenant's statutory chance to pay is the demand period itself (at least 5 days): full payment of the rent demanded within it keeps the lease. Illinois has no statute that lets a tenant redeem the tenancy later, up to a set time before the eviction is carried out, and collecting past-due rent after you file doesn't invalidate the case. No statute says that paying a money judgment for rent bars enforcement of the eviction order; but an order not enforced within 120 days can be extended only on your motion, and the court will refuse if the tenant shows the tenancy was reinstated, the breach was cured or waived, or a post-judgment agreement with you was kept. Third-party payments: no Illinois statute requires an ordinary landlord to accept rent paid by a charity, government agency or other third party on the tenant's behalf, or bars you from restricting how such a payment is made; the state emergency rental assistance law says nothing in it requires a landlord to accept program funds. The exception is a receiver appointed in a mortgage foreclosure, who must accept rent from an occupant and payments from a third party or a rental assistance program in support of the occupant's housing. Whether a full payment tendered by someone else within the demand period counts as the tenant's payment is case law. Separate payment-method rules still apply to every payment: if you use a third-party payment portal that charges a fee, you must allow a way to pay without the fee, and a large complex with an on-site office must accept rent there. Cautious course: put the statutory statement in every rent demand, accept full payment of the amount demanded from any source within the notice period, and put any agreement to continue the lease for less in writing. For a property with a federally backed mortgage or in a covered federal housing program, federal law may also require at least 30 days' notice to vacate before you file (see "Federal 30-Day Notice to Vacate for Federally Backed Properties").

title: Possession Bonds
bodyText: Illinois has no statutory possession bond: nothing lets you take from a tenant a bond to deliver possession at the end of the term, with a confessed judgment for possession if the tenant stays. Article IX gives no confessed judgment for possession at all; possession is recovered only through an eviction case. A confession-of-judgment clause (a warrant authorizing someone to confess a judgment against the tenant without a suit) is void in any instrument used in a consumer transaction made after September 24, 1979. Whether that bar reaches a residential lease of real property is unresolved by statute (see "Confession of Judgment"), so the cautious course is never to put one in a residential lease. The only bond in Illinois's landlord statutes is a tenant's bond, in double the rent claimed, to release property you have seized by distress for rent. Appeal and stay bonds in eviction cases are set by the Supreme Court's rules, which we did not review. The library doesn't offer a possession bond for Illinois. To make sure you get possession at the end of the term, rely on the lease's end date (no notice to quit is needed when a fixed term expires), the holdover remedies, and an eviction case if the tenant stays.

title: Stays of Eviction
bodyText: We found no Illinois statute that lets a court postpone a tenant's eviction for hardship, such as illness, age, children in the home, winter weather or inability to find housing. The statutes that do affect timing: in a residential eviction, if military service materially affects a service member tenant's ability to pay, the court may on its own motion, and must on the tenant's motion, stay the case for 90 days (longer or shorter if justice and equity require) or adjust the rent obligation, and may give you relief equity requires. In evictions after a lease is voided for drug or criminal use of the premises, and in the emergency public-housing and subsidized-housing evictions, the eviction order may not be stayed for more than 7 days (in the criminal-activity case, unless all parties agree). Installment buyers and condominium owners have their own longer stays; they don't apply to tenants. The statutes assume that ordinary eviction orders may be stayed: you may ask for the pro rata rent for any period the order is stayed, and an order not enforced within 120 days needs an extension. How long a stay the court sets, and on what grounds, is decided under the Supreme Court's standardized eviction order and rules, and by local practice and mediation programs, none of which we reviewed. Cautious course: ask in the complaint for the pro rata rent during any stay, expect the court to set the enforcement date, and point a tenant in crisis to the state's homelessness-prevention and crisis-assistance programs.

title: Service of Eviction Papers
bodyText: We found no Illinois statute that lets a lease, or a tenant, name a person or agent to accept the summons in an eviction case on the tenant's behalf. Service of a summons on an individual is made, except where a statute expressly provides otherwise, by handing it to the tenant personally, or by leaving it at the tenant's usual home with a family member or resident aged 13 or older, telling that person what it is, and also mailing a copy to the tenant there. Service is made by the sheriff, a licensed private detective or registered employee of a detective agency, or a person the court appoints. Eviction cases add three rules: occupants who aren't parties to any lease can be named and served as "unknown occupants" through any occupant 13 or older; if personal service fails and you file an affidavit that the tenant can't be found, the tenant can be notified by posting and mailing, or publication and mailing, but then the court decides only possession, not a rent claim, unless the tenant appears; and pre-suit demands and notices have their own service methods (see "Notice and Cure Before Eviction"). Address confidentiality: a tenant enrolled in the Attorney General's Address Confidentiality Program has designated the Attorney General as agent for service of process and receipt of mail. If a tenant tells you they are a participant, talk to a lawyer about how to serve them; the program's procedures weren't reviewed here. The library doesn't offer a clause naming a person to accept eviction papers for Illinois; the shared notices clause records each party's notice address.

title: Cold-Weather Vacating Notice
bodyText:
We found no Illinois statute that requires a tenant to warn you before vacating, or before leaving the unit empty, in cold weather, or that sets a duty to keep the heat on to stop pipes freezing. Illinois's statutory heating rule runs the other way and is narrow: in housing limited to people 55 or older, a landlord whose building has a premises-wide heating system must keep the units at set minimum temperatures during the heating season (October 1 through May 31).

If you want notice before a tenant leaves the unit empty, or want the tenant to keep the heat at a minimum setting while away, that is a lease term you choose; Illinois has no statute that supplies or limits it.

The library offers an optional winter clause (keep the heat at 55 degrees or more from October 1 to May 1, and give written notice before an absence of more than 3 days in that period) and an optional year-round "Notice of Extended Absence" clause for Illinois.

title: Late Benefit or Voucher Payments
bodyText: We found no Illinois statute that gives a tenant a defense, a continuance or reinstatement in an eviction because a Social Security check, another government benefit or a housing voucher payment arrived late. For the tenant's own share of the rent, the ordinary rules apply: a written demand giving at least 5 days to pay, and full payment within that time keeps the lease. One federal rule protects voucher tenants. In the Housing Choice Voucher program, the family isn't responsible for the part of the rent covered by the housing authority's payment, the housing authority's failure to pay it isn't a lease violation, and during the lease term you may not terminate the tenancy for the authority's nonpayment. Your remedy is against the housing authority under your payment contract with it. Other points: a tenant whose household faces eviction because of a temporary crisis such as a loss or delay of public benefits may qualify for state homelessness-prevention assistance; and refusing to rent because a tenant pays with a voucher or other lawful source of income is covered in "Source of Income". Practical course: when a tenant tells you a benefit or assistance payment is late, document it, consider accepting a dated payment plan in writing, and don't serve a demand for any portion a housing authority owes. For a property with a federally backed mortgage or in a covered federal housing program, federal law may also require at least 30 days' notice to vacate before you file (see "Federal 30-Day Notice to Vacate for Federally Backed Properties").

title: Tenant Bankruptcy
bodyText: A tenant's bankruptcy is governed by the federal Bankruptcy Code, and Illinois law adds nothing specific: we found no Illinois statute on a tenant's bankruptcy, on lease clauses that make bankruptcy or insolvency a default, on collecting rent or seeking possession from a bankrupt tenant, or on whether an eviction order is enforced after the landlord learns of the tenant's bankruptcy filing. Under federal law, the filing automatically stops (stays) any lawsuit or collection of a pre-filing debt against the tenant, and any act to take possession of property of the bankruptcy estate, which includes the tenant's lease. Two exceptions matter to landlords. First, if you got a judgment for possession before the tenant filed, you may generally continue the eviction, but the tenant can delay that for 30 days by certifying that Illinois law would let them cure the whole rent default and depositing the next 30 days' rent with the bankruptcy court clerk; if the tenant then cures the whole default within those 30 days, the exception does not apply unless the court orders otherwise. You may object, and the court must hold a hearing within 10 days. Second, an eviction based on the tenant endangering the property or illegal drug use on it may proceed 15 days after you file and serve a sworn certification, unless the tenant objects and shows the situation did not exist or has been fixed. A lease clause that ends the lease because the tenant becomes insolvent or files for bankruptcy can't be enforced after the filing. In a Chapter 7 case, the residential lease is treated as rejected if the trustee does not assume or reject it within 60 days (or a longer time the court sets); in Chapter 11, 12 or 13 the decision can wait until the plan is confirmed unless the court sets a deadline on request. Cautious course: once you learn a tenant has filed for bankruptcy, stop any eviction filing, rent demand for past rent, collection or lockout, and talk to a lawyer before taking any step against the tenant or the lease; don't rely on a bankruptcy-default clause.

title: Entity Landlords in Court
bodyText: Who may appear in court: an individual landlord may bring an eviction or a money claim in person. A corporation may not practice law or appear as an attorney in any court, and only a licensed attorney may practice law. An Illinois statute lets a corporation prosecute or defend a small claim (up to $2,500 in that statute) through an officer, director, manager, department manager or supervisor, but the Supreme Court's small-claims rule says no corporation may appear as a claimant in a small claims proceeding unless represented by a lawyer, and lets a corporation defend through an officer or manager. No statute or rule we read lets a property manager or other non-lawyer appear for an entity landlord in an eviction case, and none speaks to limited liability companies. Cautious course: if your landlord is a corporation, LLC, partnership or trust, file evictions and claims through a licensed Illinois attorney. You or your manager may still sign and serve the pre-suit demands and notices, which the statutes let an agent sign. Out-of-state entities: a foreign LLC or corporation transacting business in Illinois may not maintain a civil action in any Illinois court until it is admitted (registered) to do business here. Its leases stay valid and it may defend a suit, and it faces back fees and penalties. Merely owning real property isn't transacting business, but renting out property may be, so register before you file an eviction. Assumed names: an individual or partnership that rents property under a name other than the owners' real names must file a certificate with the county clerk and publish notice, and failing to do so is a misdemeanor. A corporation or LLC using a name other than its true name must file an assumed-name application with the Secretary of State before doing business under it. Put your true legal name in the lease and the court papers.

title: Time Limits for Lawsuits
bodyText: Written lease: you have 10 years after a claim accrues to sue on a written lease, for unpaid rent or other money the lease makes the tenant owe. If the tenant makes a payment or a new promise to pay in writing, within or after those 10 years, you have 10 years from that payment or promise. Oral lease and property damage: claims on an unwritten agreement, claims for injury to property, and other civil actions not otherwise provided for must be brought within 5 years. Whether a payment restarts that 5-year period isn't stated in the statute. Personal injury and statutory penalties: 2 years. Time a defendant spends out of Illinois after the claim accrues generally doesn't count, unless the defendant could be served under Illinois's long-arm and similar service statutes. The lease can't be relied on to change these periods: no Illinois statute lets a residential lease shorten or lengthen a limitation period (only the commercial code does that, for sales and leases of goods), and whether a court would enforce such a clause is case law. Cautious course: don't put a shortened period in the lease, keep the lease, rent ledger and move-out records for at least 10 years after the last charge, and get any payment plan or acknowledgment of the debt in writing. Claims a tenant may bring against you have their own periods, not covered here.

title: When Rent Cannot Be Demanded or Collected
bodyText: Illinois has no general rule that bars you from demanding or collecting rent, or serving a rent demand, because a unit has code violations or is in poor condition. Whether rent is fully owed for a defective unit turns on the lease and on case law (the implied warranty of habitability), which this library hasn't reviewed. A few statutes do stop or redirect rent: Dangerous conditions: if residential property is kept in a condition that endangers anyone's health or safety, the State's Attorney may get a court order barring the owner or manager from collecting, receiving or benefiting from the rents while the condition lasts, and the court may order rents paid into an escrow account used for repairs, taxes and other property debts. The statute says it doesn't authorize tenants to stop paying rent on their own. Lead hazards: if you don't complete ordered lead mitigation, the State's Attorney must take measures to have tenants of the affected units withhold rent until you comply, and no tenant may be evicted for that withholding. Foreclosure successors: a foreclosure buyer or holder, a mortgagee in possession or a receiver who doesn't give occupants the required written notice may not collect rent due from a known occupant, or end the tenancy for not paying it, until the notice is served; and an occupant who already paid the current period's rent to the owner or manager isn't liable for it again. Other statutes let a tenant pay less rather than barring your demand: repair-and-deduct, paying a landlord's unpaid utility bill and deducting it, and radon mitigation with your consent (see their rows), and penalties apply in large counties for collecting rent on an illegal extra apartment. Cautious course: fix dangerous conditions promptly, don't demand rent covered by a withholding order or escrow, and if you take over a building through foreclosure, serve the occupant notice before collecting rent.

title: Double Letting
bodyText: We found no Illinois statute on "double letting" (renting the same room or unit to two tenants for the same period), on failure to deliver possession at the start of a lease, or setting a rent abatement or other remedy when either happens. A landlord who promises the same unit to two people breaks a contract with at least one of them, and the ordinary remedies for breach of contract apply. The library's "Possession Delay" clause, which carries Illinois, covers the tenant's side: no rent while you can't deliver possession, and the tenant may cancel and get everything back if possession isn't delivered within 30 days. Cautious course: we treat the Consumer Fraud Act as possibly reaching residential leasing, so don't advertise or sign a unit you have already let; keep one booking record per unit; don't take a second deposit or application fee for a unit already promised; and refund promptly if a booking falls through.

title: Barring Non-Tenants and Trespass Warnings
bodyText: Illinois gives you a statutory way to bar a non-tenant from your property. Barring a person: you may bar from premises you own anyone who isn't a tenant or a member of the tenant's household. To make it bind the tenant, give the tenant written notice that the person is no longer allowed on the premises; the notice must say that if the tenant invites the barred person onto any part of the premises, you may treat it as a breach of the lease, and that works whether or not the lease contains such a term. You may then evict, except that a tenant or household member who is a victim of domestic violence, sexual violence, stalking or dating violence has a defense if the victim didn't knowingly consent to the barred person's entry or a valid court order allowed it. Criminal trespass: you may also give the barred person notice directly, in person (orally or in writing), or by a written notice conspicuously posted at the main entrance. A person who enters after that notice commits criminal trespass to real property, and a later invitation from a tenant or household member is void and no defense. Outside that procedure, Illinois's criminal trespass law doesn't apply to anyone living on the land by a lease or other arrangement with the owner, or to anyone they invite to visit them there, so a tenant's invited guest is not a trespasser unless you have barred that person. It also doesn't apply to a building open to the public during its normal hours, to entry in an emergency, or to process servers. Nothing in the eviction Article stops police from enforcing criminal trespass or removing trespassers. Cautious course: bar people only for conduct-based reasons you can document, apply the same standard to everyone, keep copies of both notices, never bar a tenant or household member, and handle a domestic-violence situation with the victim's protections in mind. Fair housing limits on guest bans weren't reviewed here. The library doesn't offer a barred-person clause for Illinois, because the statute applies whether or not the lease says so.

title: Notice of Extended Absence
bodyText:
We found no Illinois statute that requires a tenant to tell you before an extended absence, that invites the lease to require it, or that gives you a right to enter during a tenant's absence. Illinois also has no statute defining when a house or apartment is abandoned, so a tenant's absence alone doesn't end the lease or let you retake the unit.

An absence-notice duty is therefore a lease term you choose. The library offers an optional Illinois "Notice of Extended Absence" clause: the tenant gives written notice by the first day of an absence longer than the number of days you set, and is responsible for actual damage the notice would have let you prevent. It charges no fee and doesn't treat an absence as abandonment.

An optional winter clause also asks for notice before an absence of more than 3 days between October 1 and May 1 (see "Cold-Weather Vacating Notice"). Entry during an absence follows the lease's entry clause.

title: Tenancy at Will
bodyText: Illinois statutes don't use the terms "tenancy at will" or "tenancy at sufferance" and set no notice for ending one. They work by rental period instead: where a tenant holds over without special agreement, you may end a week-to-week tenancy with 7 days' written notice and any other tenancy of less than a year, including month to month, with 30 days' written notice; a year-to-year tenancy takes 60 days' written notice ending at the end of the year. For these rules a "lease" includes every letting, oral or written. Where someone holds and occupies land without any special agreement for rent, you may sue for a fair and reasonable payment for its use and occupation. Whether a particular informal arrangement is a tenancy at will, a periodic tenancy or something else, and what notice ends a true tenancy at will, is decided by Illinois case law. Cautious course: treat an open-ended residential occupancy for which rent is paid by the week or month as a periodic tenancy and give the matching written notice (7 or 30 days), served by a statutory method; for an occupant with no agreement and no rent, serve a written demand for possession before filing; and in every case recover possession only through an eviction case. For a property with a federally backed mortgage or in a covered federal housing program, federal law may also require at least 30 days' notice to vacate before you file (see "Federal 30-Day Notice to Vacate for Federally Backed Properties").

title: Seasonal and Short-Term Rentals
bodyText: We found no Illinois statute that creates a special category of seasonal or vacation tenancy, such as one that ends automatically at the end of a season or is exempt from the eviction process. Illinois's eviction Article applies to any lease or letting, so a seasonal rental is treated like any other: a fixed term ends on its stated date with no notice to quit needed, and an occupant who stays on must be removed through the courts. If you rent by the week or month with no fixed end date, it's a periodic tenancy ended by written notice (7 days for weekly, 30 days for monthly). So state the exact start and end dates in a seasonal agreement. Short stays bring different rules. A building held out to the public for lodging with 25 or more rooms is a "hotel" under the Innkeeper Protection Act, and its operator may remove a guest who refuses to pay or breaks its posted rules, refunding any unused advance payment; but that power can't be used as a pretext to end a month-to-month, yearly or other lease of a permanent resident without the legal process a lease termination requires. For the hotel tax, a dwelling rented for less than 30 consecutive days is a short-term rental and anyone occupying for at least 30 consecutive days is a permanent resident. Whether a particular short stay is a tenancy or a hotel-type license is case law, and local ordinances often regulate short-term rentals. For a property with a federally backed mortgage or in a covered federal housing program, federal law may also require at least 30 days' notice to vacate before you file (see "Federal 30-Day Notice to Vacate for Federally Backed Properties").

title: Tenant Early Termination Rights
bodyText:
Illinois statutes let a residential tenant end a lease early in these cases (each has its own row):
- Military service: a service member tenant (or a family member living with them) who enters military service for more than 29 days after signing, or gets orders for a permanent change of station or a deployment of at least 90 days, may end the lease by giving you the orders; a second statute adds that the tenant then owes rent only to the termination date and no other rent or liquidated damages, though still liable for damage the tenant caused.
- Domestic or sexual violence: a tenant who leaves because of a credible imminent threat, or after sexual violence on the premises, and gives the statutory written notice isn't liable for rent after leaving.
- Flooding: if you didn't give the required flood-zone disclosure, the tenant may end the lease within 30 days of learning the property is in the 100-year floodplain, or within 30 days after a flood that damages belongings or affects habitability or access, and you must refund rent and fees paid in advance within 15 days.
- Radon: for leases since January 1, 2024, a tenant whose test within the first 90 days shows a hazard you choose not to mitigate may end the lease, and a tenant who never got the radon pamphlet and disclosure may test and end the lease later.
- Utilities: if you are required to pay for water, gas or electric service and don't, the tenant may end the lease.
- Retaliation: a tenant you retaliate against may end the lease and recover the deposit, interest and prepaid rent.

There's no Illinois statute letting a tenant end a lease because the landlord made a fraudulent misrepresentation; a misled tenant's remedies come from contract and fraud law and possibly the Consumer Fraud Act.

And one statute runs the other way: a tenant who didn't tell a resident landlord who is a child sex offender that the tenant has children can't end the lease on discovering the landlord's status.

Leaving out a required lease term doesn't release the tenant from the lease in Illinois, but it can cost you money: a non-optional fee not stated on the lease's first page isn't owed.

Outside these cases, a tenant who leaves early remains liable under the lease, subject to your duty to mitigate.

title: Early Termination for Illness or Care
bodyText: We found no Illinois statute that lets a residential tenant end a lease early because of age, illness or disability, or because the tenant must move into a nursing home, assisted living or other care facility, and none that ends a month-to-month or other open-ended tenancy on a party's incapacity. So unless the lease gives that right, a tenant who leaves early for those reasons is treated like any other tenant who ends a fixed term early (your duty to mitigate applies), and a month-to-month tenant can end the tenancy with the ordinary 30 days' written notice. Two cautions. A request from a tenant with a disability to be released early, or to leave on shorter notice, may be a request for a reasonable accommodation in your rules, policies or practices; consider it in good faith rather than refusing automatically (see "Disability Modifications and Accommodations"). And Illinois's statutory early-termination rights for service members and for victims of domestic or sexual violence, and its other statutory release rights, apply whatever the tenant's age or health (see "Tenant Early Termination Rights"). The library doesn't offer an infirmity-termination clause for Illinois; the shared early-termination option already lets a tenant end a fixed term for a fee.

title: Environmental Events and the Lease
bodyText:
We found no Illinois statute that lets either side end a residential lease because of an environmental or public-health event, such as contamination, a hazardous-material or fuel spill, a sewage or water-system failure, or a government order to vacate. Illinois has no general casualty statute for leased homes either.

The related statutory rights are narrower: a tenant may end the lease over undisclosed flooding or an unmitigated radon hazard, and lead-hazard enforcement can redirect rent (see their rows). Whether a lease ends, or rent abates, when the home becomes unlivable without a lease term is case law.

So a right to end the lease after an environmental event is a lease term you choose. The library offers two optional Illinois clauses: "Fire or Other Casualty" and "Termination After an Environmental Event", which lets either side end the lease if, through no fault of the tenant's household or guests, a government authority orders the property vacated or declares it unfit to live in because of an environmental event, with rent prorated, prepaid rent refunded and the deposit returned.

title: Owner Move-In Terminations
bodyText:
We found no Illinois statute that gives a landlord a right to end a lease early so the owner or a family member can move in, or that sets a minimum ownership period, notice or relocation payment for doing so. Illinois has no statewide just-cause rule either, so a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy can be ended on the ordinary written notice without a reason (30 days for month to month), as long as the reason isn't retaliatory or discriminatory.

For a fixed-term lease, the right to end early for owner occupancy exists only if the lease reserves it; a silent lease binds you to the full term.

Three limits apply even with a reservation. After a mortgage foreclosure, an individual who buys the property at the judicial sale and will live in it as a primary residence may end a tenant's bona fide lease only on at least 90 days' written notice, and other foreclosure successors may end it only at the end of its term on 90 days' notice. Under federal Housing Choice Voucher rules, an owner may not end the tenancy during the initial lease term for the owner's personal or family use. And multi-family housing assisted by the Illinois Affordable Housing Trust Fund may not evict without good cause. Some local ordinances add their own rules (not covered).

The library offers an optional Illinois "Owner Occupancy" clause for a fixed term: you name who will move in, give written notice of at least the period you choose (not less than 30 days, or 90 days if you bought at a foreclosure sale while the lease was in effect) ending on the last day of a monthly rental period, refund rent paid for later periods, and regain possession only through the court if the tenant doesn't leave.

title: Electric Submetering: No Disclosure Statute, and Resale Is Unsettled
bodyText: No Illinois statute sets a disclosure, form or rate rule for a landlord who submeters electricity or gas and bills tenants for their metered use. Two rules still apply. First, if the lease makes the tenant pay a share of a master-metered public utility service, you must give the tenant the formula you use to allocate the bill, in writing in the lease or another written agreement, before you demand payment; the formula must include everyone who uses the service and may reflect differences in unit size or usage, the total you collect for the building for a billing period may not exceed what the utility billed, and you must show the utility bill on request (see the shared master-metered utilities clause). Second, the Public Utilities Act treats a business that furnishes electricity for public use as a public utility, counts resellers of electricity to retail customers as alternative retail electric suppliers, and recognizes resale or redistribution of electricity inside a building only for arrangements in place before 1957 (or lighting service to tenants), and then only as far as the electric utility's tariffs allowed. No statute says whether a landlord who bills tenants by submeter is a reseller or a public utility, and the Illinois Commerce Commission's rules and the utilities' tariffs may restrict resale. The cautious course: do not sell electricity or gas to tenants at a rate or markup of your own; either include it in the rent, have tenants take service in their own names, or use a written allocation formula under which the building total never exceeds the utility's bill. Electric vehicle charging is separate: the law lets you charge a tenant for charging-system electricity based on an embedded submetering device or a reasonable calculation (see the EV charging rows).

title: Energy Upgrade Charges on the Electric Meter
bodyText:
Illinois law sets up two kinds of on-bill programs for energy upgrades, and they treat rental property differently. Under the Equitable Energy Upgrade Program, which the Illinois Commerce Commission must direct electric utilities to adopt on the Pay As You Save model, a property owner, or a renter with the owner's permission, can have an energy project (solar, efficiency, storage or demand-response equipment) installed and pay for it through an optional tariff charge on the electric bill.

The law says these charges create no personal debt and no lien, stop while an upgrade is not working (the utility may restart them once it is repaired and extend the payment term to recover what was missed), and, if they go unpaid, the remaining balance stays with the utility meter at the upgraded location, so whoever later holds the electric account at that meter, such as your next tenant, may be billed the charge.

The older on-bill loan programs for electric and gas efficiency measures are open only to customers who own the building; the loan is the borrower's own responsibility, must be paid off when the borrower sells or ends service, and an owner of a multifamily building may not use them so that repayment comes through tenants' utility bills (the electric loan program is set to be repealed on January 1, 2027).

No Illinois statute requires you to tell a tenant or the next customer about an on-bill charge on the meter; the Commission's program guidelines and the utility's tariff may.

The cautious course: if a Pay As You Save charge is on the meter for a rental, tell a prospective tenant in writing before the lease is signed, and use the optional clause to say whether the tenant pays it with the electric bill or you reimburse it.

If the tenant pays the charge, list it on the first page of the lease as a utility charge the tenant pays.

title: Utility Allowances and Caps on Utility Charges
bodyText:
No Illinois statute sets a utility allowance or caps what you may charge a tenant for utility use above an allowance.

One statute caps utility charges you pass through. If the lease makes tenants pay a proportionate share of a master-metered public utility service, you must first give the tenant the allocation formula in writing (in the lease or another written agreement); the formula must include everyone who uses the service and may reflect unit size or usage; the total you collect from the building for a billing period may not exceed what the utility demanded; and you must make the utility bill available on request.

So an allowance-with-overage arrangement on a meter that serves more than one unit is a formula allocation and must meet those rules; use the shared master-metered utilities clause for it. The statute names no fine; a tenant who overpays would sue for the excess.

On a meter that serves only the rented unit, no statute limits an allowance with a tenant-paid overage, and the optional allowance clause keeps the overage at the utility's actual charge. Any utility charge the tenant must pay you is listed on the first page of the lease under the rental fee law.

In public housing, federal rules let the housing authority charge for excess utility use only on an individual check meter or for major tenant-supplied appliances, and the lease must state how the charge is figured; in the voucher program, the housing authority sets a utility allowance schedule for tenant-paid utilities, reviewed yearly, and may base its allowance on a flat utility fee you bill directly only if your fee is no greater than its allowance for the utilities covered.

title: Utility Disclosures That Go With the Lease
bodyText: Illinois has three utility disclosures, each with its own vehicle. (1) Under the rental fee law, the lease (or the listing) must say whether utilities are included in the rent, and every non-optional utility charge you bill must be on the lease's first page; the first-page fee box does both. (2) If the lease makes tenants pay a share of a master-metered public utility service, you must give the allocation formula in writing, as part of the lease or in another written agreement, before you can demand payment; the shared master-metered utilities clause is that writing. (3) If a tenant will pay a utility account in the tenant's own name that also serves common areas or other units, you must, before offering the lease or a renewal, taking a deposit or otherwise agreeing to rent, give a written statement of the areas and uses that meter serves and copies of the unit's bills for the previous 12 months (unless the tenant waives them in writing), and state in writing any rent reduction offered for that outside use. Because that statement must come before the lease offer, it is a separate document, not a lease attachment signed with the lease. No Illinois statute prescribes a utility form or schedule to attach to the lease beyond these.

title: Copies of a Tenant's Utility Shutoff Notices
bodyText:
No Illinois statute lets a tenant name the landlord, or lets a landlord arrange with a utility, to receive copies of the notices a utility sends before disconnecting the tenant's own gas, electric or water service.

The statutes run the other way: when you are the customer and fail to pay for service the tenants depend on, the utility must notify all tenants of a building with 3 or more apartments, at least 10 days before the shutoff date, of their rights to pay the bill and deduct it from rent or to ask a court for a receiver.

The Illinois Commerce Commission's rules for the gas, electric, water and sewer utilities it regulates do let a customer, by written request to the utility, name a third party (such as you) to receive a duplicate of every disconnection notice, sent at the same time as the customer's; the utility may not disconnect until at least 10 days after the notice.
