Being named does not make you responsible for the bill: under the Commission's rule on landlord service agreements, a utility may not hold you responsible for an amount a tenant owes. Municipal and cooperative utilities outside the Commission's rules may or may not offer this. The optional clause has the tenant name you. We read the Commission's disconnection-notice rule.

title: Interrupting Utilities: No Submeter Rule, One General Rule
bodyText:
Illinois has no separate rule for interrupting electricity or other utilities that you submeter or bill to tenants.

One rule covers every arrangement: you may not cause or ask for utility service to tenants in an occupied building to be interrupted, discontinued or terminated by not paying a utility bill you took on (by agreement or by implication, as with a master meter) or by tampering with equipment or lines.

You may shut service off temporarily in an emergency such as a gas leak or fire, and for building repairs or rehabilitation on at least 7 days' written notice to each affected tenant.

A tenant whose service you cut off unlawfully recovers a full rent abatement for the time it was off plus consequential damages, and if you acted deliberately, recklessly or in bad faith, statutory damages of up to $300 per tenant (or $5,000 divided among the affected tenants, if less).

So you may never use a submeter, valve or shutoff device to cut a tenant's service for unpaid rent or an unpaid utility charge; collect those as money owed. The optional repair-shutoff clause states the 7-day notice rule in the lease. Utility companies' own shutoffs for nonpayment follow separate rules (see the utility shutoff row).

title: When a Utility May Shut Off Service at a Rental
bodyText: Illinois limits when gas and electric utilities may shut off residential service, including service to all tenants of master-metered apartment buildings, for nonpayment. Temperature: where gas or electricity is the only source of space heating, or runs the only heating equipment, no shutoff on a day when the 24-hour forecast is 32 degrees Fahrenheit or below, or before a holiday or weekend forecast at that level; where it is the only source of cooling, no shutoff on a forecast of 90 degrees or above, before such a holiday or weekend, or during a National Weather Service excessive heat watch, heat advisory or excessive heat warning. Winter: from December 1 through March 31, where gas or electricity is the primary heat source, a utility may not disconnect a residential customer or a master-metered apartment building unless it has offered a deferred payment plan of at least 4 months (down payment no more than 10%) and a list of assistance agencies, the customer has refused or failed to enter the plan, and all notices have been given; and it must wait 6 business days after its winter contact. Customers in the state energy assistance program, and customers who have told the utility they are a service member or veteran, may not be disconnected in that period at all. Landlord-paid service: if you fail to pay for water, gas or electricity you are required to pay, the utility must notify all tenants of a building with 3 or more apartments at least 10 days before the shutoff date, on red paper in bold type, of their rights to pay and deduct from rent or to seek a receiver, and it is a misdemeanor for you to remove or deface that notice; tenants may also end the lease or pay and deduct. You may not cause a shutoff yourself (see the interruption row). No statute found bars shutoffs during a declared storm or disaster emergency. The Illinois Commerce Commission's disconnection rules add notice requirements.

title: Billing Tenants for Utilities: What Illinois Requires
bodyText:
Illinois has no submetering statute, no prescribed submetering disclosure form and no regulator-set billing fee. Billing tenants for utilities is governed by two landlord-tenant statutes.

(1) Shared master meter: before you can demand that a tenant pay a proportionate share of a master-metered public utility service, you must give the tenant your allocation formula in writing, in the lease or another written agreement. The formula must include everyone who uses the service and may reflect unit size or usage (so a usage reading from a submeter can be part of it); the total collected from the building for a billing period may not exceed what the utility demanded; and you must give a copy of the utility bill on request. Because of that cap, the cautious course is not to add a billing or administration fee to a utility allocation. Leasing with utilities included in the rent, without allocating them, is unaffected.

(2) Changing who pays: you may not switch a tenant from landlord-paid to tenant-paid utilities, or from a landlord-paid master meter to tenant-paid individual meters, during a lease term. You must give at least 30 days' notice, and a tenant under a lease must get it at least 30 days before the lease expires, unless you and the tenant sign a written lease amendment; lease terms to the contrary are void.

A tenant-paid meter that also serves common areas or other units needs a written statement and 12 months of bills before you offer the lease (see the shared-meter row). Any utility charge the tenant pays you is listed on the lease's first page. No statute lets you shut off service or evict specially for unpaid utility charges, and you may not interrupt service yourself.

title: Putting Utilities in the Tenant's Name
bodyText:
No Illinois statute requires a tenant to transfer utility accounts into the tenant's name, and none lets you cut off service that stays in your name because the tenant has not transferred it. The lease decides who holds each account, and the optional transfer clause has the tenant open the accounts and repay you for service billed to you meanwhile.

Do not close, stop paying or ask a utility to disconnect an account serving an occupied unit to force a transfer: Illinois bars a landlord from causing utility service to tenants in an occupied building to be interrupted by not paying bills the landlord has taken on, by agreement or by implication, and a tenant whose service is cut off can recover a full rent abatement plus damages. Recover the cost as money owed instead.

If a meter in the tenant's name would also serve common areas or other units, the written statement and 12 months of bills must come before the lease offer (see the shared-meter row), and you may not shift a utility from you to the tenant during a lease term without a signed written amendment.

Between tenants: under the Illinois Commerce Commission's rules, you and a utility may agree in writing in advance that service at a unit goes into your name when a tenant leaves and no one else has applied; the utility must tell you within two business days, separately from the bill, that you are being billed from then on, and a utility may not hold you responsible for any amount a tenant owes it.

A tenant who opens an account may be asked for a utility deposit under the Commission's deposit rules. Of the Illinois Administrative Code we read only the Commission's landlord-agreement and deposit rules.

For leases the rental fee law covers, list the tenant's repayment of service billed to you among the conditional charges on the first page of the lease.

title: Water and Sewer Liens for a Tenant's Unpaid Bills
bodyText:
In Illinois, unpaid charges for municipal water, sewer and combined water-and-sewer service, and for county, township, public water district and sanitary district water or sewer service, become liens on the property served once they are delinquent under the provider's ordinance, whoever ran up the bill, including a tenant who held the account. No Illinois statute exempts an owner because a tenant held the account, and none lets you file an affidavit or a copy of the lease to keep a tenant's bill off the property.

The protections are procedural. Under the municipal sewer and combined water-and-sewer statutes, and the county, public water district and sanitary district statutes, the provider creates a lien only if it sends the owner of record a copy of each delinquency notice (or other notice that the charges are delinquent) and a notice that unpaid charges may become a lien; the statute for a municipal waterworks alone has no such owner-notice condition.

A lien has no priority over a buyer, mortgagee or other lienholder whose rights arose before the provider records a sworn notice of lien, and the provider may foreclose it like a mortgage. Under the municipal statutes the provider may instead sue the occupant or user, and a judgment against the occupant releases the lien for that amount.

Delinquent sewer charges (more than 30 days overdue) may also be enforced by shutting off water service, after notice to the sewer user and a chance to be heard.

Practical steps: keep your mailing address current with the water and sewer provider so you get the owner notices, ask a tenant who holds the account for proof of payment, and use the optional clause so the tenant repays any lien amount you pay. Home-rule municipalities, including Chicago, have their own water and sewer ordinances, not reviewed here.

For leases the rental fee law covers, list the tenant's repayment of a lien amount among the conditional charges on the first page of the lease.

title: Tenants' Cable, Internet and Antenna Access
bodyText:
Illinois protects a tenant's choice of cable and related services. In an apartment, condominium or cooperative building, or a centrally managed development such as a garden-apartment complex, gated community or mobile home park (hotels, rooming houses, dormitories, nursing homes and similar places are excluded), you and your agents may not unreasonably interfere with a tenant's right to have cable or video service, or voice, internet or other broadband service carried over those facilities, installed and maintained by a provider holding a State authorization.

You may not ask, demand or accept any extra payment, service or gratuity from the tenant for allowing or cooperating with the installation, and you may not penalize, charge or surcharge, threaten the rights of, or discriminate against a tenant who asks for or receives the service.

You may require the provider's facilities to meet reasonable conditions that protect the safety, functioning, appearance and value of the property and the convenience and safety of people and property; require the provider to indemnify you for damage from installation, operation or removal; and seek just and reasonable compensation from the provider (not the tenant) for its use of the property.

Where a city, village or county has granted a cable franchise, separate statutes likewise bar you from preventing a tenant from receiving franchised cable, from taking payment from the tenant for it, or from charging different rent to tenants who receive it, and let you claim compensation from the franchisee by written notice within 20 days of the franchisee's notice to you.

In a mobile home park, the park owner may not make a tenant remove an outside conventional television antenna or subscribe to master antenna service, unless that service is provided free and not as part of the rent.

Under a federal rule, a lease provision may not unreasonably delay, prevent or raise the cost of a tenant installing a satellite dish of one meter or less, a similar fixed-wireless antenna, or a TV broadcast antenna (and its mast) in an area the tenant alone uses or controls, such as a balcony or patio; you may still apply restrictions needed for a clearly defined safety objective or historic preservation, if no more burdensome than necessary. The rule does not reach the roof, exterior walls or other common areas.

The State-authorization statute is scheduled to be repealed on January 1, 2030. We read the federal antenna rule.

title: Tenant Solar Devices: No Illinois Right to Install
bodyText:
No Illinois statute gives a tenant a right to install a plug-in, portable or balcony solar device, or any other solar equipment, at a rental, and none limits what a lease may say about it. So the lease decides: under the No Alterations clause, a tenant needs your written consent before attaching or installing equipment, and the optional solar clause sets conditions for any device you allow.

Three solar laws exist but do not reach your lease. Homeowners', common-interest community and condominium associations may not prohibit a property owner from installing a solar energy system; that protects owners against their association (including you as owner of a unit or lot), not tenants against landlords.

Since June 1, 2026, municipalities and counties may not adopt or use any ordinance or power that prohibits or has the effect of prohibiting the installation of a solar energy system or of low-voltage solar-powered devices such as solar doorbells, security systems and lights; those provisions bind local governments and do not apply to buildings over 60 feet tall or (with exceptions) buildings with a shared roof.

And under the Equitable Energy Upgrade Program a renter may take part in an on-bill solar or efficiency project only with the property owner's permission.

A tenant with a disability may still be entitled to a reasonable modification under fair housing law, not reviewed here.

title: Rent Statements for a Tenant's Property Tax Relief Claim
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires you to tell a tenant what part of the rent goes to property taxes, in the lease or otherwise. Illinois's property tax relief grant for older adults and people with disabilities (the Circuit Breaker Act) lets an eligible renter claim relief on rent, and it fixes the property-tax share by formula: 25% of the gross rent paid in the year for a residence subject to property tax. The Department on Aging may require proof of rent paid, and the Act lets the Department, by rule, require landlords to give tenants statements of gross rent or of rent constituting property taxes. No such rule was found: the Department of Revenue's rules for the program (Title 86, Part 530) and the Department on Aging's rules (Title 89) contain no landlord-statement requirement. Whether grants are being paid depends on state appropriations. The cautious course: if a tenant asks for a written statement of rent paid for a property tax relief claim, give an accurate one promptly, and do not charge for it (the Act bars anyone from charging a claimant a fee for help with the application).

title: Parking Rules and Towing Notice: What Illinois Requires
bodyText:
No Illinois statute requires you to give tenants parking rules before the lease is signed, to put them under any heading, or to limit changes to them during the lease; the lease and any parking addendum govern, and the shared parking-rules clause can carry them.

Three statutes touch parking at rentals. First, under the rental fee law, any parking fee a tenant must pay is a non-optional fee that must appear on the first page of the lease, or the tenant does not owe it; a parking fee added later without amending the lease is therefore unsafe to collect, and the law separately bars charging a fee for modifying or renewing a lease.

Second, before you or a commercial relocator tow an unauthorized vehicle from private property, the Vehicle Code requires a posted sign at least 24 by 36 inches, mounted 4 to 8 feet off the ground, lit or reflective, naming the relocator (with address and phone) and stating the towing charges; no sign is needed on residential property that, given the circumstances and surroundings, is clearly reserved for residents and their vehicles. Local governments may add notice rules. No statute gives residents a waiting period or posted notice before a tow for expired registration.

Third, the state parking excise tax does not apply to residential off-street parking for apartment or home tenants when the parking arrangement is in the lease or a separate writing with the landlord.

Towing a tenant's own permitted vehicle may need authority beyond the abandoned-vehicle rule (see the towing row).

title: Renting Parking Separately From the Unit
bodyText:
No Illinois statute requires you to rent parking separately from the unit (unbundle it) or forbids you to. Two laws matter.

Under the People Over Parking Act (in effect since June 1, 2026), a city, village or county may not impose minimum parking requirements on a development within half a mile of a public transportation hub or an eighth of a mile of a frequent-bus corridor; if such a project provides parking voluntarily, the local government may require spaces to be shared with the public, set aside for car-share vehicles, or made available only for a fee, and may not require the parking to be free. So a local approval for a newer building near transit may itself require paid, separately rented parking; check the building's approvals and local ordinances.

Under the rental fee law, a parking charge the tenant must pay is a non-optional fee that must be on the first page of the lease; a space the tenant chooses to rent is optional, and the optional unbundled-parking clause records that choice.

The state parking excise tax does not apply to residential off-street parking for tenants when the arrangement is in the lease or a separate writing between landlord and tenant.

title: Entry for Regularly Scheduled Services
bodyText:
No Illinois statute regulates a landlord's entry to provide regularly scheduled services such as pest treatment, filter changes or grounds work, and none requires that right to be stated conspicuously in the lease. As with entry generally, Illinois has no entry statute, so the lease sets the terms; without a lease term, the tenant's right to possession governs.

If you want to enter on a fixed schedule, say so in the lease: the optional scheduled-services clause lists the services and their schedule, the hours, and the advance notice you will give. Set that notice at no less than the notice in the lease's general entry clause so the two agree.

A fee for routine maintenance and upkeep of the unit, or for pest treatment where the tenant did not contribute to the infestation, is barred by the rental fee law, so the clause carries no charge. Some cities, including Chicago, set entry notice rules by ordinance.

title: Automatic Lease Renewal
bodyText:
No Illinois statute written for residential leases governs a clause that renews the lease automatically, and nothing bars one: a lease may renew for another term, or continue month to month, unless you or the tenant gives notice by a stated deadline. The one Illinois landlord-tenant rule on automatic renewal is for mobile home parks, whose leases must contain an automatic renewal option (that Act is outside this library).

Illinois does have a general Automatic Contract Renewal Act. It covers anyone who sells or offers to sell products or services to a consumer under a written contract that renews automatically unless the consumer cancels.

It requires the renewal terms (that the contract continues until cancelled, the deadline to cancel, the recurring charge and any change in it, and the renewal length) to be stated clearly and conspicuously, for example in bold or larger type, near the signature; and where the original term is 12 months or more and it renews for a term of more than one month, a written reminder sent no less than 30 and no more than 60 days before the cancellation deadline, saying the contract will renew unless cancelled, how to cancel, and the deadline. A violation is an unlawful practice under the Consumer Fraud and Deceptive Business Practices Act.

The Act doesn't say whether a residential lease is a sale of "services" to a "consumer", and that is for the courts.

Cautious course: if you use an automatic renewal clause, put the renewal terms in bold, and send the tenant a written reminder 30 to 60 days before the tenant's deadline to give notice of non-renewal. The library's optional Illinois "Automatic Renewal" clause does both. A tenancy that continues month to month after renewal still takes 30 days' written notice to end.

A consumer who accepts an automatic renewal online must be allowed to cancel it online, so give an email address for notices of non-renewal if the tenant signs the lease online.

title: Lease Guarantors
bodyText:
No Illinois statute governs residential lease guaranties: none says whether a guarantor stays liable after the lease renews or continues month to month, none requires a guaranty to state a maximum amount or an end date, none limits a deposit or other payment you take from a guarantor, and none says when a guarantor may revoke a guaranty for future rent. Those questions turn on the guaranty's own wording and Illinois case law.

Two statutes do apply. First, a promise to answer for another person's debt can be enforced only if it, or a note of it, is in writing and signed by the guarantor.

Second, under the Consumer Fraud and Deceptive Business Practices Act, no one may report adverse information about a cosigner to a credit bureau, send the cosigner's account to a collection agency or take any collection action against the cosigner without first mailing the cosigner, by first class mail, a notice that the main obligor is delinquent or in default, that the cosigner is responsible for paying, and that the cosigner must pay or make arrangements to pay within 15 days from the date the notice was sent; if the cosigner does, nothing adverse may be reported. A violation is an unlawful practice and carries actual damages up to $250 plus attorney's fees. The section speaks of a loan, so whether it covers a lease guarantor is for the courts; treat it as covering one.

Separately, you may not try to collect a tenant's debt from the tenant's spouse unless the spouse cosigned, the debt is at least 30 days in default, or it was for necessaries.

Cautious course: have the guarantor sign the lease or a written guaranty; state plainly whether the guaranty covers renewals, extensions and month-to-month continuation (and any rent change); and mail the 15-day notice before reporting or collecting from a guarantor. The library's optional Illinois "Guaranty" clause does all three.

title: Paying Rent in Installments
bodyText:
No Illinois statute says whether a residential lease may split each month's rent into smaller scheduled installments (for example, half on the 1st and half on the 15th), or whether scheduled installments count as partial payments. It is a matter of agreement: the lease may set rent in installments, and the library's optional "Rent Installments" clause does so and says installments paid on schedule are not partial payments.

Illinois law speaks of partial payment only in the 5-day rent demand: a demand is not invalidated by partial payments of the rent it demands if it prominently carries the statutory sentence that only full payment of the rent demanded will waive your right to end the lease unless you agree in writing to continue the lease in exchange for partial payment. If an installment goes unpaid, the demand should name the unpaid amount that is due under the schedule.

One timing rule refers to installments: when a service member ends a lease under the Illinois military termination right, termination takes effect 30 days after the notice is delivered, but if rent is paid in monthly installments it takes effect 30 days after the next rent due date after the notice; a lease with installments more often than monthly should be read with that rule in mind.

Whatever the schedule, you may not require payment by electronic funds transfer, and the payment-method rules in "Rent Payment Methods" apply.

title: While a Notice to Vacate Is Pending
bodyText: Illinois has no statute on a landlord-supplied move-out form that adds terms not in the lease (no required warning, and no rule on whether added terms bind a tenant who signs), and no statute that bars alterations or renovation work while a notice to vacate is running. What Illinois does regulate: a 5-day rent demand must prominently carry the statutory sentence about partial payment, and the 10-day notice for other lease breaches follows the statute's suggested form; at the natural end of a fixed-term lease no notice to quit is needed, because the tenant is bound to surrender possession. Until the tenant leaves, the tenancy and your duties continue. You may not cut off or interrupt utility service to an occupied building, except temporary shutoffs for emergencies or, on 7 days' written notice to each affected tenant, temporary shutoffs required for building repairs or rehabilitation. You may not retaliate against a tenant for protected activity, and you recover possession only through an eviction case, not by making the unit unusable. Cautious course: while a notice is pending, keep services and repairs going, put any move-out instructions in a separate letter that adds no new obligations, and schedule renovation that would disturb the tenant for after the tenant moves out.

title: Telling Tenants About a Foreclosure
bodyText:
No Illinois statute requires a landlord to tell a prospective tenant, before the lease is signed, that the property is in foreclosure, or to tell current tenants when a foreclosure case is filed.

The foreclosure law does affect what a new lease is worth to the tenant. A lease signed after the foreclosure notice (lis pendens) is recorded and before the judicial sale protects the tenant against the buyer only if its term is one year or less, and a longer written lease is treated as a one-year lease; an oral lease is treated as month to month unless the tenant proves a longer term.

A protected ("bona fide") lease can be ended by the new owner only at the end of its term, or for a month-to-month or week-to-week lease, on at least 90 days' written notice, and an individual buyer who will live in the unit may end it on 90 days' written notice. After the sale is confirmed, the buyer must notify known occupants in writing within 21 days and post a notice on each unit saying, among other things, "This is NOT a notice to vacate the premises."

Because a pending foreclosure can cut short the tenancy the tenant is paying for, keeping silent about it risks a claim of concealing a material fact under the Consumer Fraud and Deceptive Business Practices Act (whether that Act reaches a residential lease is for the courts).

Cautious course: if the property is in foreclosure, say so in writing before the tenant signs, and record it in the lease with the library's optional foreclosure disclosure clause.

title: Selling the Property or Changing Managers
bodyText: Illinois has no general statute requiring you to notify tenants when you sell the property or change managers, and no statute that releases a selling landlord once notice is given. What the law does: a sale does not end the lease. The buyer (or anyone who takes over the lease) gets the same remedies for rent and lease breaches that you had, and the tenant has the same remedies against the buyer for breach of the lease that the tenant had against you. On a sale, lease, transfer or other disposition of residential property (other than to a lienholder), the buyer becomes liable to the tenant for any security deposit, with statutory interest, and any prepaid rent, and you remain jointly and severally liable with the buyer, so transfer the deposits and keep proof. When deposits are transferred to a foreclosure buyer or certificate holder, that party must post a notice on each unit within 21 days. In a building of more than 4 units where neither the owner nor a manager lives or keeps an office, the posted (or lease or mailed) notice naming the person responsible for managing the building and the fire insurer must stay accurate, so update it when the manager changes. A court-appointed receiver may not reject an unexpired lease of a tenant who lives in the unit as a primary residence in the cases the statute lists. Selling a rented building of 1 to 4 units also triggers the seller's Residential Real Property Disclosure Report to the buyer, and an owner who has received a lead mitigation notice for a unit must give prospective buyers written notice of the lead hazard and tell the state Department of Public Health of the sale; a buyer who gets that notice must mitigate the hazard and obtain a certificate of compliance before entering a new lease for the unit. Foreclosure has its own rules (see "Tenants in Foreclosure and Receivership"). Cautious course: tell tenants in writing who the new owner or manager is, where to pay rent and where to send notices, and transfer every deposit with an accounting. Local ordinances may add notice duties (not covered).

title: Telling Tenants About Proceedings Against the Property
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires a residential landlord to tell tenants about a lawsuit, foreclosure, receivership, condemnation, code-enforcement case, tax sale or other proceeding against the property (the only such duty is for mobile home park owners, outside this library). Several proceedings reach tenants directly instead. In a mortgage foreclosure, a mortgagee placed in possession, a receiver and the buyer after the sale is confirmed must each identify the occupants and notify them in writing within 21 days, telling them control has changed, whom to contact for repairs and how to pay rent, and that the notice is not a notice to vacate. If you fail to pay a landlord-paid gas, electric or water bill, the utility must notify all tenants of a building with 3 or more apartments at least 10 days before shutting service off, on red paper, telling them they may pay and deduct from rent or ask a court to appoint a receiver; it is a crime for you or your agent to alter, deface, tamper with or remove that notice. If a condominium association evicts a defaulting unit owner, it may also evict the owner's tenant, or serve the tenant with a certificate directing rent to the association. A water supplier that finds a lead service line must notify the building's occupants as well as the owner. No Illinois statute requires a tenant to forward legal papers about the property to you; the library's shared "Notice of Proceedings Against the Property" clause asks the tenant to do so. Cautious course: tell tenants promptly in writing about any proceeding that may affect their possession or where they pay rent.

title: When the Property Is Taken by Eminent Domain
bodyText:
No Illinois statute says whether a residential lease ends, or rent stops or is reduced, when all or part of the leased property is taken by eminent domain, and none lets a court end the lease on a partial taking. Those questions are decided by the lease and Illinois case law.

The Eminent Domain Act does say how the money is handled: just compensation is distributed among all persons having an interest in the property according to the fair value of their legal or equitable interests, so a tenant with a lease may claim a share; anyone with an interest who was not named may join the case; and, unless federal funds cover it, the condemning authority must reimburse displaced persons for reasonable relocation costs, measured as under the federal Uniform Relocation Act. A sale to a government body under threat of condemnation, and a transfer by eminent domain, are also outside the seller disclosure law.

Because the statutes leave the lease's fate open, put it in the lease. The library offers an optional "Eminent Domain" clause: the lease ends if the whole property, or enough that the rest can't reasonably be lived in, is taken; rent is reduced for a smaller taking; and the award, including any value of the lease, goes to you, except the tenant's own relocation and personal-property payments. Whether a court will enforce a lease term assigning the tenant's share of the award to you is for the courts.

title: Agreeing on Extra Ways to Give Notice
bodyText:
Illinois landlord-tenant statutes have no "actual notice" standard and no rule letting the parties add a delivery method, such as text message, to the ones the law sets. Where a statute fixes the method, use it: rent demands and notices ending a tenancy are served by handing a written copy to the tenant, leaving it with someone 13 or older who lives on or possesses the premises, certified or registered mail with a return receipt from the addressee, or, if no one is in possession, posting on the premises.

Illinois' Uniform Electronic Transactions Act lets parties who have agreed to deal electronically meet a writing requirement with an electronic record the recipient can keep, but where another law requires a record to be sent by a specified method, it must still be sent by that method; and either party may refuse to conduct further transactions electronically, a right that can't be waived by agreement.

The security deposit statement is an exception written into the statute: it may be emailed to a verified email address the tenant provided.

For notices no statute governs (repair requests, entry notices, rule reminders), the lease may set any method the parties agree on, including email or text, alongside the statutory ones.

Cautious course: list in the lease the methods each party may use for ordinary notices, keep every statutory notice on its statutory method, and treat an email or text as an extra, not a substitute.

title: Online Tenant Portals
bodyText:
No Illinois statute regulates tenant portals as such, but three rules decide what a lease may say about one.

First, for leases and agreements executed after January 1, 2024, you may not require a tenant or applicant to pay any amount due under a residential lease, renewal or extension by electronic funds transfer, including automatic recurring transfers; a portal payment is an electronic funds transfer, so the portal can be offered but not required, and a violation is an unlawful practice under the Consumer Fraud and Deceptive Business Practices Act.

Second, for leases executed after January 1, 2025, if your third-party portal charges a transaction fee or other charge on rent payments, you must also let the tenant pay by delivering a paper check or cash to you or your business office, or by another means that carries no fee.

Third, under the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act, electronic signing and electronic notices work only between parties who have agreed to deal electronically, and a tenant who agreed may still refuse to conduct later transactions electronically; that right can't be waived in the lease.

Notices a statute says must be served a particular way (rent demands and termination notices) still go by that method even if the tenant uses the portal.

Any non-optional portal or technology fee must appear in the first-page fee list under the rental fee law (P.A. 104-479, effective July 1, 2026 under its Section 99, or January 1, 2027 as the General Assembly's records state; the cautious course treats it as applying to leases entered into on or after July 1, 2026). The library's optional Illinois "Tenant Portal" clause offers a portal on these terms.

title: Month-to-Month Versus Fixed-Term Terms
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires a month-to-month lease to carry the same terms as a fixed-term lease, bars terms that are more burdensome for one kind of tenancy than the other, or caps how much more rent you may charge for a month-to-month tenancy. Illinois sets no statewide rent cap at all, and local rent control is preempted. The rules that do differ by tenancy type are about ending it: a month-to-month tenancy is ended by 30 days' written notice, a week-to-week tenancy by 7 days', and a fixed-term lease ends on its own at the end of the term without notice. Whatever the structure, fair housing law and the ban on retaliation still apply, so a higher rent or harsher term offered to some tenants must not track a protected class or a tenant's protected activity, and every non-optional fee must appear on the lease's first page. Local ordinances may say more (not covered).

title: Type Size and Print Rules for Leases
bodyText: Illinois sets no minimum type size for a printed residential lease as a whole, and no rule that small print is unenforceable or inadmissible. A few placement and print rules do apply to particular parts of a lease. Every non-optional fee must be stated on the first page of the lease, or the tenant doesn't owe it, and non-optional fees must be shown clearly and conspicuously in a rental listing (rental fee law, P.A. 104-479, effective July 1, 2026 under its Section 99, or January 1, 2027 as the General Assembly's records state; the cautious course treats it as applying to leases entered into on or after July 1, 2026). A lease that grants a rent concession not stated in it must bear the legend "Concession Granted" across its face in letters at least one-half inch high, with a note of the concession's amount and nature in the margin. A 5-day rent demand must state the statutory partial-payment sentence prominently. Statutory forms such as the flood disclosure and radon disclosure must be used as printed. Type-size floors elsewhere in Illinois law (for example 12-point bold in contracts with distressed homeowners, or a utility's red-paper shutoff notice) don't govern ordinary leases. Cautious course: use a readable type size throughout, and put the fee box, rent and term on the first page in type at least as large as the body text.

title: Leases in Other Languages
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires a residential lease, or any lease notice, to be translated into the tenant's language, or to be written in the language you used to advertise or negotiate it. Illinois does impose language rules in some other dealings, and none of them reaches an ordinary lease: contracts with homeowners in foreclosure who sell and rent back must be written in the language the owner principally used to negotiate; door-to-door sales of goods and services must be documented in the language of the sales pitch; and assisted living establishments must give termination notices in a language the resident can read. A lease the tenant can't read still binds under ordinary contract rules, but whether a court would enforce a term the tenant could not understand is for the courts. Fair housing law bars treating applicants differently because of national origin, and language can stand in for national origin. Cautious course: if you negotiate in another language, offer a translation or an interpreter, keep the English lease as the signed controlling text, and have the tenant acknowledge in writing that they understood it.

title: Leases With an Option to Purchase
bodyText: Giving a tenant an option to buy is a lawful lease term in Illinois, but it brings in sale law. Seller disclosure: the Residential Real Property Disclosure Act applies to a transfer by lease with an option to purchase of residential real property, meaning property with 1 to 4 dwelling units, a unit in a residential cooperative, or a condominium unit (with its limited common elements), including a manufactured home that is real property. As the owner granting the option, you are a "seller" unless the transfer is exempt; exemptions include transfers to a spouse or a lineal relative, to or from a government body, by a fiduciary, between co-owners, by court order or in foreclosure, and of newly built property never occupied. You must complete every item of the statutory Residential Real Property Disclosure Report (it asks about known material defects, flooding and leaks, radon, asbestos, lead, methamphetamine manufacture, notices of uncorrected code violations and more; as a landlord you will answer "no" to having occupied the property in the last 12 months and explain), printed with the Act's Sections 5 to 65, and deliver it to the tenant-buyer before the signing of a contract, by hand, email or other electronic delivery, first-class mail or a delivery service. The Act defines a contract as a written agreement that would require the buyer to accept a transfer, and it doesn't say whether a lease-option is that contract when it is signed or only when the option is exercised; the cautious course is to deliver the report before the lease-option is signed, and supplement it in writing before closing if you learn it was wrong. If you don't deliver it before the conveyance, the buyer may terminate the contract; if it is delivered after signing and discloses a material defect, the buyer may terminate within 5 business days of receiving it and get back earnest money and down payments; and if you knowingly violate the Act or knowingly state something false, you are liable for actual damages and court costs, and the court may award attorney's fees to the winning side. A suit must be brought within one year of the earliest of possession, occupancy or recording, and the Act doesn't say how that applies to a tenant already in possession. You are not liable for errors you didn't know about, and you need not investigate. The sale radon disclosure (pamphlet and form) is due before the buyer is obligated under any contract to purchase, so give it no later than when the tenant exercises the option. Other statutes: Illinois has no separate lease-option or rent-to-own statute (no rules on option fees, rent credits, forfeiture, early exercise or a cure period). But if the arrangement is really a sale on installments (the tenant agrees to buy and pays the price over a year or more while you keep title or another interest), the Installment Sales Contract Act applies to a seller who makes more than 3 such contracts in 12 months: a written, notarized contract with 28 required disclosures, the Attorney General's disclosure document at least 3 full business days before signing, a non-waivable 3-business-day cooling-off period, recording within 10 business days, a 90-day right to cure a payment default, and no prepayment penalty; violations are unlawful practices under the Consumer Fraud Act. Any installment contract for a dwelling structure of 12 or fewer units is voidable by the buyer without a code-compliance certificate or a code-violation warranty, the buyer may always record it, and a contract with less than 80% of the price unpaid must be foreclosed rather than handled as an eviction. If you buy a home from an owner in foreclosure or tax distress and lease it back with an option to repurchase, the Mortgage Rescue Fraud Act's contract rules, 5-business-day cancellation right and payment rules apply, and the lease is terminable at will by the former owner. Whether a particular lease-option is an installment contract is for the courts. Cautious course: keep the option separate from rent (state the option price, any option fee and whether any rent is credited), don't bind the tenant to buy unless you comply with the installment-contract statutes, and deliver the disclosure report and lead and radon materials before signing.

title: Required Lease Disclosures in Illinois
bodyText:
Illinois has no single list of required lease disclosures, but statutes require these, each covered by its own row:
- (1) the Department of Human Rights summary of rights for survivors of domestic and sexual violence, attached as the first pages of every new written lease and renewal and signed by each tenant
- (2) every non-optional fee on the first page of the lease itself, and whether utilities are included in rent
- (3) the flood disclosure, in writing before signing and again in the signed lease
- (4) the radon pamphlet, any radon hazard reports and the radon disclosure form, before the lease is signed (not required for units on the third story or higher)
- (5) for pre-1978 housing, the state lead brochure and the federal lead disclosure, and, where a lead mitigation notice was issued, notice to tenants before renewal
- (6) the lease sentence that using the premises for a felony or Class A misdemeanor lets you void the lease
- (7) in a building of more than 4 units with no resident owner or on-site manager, the manager and fire-insurer notice, which may be put in the lease
- (8) where a tenant-paid meter also serves common areas or other units, a written statement of what the meter serves, 12 months of bills and any rent reduction, before you offer the lease
- (9) where tenants pay a share of a master-metered utility, the written allocation formula, in the lease or another writing
- (10) a "Concession Granted" legend on a lease that doesn't state a rent concession
- (11) where a waiver of the state noise rules for a commercial wind or solar energy facility is recorded for the property, disclosure of the waiver before any new lease
- (12) if you, or the agent leasing for you, hold an Illinois real estate license, written disclosure of that status and of any interest in the property.

Granting an option to purchase brings in the seller's Residential Real Property Disclosure Report (see "Leases With an Option to Purchase").

Illinois has no statewide just-cause or rent-regulation law, so no lease notice of coverage is required, and no state form other than the summary of rights must lead the lease. Local ordinances, such as Chicago's, add their own summaries and notices (not covered).

title: Emergency and Maintenance Contacts
bodyText:
No Illinois statute requires a lease to give tenants an emergency or 24-hour maintenance number, a management website or a social-services hotline notice, and none governs the emergency contact person a tenant may name for you.

Two rules touch the subject. In a building of more than 4 units where neither the owner nor a manager or agent lives or keeps an office on site, you must post near the mailboxes (or put in the lease, or mail) the name, address and telephone number of the person responsible for managing the building and of the fire insurer.

And under the rental fee law you may not charge a fee or fine for after-hours maintenance requests, for contacting the owner or manager about maintenance, service, lease questions or other tenancy matters, or for using a maintenance hotline (P.A. 104-479, effective July 1, 2026 under its Section 99, or January 1, 2027 as the General Assembly's records state; the cautious course treats it as applying to leases entered into on or after July 1, 2026).

Cautious course: give every tenant, in the lease or a move-in letter, a way to reach you or your manager for emergencies at any hour, free of charge. If you ask the tenant to name an emergency contact, use it only for emergencies; the library's shared optional "Emergency Contact" clause does this. Local ordinances may require more (not covered).

title: Landlord Insurance
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires a residential landlord to carry liability or property insurance, to register insurance with a government office, or to show tenants proof of coverage. The one insurance notice in Illinois landlord law is about fire insurance in larger buildings: an owner of a building with more than 4 living units who doesn't live or keep an office there, and has no resident or on-site manager or agent, must post near the mailboxes (or include in the lease, or mail to each tenant) the name, address and telephone number of the company insuring the building against fire or explosion, or state that the building is uninsured, and must post notice within 24 hours after learning the insurance was cancelled; failure is a petty offense with a fine of up to $100 a day. Insurance also can't do what the law forbids: a lease term exempting you from liability for injuries or property damage caused by your own negligence, or that of your agents or employees, in operating or maintaining the property is void. Cautious course: carry landlord liability and property coverage anyway, and check your lender's and any association's requirements.

title: Insurance Claims Between Landlord and Tenant
bodyText: No Illinois statute governs how insurance claims are handled between a residential landlord and tenant: none requires a tenant to report a loss to you or to make a claim, none says whose policy pays first, and none regulates waivers of subrogation in residential leases. So the lease and general insurance and contract law decide. A few statutes bear on it. A lease term exempting you from liability for injury or property damage caused by your own negligence, or your agents' or employees', in operating or maintaining the property is void, so a lease can't make the tenant's insurance the only remedy for losses you negligently cause. A tenant who installs an electric vehicle charging system with your consent must, within 14 days, give you a certificate naming you as an additional insured on the tenant's renter's policy for claims related to the charger, or, at your option, reimburse any increase in your premium caused by it. Insurers may not refuse, cancel or surcharge a renter's policy based solely on the breed of a dog the tenant keeps (with exceptions). The statutory flood disclosure warns tenants that most tenant insurance policies don't cover flood loss. Cautious course: if you want prompt notice of losses and cooperation with insurers, say so in the lease, and don't use insurance or subrogation terms to shift your own negligence onto the tenant.

title: Leases After a Declared Disaster
bodyText: No Illinois statute ends a residential tenancy, abates or freezes rent, or pauses evictions because the Governor or the President has declared a disaster. What happens to the lease when a storm, flood or fire makes a unit unlivable is decided by the lease and Illinois case law; the library's optional Illinois "Fire or Other Casualty" clause lets either party end the lease and prorates rent. A disaster proclamation does give the Governor, for up to 30 days at a time, powers that can reach rentals: to control entry into and movement within a disaster area and the occupancy of premises there, to provide temporary emergency housing, to regulate the price and distribution of commodities, goods and services, and to prohibit increases in the prices of goods and services during the disaster. Whether a given order covers rent depends on its words, so read any proclamation or executive order issued for your area. Your ordinary duties continue: you may not cut off utilities except temporarily for emergencies or, on 7 days' written notice, for repairs; you recover possession only through the courts; and you may not retaliate. Tenants left homeless by a natural disaster may qualify for state crisis and homelessness-prevention assistance.

title: Sheltering People Displaced by a Disaster
bodyText: No Illinois statute lets a tenant house people displaced by a declared disaster despite the lease's guest or occupancy limits, or bars you from enforcing those limits against displaced guests. The lease's guest and occupancy terms therefore apply, subject to fair housing law and to local occupancy codes. During a declared disaster the Governor may, by proclamation, control the occupancy of premises in a disaster area and provide for temporary emergency housing, so check any order issued for your area. Cautious course: if a tenant asks to shelter family or friends displaced by a disaster, consider agreeing in writing to a temporary exception to the guest limit with an end date, rather than treating the stay as a breach. We searched the Illinois Compiled Statutes, the Illinois Constitution and the list of the 104th General Assembly's Public Acts.

title: Tenant Rights to Buy When You Sell
bodyText: Illinois has no general tenant opportunity-to-purchase law: when you sell a rental house or apartment building, tenants have no statewide right of first refusal and no right to notice of the sale. Three Illinois rules give tenants purchase rights in particular cases. First, condominium conversion: before converting a rental building to condominiums, the developer must give every tenant written notice of intent at least 30 days and not more than one year before recording the declaration, with a schedule of selling prices and an offer to sell the tenant's unit that stays open at least 30 days (except units to be vacated for rehabilitation); for 120 days after the notice the tenant has a right of first refusal to buy the unit on the terms of any signed purchase contract, exercisable within 30 days after notice of that contract; tenants whose leases would end within that 120 days (other than for cause) may extend to the end of the 120 days on the same terms and rent by giving the developer written notice within 30 days after receiving the notice of intent; with the notice of intent the developer must tell each tenant whether the tenancy will be renewed or terminated when it expires and, if renewed, all charges and the proposed term; during the 30 days a tenant has to exercise the right of first refusal, the developer must give the tenant access to inspect the building and its reports, warranties and condition documents, subject to reasonable limits (each refusal is a $500 business offense); before the first sale, an occupied unit may be shown only a reasonable number of times, at appropriate hours, and only in the last 90 days of an expiring tenancy; an owner who skips the notice of intent, declines to renew a tenant who then moves out, and converts the unit owes that tenant moving expenses up to $1,500, 3 months' rent and attorney's fees and court costs; and any lease term waiving these rights is void. Second, Illinois Housing Development Authority financing: an owner of a development financed by the Authority's bonds or notes who wants to prepay the mortgage without extending the affordability restrictions must give tenants, on an Authority-approved form, at least 9 months' notice of the intent to prepay and of their rights, and the tenants, through a tenant association representing a majority that notifies the owner within 60 days, get a first right to purchase the development. The owner must give the association a bona fide offer stating the price and other essential terms and allowing 30 days to give written notice of intent to buy. The owner must then sign a purchase contract that the association delivers within 90 days, at an agreed price or one set by appraisal, with closing within 90 days after signing. The owner must also forward a copy of every notice to the Authority. The rule does not cover developments under the federal Low-Income Housing Preservation and Resident Homeownership Act of 1990. Third, federally assisted housing as the Federally Assisted Housing Preservation Act defines it, which covers developments with project-based Section 8 assistance, Section 221(d)(3), 236 or 202 mortgages, federal rent supplements, Section 514 or 515 rural housing loans, or low-income housing tax credits: before selling or otherwise disposing of the development, completing a prepayment of a covered federal mortgage, or completing the end of its project-based Section 8 participation or of its tax-credit affordability restrictions, the owner must give written notice at least 12 months ahead to all tenants and to the mayor (or county board chair), the local housing authority and the Illinois Housing Development Authority, delivered in person or by certified or registered mail, return receipt requested. The notice must give the property's address, its characteristics including the number of units, the owners' names and addresses, the date the owner intends to sell, lease, prepay, end assistance or otherwise dispose of the property, and a detailed list of the affordability restrictions that apply to it. If, within 60 days after that notice, the tenants tell the owner they have formed a tenant association representing a majority of the tenants, the owner must, within 60 days and before selling, leasing or otherwise disposing of the property or completing the prepayment or the end of assistance, give the association a bona fide offer to sell, stating the price and other essential terms. The association then has 90 days to give written notice of its intent to buy. After that notice, the owner must, within 15 days of a reasonable request, make documents available at the owner's principal place of business during business hours, such as floor plans, operating and capital expenses, reserves, utility consumption, inspection reports, the rent roll, a tenant list and vacancy figures. The association has 90 more days to deliver a purchase contract with a 5% earnest money deposit, and must agree to close within 90 days after the contract is signed. The price is set by appraisal if the parties can't agree within the first 60 days; if it misses a step, the owner is released from the Act. The Act does not apply to a government taking by eminent domain or negotiated purchase, a foreclosure sale, a transfer by gift, devise or operation of law, or a sale after which the property stays assisted housing. An owner found in a tenant's or the association's lawsuit to have violated the Act owes each tenant a $500 civil penalty, on top of any damages, plus attorney's fees and costs. Separately, an owner of housing with certain HUD- or FmHA-insured or HUD-held mortgages, or with a Section 8 contract, has notice duties. The owner must give the municipal (or county) clerk and the Authority notice of the earliest date the mortgage may be prepaid at least 12 months before that date, post it in the building, and deliver it to every tenant and prospective tenant. The owner must then give a further notice of intent to prepay at least 9 months before prepaying, to the clerk and the Authority, posted in the building, delivered personally or by certified mail to every tenant, and given in writing to prospective tenants, on the Authority's forms; it is good for 15 months. An owner of a building with a Section 8 contract that the Authority does not administer must tell each prospective tenant in writing, before signing a lease, when the contract expires. Missing a 9-month or Section 8 notice to a tenant costs $1,000 per tenant, and missing the 9-month notice to the local government costs $25,000. Mobile home parks have their own right of first refusal (outside this library). California-style notices of rent-cap or just-cause coverage don't exist in Illinois: there is no statewide rent cap or just-cause law.

title: Exemption Notices for Tenant Purchase Rights
bodyText: Because Illinois has no general tenant opportunity-to-purchase law, there is no exemption notice, exempt-sale statement or exemption filing for an owner to give tenants or an agency. The three Illinois tenant purchase rights carry their own limits, with no separate notice of exemption. For federally assisted housing, the Act as a whole, including its 12-month notice and the tenant association's right to an offer to buy, does not apply to a government taking by eminent domain or negotiated purchase, a forced sale in foreclosure, a transfer by gift, devise or operation of law, or a sale after which the property remains assisted housing; and if the tenants miss the Act's deadline to give notice of a tenant association or of intent to buy, or to sign a purchase contract, the owner is released from the Act. In a condominium conversion, the developer's offer to sell need not cover units to be vacated for rehabilitation after the notice of intent, and the tenant's right of first refusal ends when a deed is recorded stating that the tenant waived it, failed to exercise it or had none (the tenant keeps any damages claim). For Housing Development Authority financed developments, the tenants' first right to purchase does not apply to a government taking, a forced sale in foreclosure, or a transfer by gift, devise or operation of law; it also doesn't arise if the owner agrees with the Authority to extend the affordability restrictions on the low-income units to the full term of the mortgage loan, or to create a comparable number of new affordable units; and the owner may prepay if the Authority finds the tenants did not form a qualifying association or missed a step. Nor does Illinois require a notice telling tenants that a unit is exempt from a rent cap or just-cause law, since it has neither statewide.

title: Sunset Dates in Illinois Tenant Law
bodyText: No Illinois tenant-protection statute is on a dated repeal or expiry clock: the Landlord and Tenant Act, the security deposit Acts, the Landlord Retaliation Act, the Safe Homes Act, the repair-and-deduct Act, the eviction Article of the Code of Civil Procedure, the Rent Control Preemption Act and the Human Rights Act's housing provisions carry no sunset date. Three dated items are worth knowing. The Real Estate License Act of 2000, including its rules that a licensee leasing property must disclose licensee status and any interest in writing, is scheduled to be repealed on January 1, 2030, unless the General Assembly extends it. The COVID-19 rule sealing eviction files covered only cases tied to the period that ended March 31, 2022. And the rental fee law's start date is itself unsettled: P.A. 104-479 says July 1, 2026 in its Section 99, while the General Assembly's records say January 1, 2027; the cautious course treats it as applying to leases entered into on or after July 1, 2026.

title: Rent Changes During the Lease Term
bodyText:
No Illinois statute regulates rent escalation clauses in residential leases: nothing requires, bars or caps a scheduled increase, an index-based adjustment or a clause letting you raise rent during the term, and no statute sets notice for a mid-term increase. During a fixed term, rent changes only as the lease provides; without an escalation clause, the rent is fixed until the term ends. Local rent control is preempted statewide.

The limit that matters is retaliation: you may not knowingly increase rent because a tenant in good faith complained about code violations, asked for required repairs, joined a tenants' union, testified, or used any legal right, and if the tenant's protected activity came within one year before the increase, retaliation is presumed unless you show a legitimate, non-retaliatory reason or that you began the action before the tenant's activity. A schedule written into the lease at signing is the clearest proof that an increase was set before any later complaint.

You also may not raise rent to recover utility payments a tenant lawfully deducted.

The library offers two optional clauses: "Rent Escalation" (a fixed schedule, or an index adjustment with a stated cap and notice) and "Mid-Term Rent Increase" (an increase on 30 days' written notice, with the tenant free to end the lease instead). Whether a court will enforce a clause letting you raise rent on notice during a fixed term is decided by case law; the fixed schedule is the safer choice.

title: Passing Property Tax and Insurance Increases to Tenants
bodyText:
No Illinois statute generally regulates a residential lease term that passes increases in property taxes or insurance premiums to the tenant: nothing requires the lease to state the tenant's exact share, refund abatements or limit the amount, and no deposit rule lets you deduct a tax share. Such a term is a contract matter, with three Illinois overlays.

First, the rental fee law: every non-optional fee or charge must be listed on the first page of the lease, or the tenant doesn't owe it, and a charge can't be renamed to avoid that rule; list any tax or insurance share in the first-page fee box (P.A. 104-479, effective July 1, 2026 under its Section 99, or January 1, 2027 as the General Assembly's records state; the cautious course treats it as applying to leases entered into on or after July 1, 2026).

Second, retaliation: an increase made because of a tenant's protected activity is unlawful, so tie any pass-through to a formula fixed at signing.

Third, the Property Tax Code has its own lease wording for a single-family residence whose tenant lives there and is liable for the property taxes: such a tenant may claim the general homestead exemption (and the senior citizens and returning veterans exemptions if eligible), and the county assessment officer may require a notarized application signed by owner and tenant each year, a copy of the lease, a lease statement that the tenant is liable for the taxes, and statutory wording under which the monthly rent rises or falls pro rata each January 1 with the real estate taxes.

The library offers two optional Illinois clauses: "Tax and Insurance Increases" (a share of increases over a base year, listed in the fee box, with abatements credited back) and "Tenant Liable for Real Estate Taxes" (the statutory homestead-exemption wording).

title: House Rules
bodyText:
No Illinois statute governs a residential landlord's house rules: none says when a rule is enforceable, requires rules to be reasonable or applied equally, sets notice for adopting or changing rules, or lets a written notice alone change the rules of a month-to-month tenancy. So house rules bind a tenant as part of the lease, and whether a rule adopted after signing binds the tenant, and whether an unreasonable rule is enforceable, is decided by contract principles and Illinois case law.

Some statutes still shape rules. A month-to-month tenancy can be ended on 30 days' written notice, so new rules can be put in a new tenancy that way. You may not change rules or other terms in retaliation for a tenant's protected activity. A rule can't impose a fee or fine the rental fee law bars, and any non-optional fee must be on the lease's first page (P.A. 104-479, effective July 1, 2026 under its Section 99, or January 1, 2027 as the General Assembly's records state; the cautious course treats it as applying to leases entered into on or after July 1, 2026). Fair housing law applies to rules too.

In a condominium, the association's declaration, bylaws and rules on use of the unit and common elements are deemed part of every lease, and the board may evict a tenant who breaches them; other common interest communities have similar rules.

Cautious course: attach the rules in force at signing; adopt later rules only for health, safety, protection of the property or fair sharing of facilities, give written notice before they take effect, apply them to all tenants alike, and have any rule that substantially changes the tenant's rights or obligations take effect only with the tenant's written agreement or at renewal. The library's optional Illinois "Rules" clause does this. Mobile home parks have their own statutory rules regime (outside this library).

title: Owners Who Live Outside Illinois
bodyText: Illinois has no rule that an owner who lives outside Illinois must appoint an Illinois agent, name one in the lease, or file an agent designation before suing a tenant, and no rule that a tenant must withhold Illinois income tax from rent paid to an out-of-state owner. Four rules do reach an out-of-state owner. (1) If the building has more than 4 units and neither you nor a manager or agent you employ lives or keeps an office there, you must post a notice near the mailboxes (or inside, where all residents can see it) giving the name, address and phone number of the person managing the building and of the company insuring it against fire or explosion (or saying it is uninsured), and post notice within 24 hours if that insurance is cancelled. Your managing agent may instead put the notice in the lease or mail it to each tenant (see the building manager and insurer notice clause). Not giving it is a petty offense with a fine of up to $100 a day. (2) Owning Illinois real estate submits you to the Illinois courts for claims arising from it, and a tenant can have you served with a summons outside Illinois. (3) If you own through a limited liability company or corporation formed in another state, it can't bring a civil action in an Illinois court, including an eviction, until it is admitted (registered) to do business in Illinois. Merely owning property isn't transacting business, but renting it out may be, so register before you file (see the row on entity landlords in court). (4) Rent from Illinois property is Illinois income for a nonresident, and a partnership, S corporation or trust that owns the property must generally withhold Illinois tax for its nonresident partners, shareholders or beneficiaries. Federal withholding on rent paid to a foreign person is federal law we haven't reviewed. What to do: if you live out of state, name a local manager or contact for repairs and notices in the lease, keep the manager and insurer notice current, and get tax advice on withholding.

title: Checked Across All of Illinois Law
bodyText: Points checked across all Illinois statutes, not only the landlord-tenant laws. (1) Squatters: Illinois has no fast-track removal of squatters or unauthorized occupants. You recover possession through an eviction case, which covers entry into vacant property without right or title and forcible entry, and unknown occupants can be named and served as "unknown occupants". Police may still enforce criminal trespass and remove people when there is a criminal trespass, but don't remove anyone who may be a tenant without a court order (see the unauthorized occupants row). (2) Receipts: no Illinois statute requires a landlord to give a receipt for rent, whether paid in cash or otherwise, and there is no general rule that every creditor must give one; the receipt duties we found bind retail installment sellers, motor-vehicle lessors, debt-management and debt-settlement providers and court-appointed receivers of nursing homes, not landlords. Give a dated written receipt for every cash payment anyway, and check local ordinances (Chicago's, for example). (3) Registration before eviction: no state law makes landlord registration or a rental license a condition of filing an eviction or getting a possession order (local ordinances may, and are not covered). One exception: a mobile home park that hasn't applied for its license or renewal and paid its fees can't evict a tenant for not paying rent. (4) Out-of-state entities: a limited liability company, corporation, limited partnership or limited liability partnership formed in another state can't bring a case in an Illinois court while it is transacting business here without being admitted or qualified; its leases stay valid. Owning property alone isn't transacting business, but renting it out may be, so register before you file (see the row on entity landlords in court). (5) Business names: an individual or partnership renting property under a name other than the owners' real names must file a certificate with the county clerk and publish notice; failing to is a misdemeanor. A corporation or limited liability company must file with the Secretary of State before doing business under an assumed name. The Act doesn't say whether an unregistered business may sue; use your true legal name in the lease and in court. (6) Out-of-state owners: owning Illinois real estate submits you to Illinois courts on claims arising from it, and you can be served outside Illinois (see the row on owners who live outside Illinois). (7) Reporting duties: no statute makes a landlord a mandated reporter of child or adult abuse, but anyone may report. Rules that bind any person do reach you: anyone who knows a person has been bitten by an animal must notify the county animal control administrator within 24 hours; a person with custody of the body after a sudden, violent or unattended death must notify the coroner promptly; and no one may move a body or the dead person's belongings from the place of death without the coroner's permission unless necessary to protect them or for safety.

title: Liens for Work a Tenant Orders
bodyText:
Illinois's Mechanics Lien Act gives a contractor a lien when the contract is with the owner or with someone the owner has authorized or knowingly permitted to contract for the work. So if your tenant hires a contractor and you authorized or knowingly allowed the work, the contractor may claim a lien on your interest in the property, not only on the tenant's.

Illinois has no notice of nonresponsibility you can post or record to protect yourself, and no statute that lets a lease keep your interest free of liens; a no-liens clause in the lease binds your tenant but not the contractor. Whether consenting to an alteration in the lease counts as knowing permission is decided by the courts.

What helps: keep the lease's no-alterations rule, and if you approve work, say in writing that your consent is not an agreement to pay and require the tenant to pay every contractor and tell each one that the tenant, not you, is responsible (see the optional no-liens clause).

Repairs a tenant makes under Illinois's repair-and-deduct law are not treated as done with your permission for lien purposes.

If a lien is filed: a contractor must record its claim, or sue, within 4 months after completing the work to enforce it against other creditors and purchasers, and within 2 years as to the owner. Once a recorded claim is paid, or the claimant fails to sue after the owner's demand, you can demand a written release, and a claimant who neglects to give it for 10 days owes the owner $2,500 plus attorney's fees. An owner, or anyone liable for the claim, may also replace the lien with a surety bond of 175% of the claim.

title: Foreign and Noncitizen Owners and Tenants
bodyText: Illinois doesn't restrict who may own or rent property because of citizenship or nationality: noncitizens may acquire, hold and dispose of real property on the same terms as citizens, and we found no Illinois ban on foreign adversaries or other foreign persons buying or leasing land. Illinois law puts no duty on you to find out a prospective tenant's citizenship or nationality for this purpose. Don't base a rental decision or an eviction on it: Illinois bars a landlord from evicting because of a tenant's immigration or citizenship status or using that status to harass or intimidate (see the immigration status row), and fair housing law also applies. Two Illinois rules do touch foreign or noncitizen ownership. (1) A foreign person (a non-U.S. individual without permanent residence, a foreign company or government, or an Illinois entity a foreign person substantially controls) that acquires or transfers an interest in Illinois agricultural land (land used for farming, forestry or timber) must report it to the Director of Agriculture within 90 days. A lease of 10 years or less is excluded, so an ordinary residential or farm lease is not reportable, and filing a copy of the federal report satisfies the state rule. Knowingly failing to report can bring a civil penalty of up to 25% of the land's value, counting any federal penalty. (2) If a noncitizen landlord leases land for farming, the lease can't require the tenant to pay the property taxes; that term is void and the tenant can recover any money paid for the taxes.

title: When Illegal Use Voids the Lease
bodyText: Several Illinois statutes let you treat a residential lease as void when the home is used for a prohibited purpose; each works at your option, so the lease doesn't end by itself. (1) If any tenant or occupant uses the premises, or lets them be used, for a felony or Class A misdemeanor, the lease becomes void at your option, and a written lease must tell the tenant so (see the criminal activity clause and the expedited criminal eviction row). (2) If any tenant or occupant uses the premises, or lets them be used, for lewdness, assignation or prostitution, the lease becomes void at your option and you may recover possession as against a tenant holding over. (3) If the premises are used for unlawful drug activity, the lease becomes void at your option and you may post a 5-day notice to vacate (see the drug use row). (4) If a tenant or occupant is charged with a Class X felony on the premises and there is a probable-cause finding or indictment, you may void the lease only if you and the tenant signed the federal drug-free housing addendum or a similar document (see that addendum clause). After voiding, you still need a court order to remove anyone who doesn't leave. These laws also reach you as owner: a building used for prostitution, lewdness or assignation is a public nuisance, and its owners and agents may be enjoined; a building used for listed crimes (including drug, gambling and prostitution offenses) is a public nuisance, and if you intentionally, knowingly, recklessly or negligently permitted it, a court may bar all use of the building for a year unless you post a bond. Your lease's residential-use clause limits the tenant to residential use; act promptly on known illegal use.

title: Hunting on Rented Land
bodyText:
Illinois has no statute that gives hunting rights on rented land to the landlord or to the tenant; the lease can decide (see the optional hunting clause).

Illinois wildlife law does set who may give permission. To hunt or trap on the land of another, a person needs permission from the owner or the owner's designee, and a designee must hold the owner's written authorization describing the property and how far the designee may decide who hunts, with the owner's notarized signature. So if you want your tenant to be able to let others hunt, sign that kind of authorization.

Hunting with a gun or dog, or firing a gun to take wildlife, within 300 yards of an occupied home needs permission from the owner or tenant, with exceptions for some methods. Taking other wildlife not covered by the Wildlife Code needs the landowner's or tenant's permission. A trespass notice may come from the owner or the occupant.

Your farm tenant also has statutory privileges: owners living on farm land and bona fide tenants of farm land, with certain family members living there, may hunt and trap on that land without a license, and owners or bona fide tenants living on land may fish its waters without a license, all within seasons and methods. Resident tenants of at least 40 acres of commercial agricultural land can get free landowner deer and turkey permits for the land they rent (from January 1, 2027 the tenant must rent under a written notarized agreement with the landowner).

Liability: an owner of land, which includes a tenant or anyone in control of it, owes no duty to keep land safe for people entering for recreation such as hunting, unless the owner charged them, invited them, or acted willfully and wantonly; this protection does not cover residential buildings or residential property.

title: Housing an Employee
bodyText: Illinois has no general statute on housing you provide to an employee, such as a resident manager, janitor or farm hand: no required disclosure of occupancy terms, no rule that the housing ends when the job ends, and no special eviction procedure for employees. Whether an employee who lives on the property is a tenant entitled to the usual notices is decided by the courts. Cautious course: put the housing terms in a written agreement separate from the job terms (rent or rent-free, what happens to the housing when the job ends, and how much notice you'll give), give at least the written notice Illinois requires to end a periodic tenancy (7 days for week-to-week, 30 days for other tenancies of less than a year), and recover possession only through an eviction case if the person doesn't leave. Illinois's eviction law covers anyone who holds possession without right after a tenancy ends, and police may not treat a worker living on the land with the owner's permission as a criminal trespasser.
