Farm labor housing: housing for 10 or more migrant agricultural workers, or 4 or more families with migrant workers, is a migrant labor camp that needs a Department of Public Health license, smaller housing must meet the Department's minimum standards, and you may not evict or discharge a migrant worker for complaining or giving information to an enforcement agency.

title: Trying to Settle Disputes Before Court
bodyText:
Illinois has no statute that requires, permits or bars a lease term asking the parties to try to resolve a dispute informally before going to court. You may use the library's optional informal dispute resolution clause, which leaves eviction (possession) cases out and does not delay or limit any notice, deadline or remedy the law gives either side. Don't turn it into a waiting period or a condition on the tenant's statutory claims, such as a security deposit or rental fee claim.

Binding arbitration is a different matter: this library doesn't offer an arbitration clause for Illinois (see the arbitration row). Some Illinois circuit courts run eviction mediation or diversion programs under a Supreme Court rule; if your county has one, the court may refer your eviction case to it, whatever the lease says.

title: Leasing From a Life Tenant
bodyText:
Illinois has no civil-law usufruct, but a landlord may hold property only for life (a life estate), with someone else (the remainderman) taking it afterward. Illinois statutes cover two points.

Rent: if a life tenant who has leased the property dies on or after a rent due date, the life tenant's executor or administrator collects that rent; if the life tenant dies before the rent is due, the executor collects the share that built up before death and the remainderman collects the rest.

Farmland: a year-to-year farm lease from a life tenant continues to the end of the lease year in which the life estate ends, unless the lessor and lessee agreed otherwise in writing, and if the life estate ends within 6 months before the end of the lease, but before the next crop year begins, the farm tenant is entitled to reasonable field preparation costs from the next life tenant or the remainderman.

No Illinois statute says whether a residential lease from a life tenant survives the life tenant's death; that is decided by the courts.

Cautious course: if you lease as a life tenant, say so in the lease and either have the remainder holders sign it or make clear the lease ends with your life estate (see the optional life estate clause). If you're renting from someone, check whether they own the full interest.

title: No Special District Statement in Illinois Leases
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires a lease to say that the property lies in a special service area, tax increment financing district, business improvement district or other special district, or to have the tenant acknowledge district laws, charges or plans. Two points still touch tenants. Special service areas: the hearing notice for a proposed special service area is mailed to whoever paid the property taxes, so you get it, not your tenant; but the area can be blocked or a tax increase stopped by an objection petition signed by at least 51% of the electors residing in the area and at least 51% of the owners of record, so tenants who are registered voters living there count toward the residents' half. Business improvement districts: a business improvement district's board includes property owners, their managers or their tenant designees, and after its first year at least 25% of the board must be tenant designees (this mainly matters for commercial tenants). If a special service area tax or other district charge raises your costs, you can't pass it to the tenant as a separate fee unless the lease provides for it and the Illinois fee rules allow it (see the rental fee law row).

title: No Communal-Land Lease Approval in Illinois
bodyText: Illinois has no communal, tribal or native-owned land system under which a residential lease needs a government officer's approval before it is valid, and no Illinois statute requires such approval. A lease of privately owned land in Illinois takes effect when the parties sign it. Land held in trust by the United States for a tribe is governed by federal law, which we did not review; if you are ever asked to lease such land, get legal advice first.

title: Other Rules Illinois Does Not Have
bodyText: Rules found in some other states for which we found no Illinois statute, each explained in its own row: no statewide just-cause requirement to end a private tenancy ("edu-no-just-cause-il"); no statewide cap on security deposits ("edu-no-security-deposit-cap-il") or late fees ("edu-no-late-fee-limit-il"); no general statute on landlord entry ("edu-no-entry-statute-il"); no statewide rent-increase notice rule ("edu-no-rent-increase-notice-il"); no lockout for unpaid rent ("edu-no-lockout-for-rent-il"); no possession bond ("edu-no-possession-bond-il"); no rent-into-court rule ("edu-rent-into-court-counterclaim-il"); no early termination for illness or a move to care ("edu-no-infirmity-termination-il") or because repairs cost too much ("edu-no-repair-cost-termination-il"); no seasonal-tenancy regime ("edu-no-seasonal-tenancy-rule-il"); no rule ending a lease when a tenant dies ("edu-no-tenant-death-rule-il"); no statewide landlord registration ("edu-no-landlord-registration-il"); no required disclosure of mold, bed bugs, methamphetamine contamination or a death or crime on the property ("edu-no-mold-disclosure-il", "edu-no-bed-bug-rule-il", "edu-no-meth-disclosure-il", "edu-no-stigmatized-property-rule-il"); no rule on requiring renter's insurance ("edu-no-renters-insurance-rule-il"); and no special-district statement or communal-land approval ("edu-no-special-district-statement-il", "edu-no-communal-land-approval-il"). For lease form, we found no Illinois rule setting type size or print for residential leases ("edu-no-lease-type-size-il"), requiring plain language ("edu-no-plain-language-rule-il"), initials ("edu-no-lease-initials-requirement-il"), a translation ("edu-no-translation-duty-il") or a copy of the signed lease for the tenant ("edu-no-lease-copy-rule-il"). Give every tenant a signed copy anyway. Where no statute speaks, Illinois courts apply case law, which this library hasn't reviewed; each row gives the cautious course. Local ordinances (for example Chicago's and Cook County's) often fill these gaps and are not covered.

title: Arbitration Clauses in Illinois Leases
bodyText: Illinois law allows a written contract to send future disputes to binding arbitration. The Uniform Arbitration Act makes such a provision valid, enforceable and irrevocable except on grounds that would undo any contract, gives each side a right to a lawyer that cannot be waived in advance, and has no exception for consumer contracts or residential leases. No Illinois statute addresses arbitration of a residential landlord-tenant dispute. Even so, this library does not offer an arbitration clause for Illinois. The rental fee law lets a tenant sue for money, an injunction and attorney's fees when a landlord or a lease requires a fee the law bans, so a lease that contains a prohibited term already carries a penalty, and asking a court to send a tenant's claim to arbitration under such a lease invites that fight. The library's rule is to offer arbitration only where state law allows it and no statute penalizes including or enforcing a prohibited lease term. An eviction case is filed in the circuit court for the county where the property is, and either side may demand a jury there whatever the lease says. Money claims up to $10,000 can go to small claims court. If you want an arbitration clause anyway, have an Illinois lawyer draft it, keep possession cases and small claims in court, and leave every statutory remedy intact.

title: The Consumer Fraud Act and Illinois Rentals
bodyText: Illinois's Consumer Fraud and Deceptive Business Practices Act bans unfair or deceptive acts and practices, including misrepresenting or concealing a material fact, in any trade or commerce. Its definition of trade and commerce covers dealing in real property, but its definition of merchandise lists real estate only when it is outside Illinois, so whether the Act reaches an ordinary Illinois apartment lease is a question for the courts, which we did not review. One statute settles it for a specific practice: requiring a tenant to pay rent or other amounts by electronic funds transfer is an unlawful practice under the Act. A person harmed by a violation may sue for actual damages and other relief, including attorney's fees, within 3 years. The Act also bars a contract for the lease of consumer goods or services from taking away a customer's right to post reviews or other statements, and makes it unlawful to threaten to enforce such a term; whether that reaches a residential lease is not settled either. The cautious course: treat your advertising, lease terms and fee disclosures as covered, never misstate rent, fees or conditions, don't require electronic payment, and don't put a no-negative-reviews clause in your lease. Separately, the rental fee law has its own civil action for fees it bans or that are missing from the lease's first page.

title: Association Rules and Documents When Renting a Unit in Illinois
bodyText: No Illinois statute requires a lease of a condominium or other association unit to disclose the association's rules or obligations to the tenant, or to include a tenant's statement about them. The law makes them apply anyway. For a condominium, the Condominium Property Act, the declaration, bylaws, other condominium instruments and the rules that relate to the use of the unit or the common elements apply to anyone leasing a unit and are treated as part of the lease. The Common Interest Community Association Act says the same for units in a common interest community. Your duty runs to the association: unless the community's instruments say otherwise, give the board a copy of the signed lease (or a memorandum of an oral lease) by the move-in date or 10 days after signing, whichever comes first. If you don't follow the leasing rules, a condominium association may sue you and your tenant together to keep the tenant out or to evict the tenant, and the board may also sue a tenant directly for breaking the association's rules. A condominium board can also evict a tenant when you, the owner, fall behind on assessments. Associations levy fines against owners, after notice and a chance to be heard. What to do: give your tenant a copy of the association's rules before signing, use the library's association-compliance clause, deliver the lease to the board on time, and keep your assessments current. If your lease makes the tenant reimburse association fines the tenant causes, list that charge on the lease's first page with your other charges.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Illinois follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (810 ILCS 5/3-311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (810 ILCS 5/1-308(b)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Illinois's landlord-tenant statutes impose no general duty of good faith of the kind in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (the Landlord and Tenant Act, the Security Deposit Return Act, the Retaliatory Eviction Act and the eviction article searched); good faith appears only in specific rules. Courts in many states read a covenant of good faith and fair dealing into every contract, a lease included; whether and how Illinois's courts do is case law, so act as if the duty applies. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.
